◆ convertRefToInitializedName()

SgInitializedName * SageInterface::convertRefToInitializedName ( SgNode * current,
bool coarseGrain = true )

Converts a reference expression node to its corresponding SgInitializedName declaration.

This function traverses various types of reference expressions in the ROSE AST and attempts to resolve them to their underlying SgInitializedName declaration. It handles a wide variety of expression types including variable references, array references, pointer dereferences, member access expressions (dot and arrow operators), cast expressions, and arithmetic operations commonly used in pointer arithmetic.

The function operates in two modes controlled by the coarseGrain parameter:

  • Coarse grain mode (default): Returns the outermost or aggregate variable, which is useful for tools like the Outliner that need to work with complete memory objects.
  • Fine grain mode: Returns the specific member or element being accessed.

Special handling is provided for C++11 lambda functions, where captured variables are represented as class members accessed through the this pointer (this->variable pattern). In such cases, the function correctly identifies and returns the captured variable.

The function uses recursive descent to handle nested expressions such as array subscripts, chained member accesses, and pointer dereferences.

Parameters
currentThe AST node representing a reference expression to be converted. Must not be NULL. Can be various expression types including SgVarRefExp, SgPntrArrRefExp, SgDotExp, SgArrowExp, SgPointerDerefExp, SgCastExp, SgAddOp, SgSubtractOp, SgFunctionCallExp, and others.
coarseGrainWhen true (default), returns the coarse-grained memory object (e.g., the struct rather than its member). When false, returns the fine-grained object (e.g., the specific member being accessed).
Returns
The SgInitializedName corresponding to the variable declaration referenced by the input node. Returns NULL for function references, SgNonrealRefExp, SgThisExp, SgIntVal, SgConstructorInitializer, or when the reference cannot be resolved to an initialized name.
Warning
The function will call ROSE_ABORT() if it encounters an unhandled reference type that is not a SgConstructorInitializer, after logging an error message.
Precondition
The parameter current must not be NULL.
Postcondition
If a valid SgInitializedName is found, the returned pointer references an existing node in the AST and should not be deleted by the caller.
Note
This function is related to AstInterface::IsVarRef() and may need to be consulted for additional cases.
For scientific applications that use pointer arithmetic patterns like *(address + offset) for array access, the function assumes the left operand of addition or subtraction operations is the variable of interest.
Lambda captured variables are detected using isLambdaCapturedVariable() to avoid incorrect backtracking through arrow expressions.

◆ copyExpression()

SgExpression * SageInterface::copyExpression ( SgExpression * e)

Creates a deep copy of a given expression node.

This function produces a complete deep copy of the specified SgExpression node and its entire subtree. The function delegates to the deepCopy utility to perform the actual copying operation. Unlike a shallow copy, a deep copy ensures that all child nodes and associated data structures are duplicated, resulting in an independent copy that can be modified without affecting the original expression.

Note that the source expression does not need to be attached to the AST (i.e., it may have a NULL parent). This allows copying of newly constructed expressions that have not yet been inserted into the AST.

Parameters
ePointer to the SgExpression node to be copied. This parameter must not be NULL. The expression may or may not be attached to an AST.
Returns
A pointer to the newly created deep copy of the input expression. The returned expression is independent of the original and can be safely modified or inserted into a different location in the AST.
Precondition
The parameter e must not be NULL.
Postcondition
A new SgExpression node is created that is a deep copy of the input expression. The original expression remains unchanged.
Note
The source expression is not required to have a parent node set, allowing copying of expressions that are newly built and not yet attached to the AST.
Warning
The caller is responsible for managing the memory of the returned expression node to avoid memory leaks.

SgStatement * SageInterface::copyStatement ( SgStatement * s)

Creates a deep copy of a given SgStatement node.

This function produces a complete deep copy of the specified SgStatement and its entire subtree. The implementation delegates to the deepCopy function, which recursively duplicates all child nodes and associated attributes of the statement. The resulting copy is independent of the original statement and can be safely modified or inserted into a different location in the AST without affecting the source statement.

Parameters
sPointer to the SgStatement node to be copied. This can be any type of statement in the ROSE AST, including declarations, expression statements, control flow statements, and compound statements.
Returns
A pointer to the newly created deep copy of the input statement. The returned statement is a completely independent copy with its own memory allocation. Returns the result of deepCopy, which may be NULL if the input is NULL or if the copy operation fails.

The input statement s should be a valid SgStatement pointer or NULL.
Postcondition
The original statement s remains unchanged.
If successful, the returned statement is a complete deep copy that shares no mutable state with the original.
Note
The caller is responsible for managing the memory of the returned statement, including proper insertion into the AST or explicit deletion when no longer needed.
This function is a convenience wrapper around the more general deepCopy template function specialized for SgStatement types.

◆ createTempVariableAndReferenceForExpression()

std::pair< SgVariableDeclaration *, SgExpression * > SageInterface::createTempVariableAndReferenceForExpression ( SgExpression * expression,
SgScopeStatement * scope )

Creates a temporary variable declaration and a reference expression for a given expression.

This function generates a temporary variable that is initialized with a copy of the provided expression, along with a variable reference expression that can be used as a replacement for the original expression. This is useful for scenarios where an expression needs to be evaluated once and its result reused multiple times, or when expression transformation requires storing intermediate values.

The function handles special cases for array types. When the expression has an array type, the temporary variable is declared with a pointer type to the array's base type instead of the array type itself. This accounts for array-to-pointer decay semantics in C/C++. The function strips any typedef layers from array types before determining the appropriate pointer type.

The algorithm proceeds as follows:

  1. Determine the type for the temporary variable, adjusting for array types if necessary
  2. Generate a unique variable name within the given scope
  3. Create a copy of the original expression for use as an initializer
  4. Build a variable declaration with an assign initializer
  5. Create a variable reference expression pointing to the new declaration
  6. Return both the declaration and reference as a pair
Parameters
expressionThe source expression for which a temporary variable and reference are created. The expression is copied for the initializer, so the original remains unmodified.
scopeThe scope statement in which the temporary variable will be declared. This scope is used for generating a unique variable name and as the declaration context.
Returns
A pair containing the newly created variable declaration as the first element and a variable reference expression referring to that declaration as the second element.
Precondition
expression must be a valid, non-null SgExpression pointer.
scope must be a valid, non-null SgScopeStatement pointer representing a valid scope context.
Postcondition
The returned variable declaration is fully constructed with a unique name and initializer.
The returned variable reference expression correctly references the new declaration.
The original expression remains unmodified.
Note
For array types, the function uses pointer types to handle array-to-pointer decay properly.
The generated variable name is guaranteed to be unique within the specified scope.
The caller is responsible for inserting the returned declaration into the appropriate location in the AST.

◆ createTempVariableForExpression()

std::pair< SgVariableDeclaration *, SgExpression * > SageInterface::createTempVariableForExpression ( SgExpression * expression,
SgScopeStatement * scope,
bool initializeInDeclaration,
SgAssignOp ** reEvaluate )

Creates a temporary variable to hold the value of a given expression.

This function generates a temporary variable declaration that can be used to store the result of evaluating the provided expression. The function handles several special cases for different expression types:

  • Reference types: If the expression has a reference type, a pointer type is used for the temporary variable to allow re-assignment. The expression is converted using address-of operator, and the resulting variable reference is dereferenced when returned.
  • Array types: If the expression has an array type, a pointer to the base type is used for the temporary variable.
  • Dereferenced pointers: If the expression is a pointer dereference, a reference type is used to hold the value.

The function generates a unique variable name within the given scope and optionally initializes the variable in its declaration. It can also provide an assignment operation for re-evaluating the expression into the temporary variable.

Parameters
expressionThe expression for which a temporary variable should be created. This expression will be copied for initialization purposes.
scopeThe scope statement in which the temporary variable will be declared. Used for generating a unique variable name and setting the declaration scope.
initializeInDeclarationIf true, the temporary variable will be initialized in its declaration statement. If false, no initializer is attached to the declaration.
reEvaluateOptional output parameter. If not NULL, an SgAssignOp node will be created and stored at this location, which can be used to re-evaluate the expression and assign the result to the temporary variable.
Returns
A pair containing the temporary variable declaration (first) and a variable reference expression (second) that can be used in place of the original expression. For reference types, the variable reference is wrapped in a pointer dereference expression.
Precondition
expression must be a valid non-NULL SgExpression pointer.
scope must be a valid non-NULL SgScopeStatement pointer.
Postcondition
A new SgVariableDeclaration is created with a unique name in the given scope.
If reEvaluate is not NULL, it points to a valid SgAssignOp for re-evaluation.
The returned pair contains valid non-NULL pointers.
Note
The function uses SageInterface::copyExpression to duplicate the input expression, so the original expression remains unmodified.
For reference types, there is a workaround that sets lvalue to false on the temporary initialization expression to avoid an assertion in ROSE.
The caller is responsible for inserting the returned declaration into the appropriate location in the AST.

◆ cutPreprocessingInfo()

void SageInterface::cutPreprocessingInfo ( SgLocatedNode * src_node,
PreprocessingInfo::RelativePositionType pos,
AttachedPreprocessingInfoType & save_buf )

Cuts preprocessing information from a source node and saves it into a buffer.

This function extracts preprocessing information (such as comments and preprocessor directives) from a source AST node based on a specified relative position and stores the extracted information into a provided buffer. The preprocessing information is removed from the source node after being copied to the buffer.

This operation is designed to be used in combination with pastePreprocessingInfo(). The cut-paste operation provides more flexibility than moveUpPreprocessingInfo() because the destination node does not need to be known at the time of the cut operation; it only needs to be specified when the paste action is performed.

The algorithm works by:

  1. Retrieving the attached preprocessing information pointer from the source node
  2. Copying elements matching the specified relative position to the save buffer using remove_copy_if with a negated position predicate
  3. Removing the copied elements from the original preprocessing info container using remove_if followed by erase
Parameters
src_nodePointer to the source located node from which preprocessing information will be cut. Must not be null.
posThe relative position type specifying which preprocessing information entries to cut (e.g., before, after, or inside the node).
save_bufReference to a buffer where the cut preprocessing information will be stored. New entries are appended to this buffer.
Precondition
src_node must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgLocatedNode.
save_buf should be initialized (may be empty or contain existing entries).
Postcondition
Preprocessing information matching the specified position is removed from src_node and appended to save_buf.
If src_node had no attached preprocessing information, save_buf remains unchanged.
Note
This function does nothing if the source node has no attached preprocessing information (null preprocessing info pointer).
The function uses C++11 lambda expressions to filter preprocessing info entries based on their relative position using the isRelPos() predicate.
Warning
The caller is responsible for ensuring src_node is not null; otherwise, an assertion failure will occur.

◆ declarationPositionString()

string SageInterface::declarationPositionString ( const SgDeclarationStatement * declaration)

Generates a unique position string for a declaration statement.

This function creates a unique string identifier based on the source location of a declaration statement. The string encodes the file ID, line number, and column number from the declaration's file information. The resulting string is formatted to be a valid C/C++ identifier component, which is useful for generating unique names in code transformations.

The format of the returned string is "_F<file_id>_L<line>_C<column>" where file_id, line, and column are the respective source location values. For compiler-generated nodes that have negative file IDs, the negative sign is replaced with the letter "N" to ensure the string remains a valid identifier (e.g., file_id -3 becomes "N3").

This function is primarily used by the generateUniqueName() function to create distinct identifiers for declarations based on their source positions.

Parameters
declarationPointer to the declaration statement for which to generate the position string. Must not be NULL and must have valid file information associated with it.
Returns
A string encoding the declaration's source position in the format "_F<file_id>_L<line>_C<column>". The string is guaranteed to contain no hyphen characters, making it suitable for use in C/C++ identifiers.
Precondition
The declaration parameter must not be NULL.
The declaration must have valid file information (get_file_info() must not return NULL).
Postcondition
The returned string does not contain any hyphen characters.
The returned string follows the pattern "_F<id>_L<line>_C<col>" where id may be prefixed with "N" for originally negative file IDs.
Note
For translation-generated SgNode objects, the file_id may be negative (e.g., -3). To maintain valid C/C++ identifier syntax, negative file IDs are converted by replacing the minus sign with "N" (e.g., -3 becomes "N3").
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if the declaration pointer is NULL or if its file information is NULL.
The function will trigger an assertion failure if the final string contains a hyphen character, indicating an unexpected format issue.

◆ declarationPreceedsDefinition()

bool SageInterface::declarationPreceedsDefinition ( SgDeclarationStatement * nonDefiningDeclaration,
SgDeclarationStatement * definingDeclaration )

Determines whether a non-defining declaration appears before its defining declaration in the AST.

This function tests the order of appearance of a non-defining declaration versus a defining declaration in a preorder traversal of the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). It is primarily used in the unparser to determine proper declaration ordering for code generation, but may be useful for general AST analysis tasks.

The implementation uses a custom AST traversal class (DeclarationOrderTraversal) that performs a preorder traversal starting from the global scope. During traversal, it tracks which of the two input declarations is encountered first. The traversal examines all declaration statements in the order they appear in the AST, which is necessary because the non-defining declaration may appear in a different scope than the defining declaration.

Note that the current implementation has the traversal disabled to avoid O(n^2) complexity during unparsing. When disabled, the function defaults to returning false (indicating the non-defining declaration does not precede the defining declaration).

Parameters
nonDefiningDeclarationPointer to the non-defining declaration statement to check. Must not be NULL.
definingDeclarationPointer to the defining declaration statement to check against. Must not be NULL and must be different from nonDefiningDeclaration.
Returns
True if the non-defining declaration appears before the defining declaration in the AST preorder traversal, or if the declarations could not be found in the AST (as a safe default). Returns false if both declarations are the same pointer, or if the defining declaration appears first.
Warning
The AST traversal is currently disabled to avoid O(n^2) complexity during unparsing. The function will always return false when the two declarations are different until the traversal is re-enabled.
The non-defining declaration can be a different type of declaration than the defining declaration, which may lead to unexpected results.
Precondition
nonDefiningDeclaration must not be NULL.
definingDeclaration must not be NULL.
Both declarations should be part of a valid AST with an accessible global scope.
Postcondition
The AST is not modified by this function.
Note
When the declarations cannot be found during traversal (hidden island problem or non-defining declarations not in the traversal), the function returns true as a safe default to avoid incorrectly assuming the non-defining declaration appears after the defining declaration.
The trivial case where nonDefiningDeclaration equals definingDeclaration is defined to return false.

The implementation relies on an underlying deepCopyNode function that handles the recursive duplication of the tree structure. This wrapper provides a convenient type-safe interface for obtaining a copy with the correct static type.

After copying, the source position information for the newly created node is set to indicate that it was generated through transformation, which is important for proper handling of compiler-generated code versus original source code.

◆ deepDelete()

void SageInterface::deepDelete ( SgNode * root)

Performs a deep deletion of a sub AST tree starting from the given root node.

This function recursively deletes an entire Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) subtree rooted at the specified node. The deletion is performed using postorder traversal, which ensures that all child nodes are deleted before their parent nodes. This traversal order is essential to prevent dangling pointers and memory corruption that would occur if parent nodes were deleted before their children.

The implementation delegates to the deleteAST function to perform the actual deletion. An alternative implementation using AstSimpleProcessing with postorder traversal exists but is currently disabled.

Parameters
rootPointer to the root node of the AST subtree to be deleted. This node and all of its descendants will be deallocated. May be nullptr, in which case the behavior depends on the underlying deleteAST implementation.
Warning
This function permanently destroys the AST subtree. All pointers to nodes within the deleted subtree become invalid after this call. Ensure that no other parts of the program hold references to nodes in this subtree.
Deleting a node that is still connected to a larger AST may leave the parent tree in an inconsistent state with dangling pointers.
Precondition
The root parameter should point to a valid SgNode or be nullptr.
The subtree rooted at root should not be referenced elsewhere in the program after this call.
Postcondition
The root node and all its descendants have been deallocated.
All memory associated with the subtree has been freed.
Note
This function is part of the SageInterface namespace which provides utility functions for manipulating ROSE compiler AST structures.
The postorder traversal ensures safe deletion by processing children before parents.

◆ deleteAllNodes()

void SageInterface::deleteAllNodes ( )

Deletes all IR nodes in the ROSE AST and clears the associated memory pools.

This function performs a complete cleanup of all SgNode objects in the ROSE Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) by traversing the memory pool and deleting each node individually. The implementation uses a custom traversal class derived from ROSE_VisitTraversal to collect all SgNode pointers from the memory pool. After collecting all nodes, the function iterates through the list and calls the delete operator on each node, invoking their destructors. Finally, it clears all memory pools using AST_FILE_IO::clearAllMemoryPools() to complete the cleanup process.

The algorithm proceeds in the following steps:

  1. Record the number of IR nodes before deletion for debugging purposes
  2. Traverse the entire memory pool to collect all SgNode pointers
  3. Iterate through the collected nodes and delete each one
  4. Clear all memory pools managed by ROSETTA
  5. Report the number of nodes before and after deletion
Warning
This function destroys the entire AST. After calling this function, all previously obtained pointers to SgNode objects become invalid. Any attempt to use such pointers will result in undefined behavior.
Calling functions like get_name() on nodes during the deletion process is erroneous as many nodes may already be in an inconsistent state.
Precondition
A valid ROSE AST exists with nodes allocated in the memory pool.
Postcondition
All SgNode objects have been deleted and their memory freed.
All memory pools have been cleared via AST_FILE_IO::clearAllMemoryPools().
The number of nodes in the system should be zero or significantly reduced.
Note
This function outputs diagnostic information to stdout showing the number of nodes in the list and the node counts before and after deletion.
The function uses a memory pool traversal mechanism specific to ROSE IR nodes rather than a standard tree traversal, ensuring all nodes are visited regardless of their position in the AST structure.

◆ deleteAST()

void SageInterface::deleteAST ( SgNode * n)

Deletes an entire AST subtree rooted at the given node, including associated symbols.

This function performs a comprehensive deletion of an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) subtree starting from the specified root node. The implementation uses a two-phase approach:

  1. A ClassicVisitor class that implements the ROSE_VisitorPattern to traverse the memory pool and count references to various symbol types (SgVariableSymbol, SgFunctionSymbol, SgClassSymbol, SgTypedefSymbol, SgMemberFunctionSymbol, SgTemplateSymbol, and SgEnumFieldSymbol). This reference counting ensures symbols are only deleted when they have exactly one reference, preventing dangling pointer issues.
  2. A DeleteAST class that performs post-order traversal of the AST, visiting each node and safely deleting it along with its associated symbols. The post-order traversal ensures that child nodes are deleted before their parents, avoiding access to already-deleted memory.

The function handles deletion of various ROSE IR node types including:

  • SgInitializedName and associated SgVariableDefinition, SgVariableSymbol, SgEnumFieldSymbol
  • SgFunctionDeclaration and associated SgFunctionSymbol
  • SgClassDeclaration and associated SgClassSymbol, SgClassType
  • SgMemberFunctionDeclaration and associated SgMemberFunctionSymbol
  • SgTypedefDeclaration and associated SgTypedefSymbol
  • SgTemplateDeclaration and associated SgTemplateSymbol
  • SgNamespaceDeclarationStatement and associated SgNamespaceSymbol
  • SgLabelStatement and associated SgLabelSymbol
  • SgEnumDeclaration and associated SgEnumSymbol, SgEnumType
  • SgInterfaceStatement and associated SgInterfaceSymbol
  • SgModuleStatement and associated SgModuleSymbol
  • Various reference expressions (SgVarRefExp, SgFunctionRefExp, SgMemberFunctionRefExp, etc.)
Parameters
nPointer to the root SgNode of the AST subtree to be deleted. This node and all its descendants will be removed from memory. The pointer should not be used after this function returns.
Warning
This function permanently destroys the AST subtree. Any pointers to nodes within the deleted subtree become invalid after this call.
The function modifies symbol tables by removing symbols that are no longer referenced. This may affect other parts of the AST that share symbols with the deleted subtree.
Some node types such as SgTemplateArgument and certain template-related constructs may not be fully cleaned up due to implementation limitations.
Precondition
The parameter n must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgNode.
The AST should be in a consistent state before deletion.
Symbol tables associated with scopes in the subtree should be accessible.
Postcondition
The node n and all its descendants are deleted from memory.
Symbols referenced only by the deleted subtree are removed from their respective symbol tables and deleted.
Types exclusively associated with deleted declarations are also deleted.
Note
This function was re-implemented by Tan in August 2010.
The function uses memory pool traversal to accurately count symbol references across the entire program, not just the subtree being deleted.
Post-order traversal is essential to avoid visiting deleted IR nodes during the deletion process.

◆ deleteExpressionTreeWithOriginalExpressionSubtrees()

void SageInterface::deleteExpressionTreeWithOriginalExpressionSubtrees ( SgNode * root)

Empty function or ill-formed function detected.

Deletes an expression tree along with all nested original expression subtrees.

This function performs a deep deletion of an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) rooted at the given node, including any original expression trees that may be attached to expression nodes within the tree. The function uses a post-order traversal to ensure that child nodes are processed before their parents, which is essential for safe deletion.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Traverse the tree starting from the root in post-order
  2. For each node visited, check if it is an SgExpression
  3. If the node is an expression, recursively traverse and delete its original expression tree (obtained via get_originalExpressionTree()) using the same post-order approach
  4. Delete the current node

Original expression trees are auxiliary AST structures that may be attached to expression nodes to preserve the original source representation before transformations. This function ensures these nested structures are also properly deallocated to prevent memory leaks.

The function does not perform any validation on the tree structure. Passing a malformed or cyclic tree may result in infinite recursion or double deletion.
Precondition
The root parameter should point to a valid SgNode or be NULL.
All nodes in the tree should be dynamically allocated and not referenced elsewhere.
Postcondition
The root node and all its descendants are deallocated.
All original expression subtrees attached to expression nodes are deallocated.
The root pointer becomes invalid and should not be dereferenced.
Note
This function uses the AstSimpleProcessing visitor pattern from ROSE for tree traversal.
The post-order traversal ensures children are deleted before parents, maintaining safe memory deallocation order.

◆ doLoopNormalization()

bool SageInterface::doLoopNormalization ( SgFortranDo * loop)

Normalizes a Fortran DO loop by making the default increment expression explicit.

This function normalizes a Fortran DO loop by ensuring that the increment expression is explicitly specified. In Fortran, when a DO loop does not have an explicit increment (step) value, it defaults to 1. This function detects when the increment expression is a null expression (indicating the default was used) and replaces it with an explicit integer value of 1. This normalization simplifies subsequent analysis and transformation passes by ensuring all DO loops have explicit increment expressions.

The function performs the following steps:

  1. Retrieves the current increment expression from the loop
  2. Checks if the increment is a null expression (SgNullExpression)
  3. If null, creates a new SgIntVal node with value 1
  4. Sets the new increment expression on the loop and establishes proper parent linkage
  5. Deletes the original null expression to prevent memory leaks
Parameters
loopPointer to the SgFortranDo node representing the Fortran DO loop to be normalized. Must not be NULL.
Returns
Always returns true indicating the normalization operation completed.
Precondition
The loop parameter must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgFortranDo node.
The loop must be part of a properly constructed AST.
Postcondition
If the loop had a null increment expression, it will be replaced with an explicit SgIntVal node containing the value 1.
The parent pointer of the new increment expression is correctly set to the loop node.
The original null expression is deallocated.
Note
This function currently always returns true regardless of whether any modification was actually performed.
There is a TODO comment in the implementation suggesting future work to normalize CONTINUE statements to ENDDO statements.
The function uses ROSE_ASSERT to verify the loop pointer is not NULL, which will terminate the program in debug builds if the assertion fails.

◆ dumpInfo()

void SageInterface::dumpInfo ( SgNode * node,
std::string desc = "" )

Dumps diagnostic information about a ROSE AST node to standard output.

This function provides a comprehensive debugging utility for inspecting ROSE Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) nodes. It outputs various categories of information about the given node to the standard output stream, including:

  1. Base information: The node pointer address and its class name.
  2. Source location information: For SgLocatedNode types, displays the filename, line number, and column number from the file info.
  3. Preprocessing information: If the node has attached preprocessing info (such as comments, include directives, define macros, etc.), it displays the total count and details of each attached preprocessing item.
  4. Name information: For named nodes such as SgFunctionDeclaration, SgVarRefExp, or SgInitializedName, it outputs the qualified name or referenced variable name.

The output is formatted with clear section delimiters to aid in debugging and understanding the structure of AST nodes during ROSE-based source code analysis.

Parameters
nodePointer to the SgNode to be inspected. Must not be NULL.
descAn optional description string that is printed before the node information. Defaults to an empty string if not provided.
Warning
This function outputs directly to std::cout, which may not be suitable for all contexts. Consider redirecting output if needed.
Precondition
node must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgNode object.
Postcondition
Diagnostic information about the node has been written to standard output. The node itself remains unmodified.
Note
This function performs dynamic type checking using isSgLocatedNode, isSgFunctionDeclaration, isSgVarRefExp, and isSgInitializedName to determine what additional information can be extracted from the node.
The function will trigger a ROSE_ASSERT failure if node is NULL.

◆ dumpPreprocInfo()

void SageInterface::dumpPreprocInfo ( SgLocatedNode * locatedNode)

Dumps all attached preprocessing information for a given AST node to standard output.

This function retrieves and displays detailed information about all preprocessing directives (such as include, define, ifdef, ifndef, endif, pragma, comments, etc.) that are attached to a specified SgLocatedNode in the ROSE AST. The output includes the node's memory address, type, source file location, and for each attached preprocessing info item: its classification type, string content, and relative position (before, after, or inside the node).

If no preprocessing information is attached to the node, a message indicating this is printed along with the node's address and type.

The function iterates through all attached PreprocessingInfo objects and prints their details in a numbered format for easy identification and debugging purposes.

Parameters
locatedNodePointer to the SgLocatedNode whose attached preprocessing information should be dumped. This parameter must not be NULL.
Warning
This function outputs directly to standard output using printf. It is intended for debugging purposes and may produce verbose output for nodes with many attached preprocessing directives.

locatedNode must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgLocatedNode object within a properly constructed ROSE AST.
Postcondition
The preprocessing information attached to the node is printed to standard output. The node and its attached information remain unchanged.
Note
The relative position of preprocessing info can be "before", "after", or "inside" the associated AST node, indicating where the directive appears relative to the node in the original source code.
This function is useful for debugging source-to-source transformations where preserving comments and preprocessor directives is important.

◆ enclosingNamespaceScope()

SgNamespaceDefinitionStatement * SageInterface::enclosingNamespaceScope ( SgDeclarationStatement * declaration)

Returns the enclosing namespace scope for a given declaration statement.

This function traverses the scope chain starting from the given declaration to find the first enclosing namespace definition statement. It iterates through nested scopes (such as class definitions or other block scopes) until it reaches either a namespace definition or the global scope. This functionality is particularly important for template handling in ROSE, specifically for ensuring that template specializations generated by ROSE are placed in the correct namespace location. Modern GNU compilers enforce strict rules about template specialization placement, making this scope resolution essential for correct code generation.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Start with the immediate scope of the declaration
  2. Traverse upward through the scope chain
  3. Stop when either a namespace definition or global scope is encountered
  4. Return the namespace definition if found, or nullptr if global scope was reached
Parameters
declarationThe declaration statement for which to find the enclosing namespace. Must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgDeclarationStatement.
Returns
A pointer to the SgNamespaceDefinitionStatement representing the enclosing namespace scope, or nullptr if the declaration is not contained within any namespace (i.e., it is at global scope or only enclosed by non-namespace scopes).
Precondition
declaration must not be nullptr.
declaration must have a valid scope chain (get_scope() must return valid scopes).
Postcondition
The returned value is either a valid SgNamespaceDefinitionStatement pointer or nullptr if no enclosing namespace exists.
Note
This function is used in the markTemplateInstantiationsForOutput functionality.
The function stops at global scope if no namespace is found in the scope chain, returning nullptr in that case since global scope is not a namespace.
Warning
The function assumes that the scope chain is well-formed and will assert if a null scope is encountered during traversal before reaching global scope.

◆ ensureBasicBlockAsBodyOfCaseOption()

SgBasicBlock * SageInterface::ensureBasicBlockAsBodyOfCaseOption ( SgCaseOptionStmt * cs)

Ensures that the body of a case option statement is wrapped in a basic block.

This function checks whether the body of the given SgCaseOptionStmt is already an SgBasicBlock. If the body is not a basic block, the function wraps the existing body statement inside a newly created SgBasicBlock, updates the parent-child relationships accordingly, and records the transformation for potential later reversal. This normalization ensures consistent AST structure where case option bodies are always represented as basic blocks, simplifying subsequent analysis and transformation passes.

The transformation is recorded using the recordNormalizations mechanism, which allows the change to be undone if needed to restore the original AST structure.

Parameters
csPointer to the SgCaseOptionStmt whose body should be ensured to be a basic block. Must not be null.
Returns
Pointer to the SgBasicBlock that serves as the body of the case option statement. This is either the original body if it was already a basic block, or the newly created basic block wrapper.
Precondition
The parameter cs must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgCaseOptionStmt.
The case option statement must have a valid body statement.
Postcondition
The body of the case option statement is guaranteed to be an SgBasicBlock.
The parent pointer of the body is correctly set to the case option statement.
If a new basic block was created, the transformation is recorded for potential later reversal.
Note
This function is part of the AST normalization utilities that ensure consistent structure across the ROSE AST representation.
The original body statement becomes a child of the new basic block if wrapping occurs.
Warning
The caller must ensure that cs is not null, as no null check is performed before dereferencing the pointer.

The new basic block is then set as the body of the catch statement, and the parent pointer of the basic block is updated to reference the catch statement. This transformation ensures a consistent AST structure where catch statement bodies are always represented as basic blocks, which simplifies subsequent AST traversals and transformations.

◆ eraseNullPreprocessingInfo()

int SageInterface::eraseNullPreprocessingInfo ( SgLocatedNode * lnode)

Removes all NULL PreprocessingInfo pointers from a subtree rooted at a given node.

This function traverses the entire AST subtree rooted at the specified SgLocatedNode and identifies all NULL entries within the attached preprocessing information lists of each located node. The function collects these NULL entries along with their indices, then removes them in reverse order to maintain correct index positions during deletion. The reverse iteration approach ensures that removing an element does not invalidate the indices of elements that are yet to be removed.

The algorithm works in two phases:

  1. Collection phase: Iterates through all nodes in the subtree using RoseAst iterator, examining each SgLocatedNode's attached preprocessing info list for NULL entries.
  2. Removal phase: Iterates through collected NULL entries in reverse order and erases them from their respective preprocessing info lists.
Parameters
lnodePointer to the root SgLocatedNode of the subtree to process. This node and all its descendants will be examined for NULL preprocessing info entries.
Returns
The total count of NULL PreprocessingInfo pointers that were erased from the subtree.
Precondition
lnode must not be NULL.
lnode must be a valid SgLocatedNode within a properly constructed AST.
Postcondition
All NULL PreprocessingInfo pointers within the preprocessing info lists of nodes in the subtree have been removed.
The relative order of non-NULL PreprocessingInfo entries is preserved.
Note
The function only processes SgLocatedNode instances; other node types in the subtree are skipped.
Nodes with no attached preprocessing info (NULL info list) are also skipped.
The removal is performed using reverse iteration to avoid index invalidation issues when multiple entries need to be removed from the same list.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if lnode is NULL.

◆ evaluateConstIntegerExpression()

struct const_int_expr_t SageInterface::evaluateConstIntegerExpression ( SgExpression * expr)

Evaluates a constant integer expression and returns its computed value.

This function evaluates a given SgExpression node that represents a constant integer expression in the SAGE III abstract syntax tree (AST). It utilizes a SimpleExpressionEvaluator to traverse the expression tree and compute the resulting constant integer value. The function is designed to handle expressions that can be evaluated at compile time, such as literal integers, arithmetic operations on constants, and other statically determinable integer expressions.

The evaluation is performed by creating a SimpleExpressionEvaluator instance and invoking its traverse method on the provided expression node. The traversal walks through the expression tree structure and computes the final integer value.

Parameters
exprPointer to an SgExpression node representing the constant integer expression to be evaluated. This expression should be evaluable at compile time. The pointer must not be null.
Returns
A const_int_expr_t structure containing the result of the constant integer expression evaluation. This structure typically contains the computed integer value and potentially status information about whether the evaluation was successful.
Precondition
The expr parameter must point to a valid SgExpression node.
The expression represented by expr should be a constant expression that can be evaluated without runtime information.
Postcondition
The returned const_int_expr_t contains the evaluated result of the expression if evaluation was successful.
Note
This function creates a temporary SimpleExpressionEvaluator object for each invocation. For multiple evaluations, consider whether a persistent evaluator would be more efficient.
The function does not modify the input expression tree.
Warning
If the expression contains non-constant elements or cannot be evaluated at compile time, the behavior depends on the SimpleExpressionEvaluator implementation.

Extracts the leading keyword from a pragma declaration.

For example, given a pragma declaration such as "%pragma omp parallel", this function would return "omp" as the keyword. The extraction is performed using a string stream to tokenize the pragma string by whitespace, retrieving only the first whitespace-delimited token.

This function is intended to be run on the body of a loop or switch statement, as it specifically stops traversal at constructs that define new break scopes.

◆ findDeclarationStatement()

template<typename T>
T * SageInterface::findDeclarationStatement ( SgNode * root,
std::string name,
SgScopeStatement * scope,
bool isDefining )

Searches for a declaration statement by name within an AST subtree.

This function performs a recursive depth-first search through the ROSE AST starting from the given root node to find a declaration statement of type T that matches the specified name. The search can optionally be constrained to a specific scope. When a matching declaration is found, the function can return either the declaration itself or its defining declaration based on the isDefining parameter.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Attempts to cast the root node to the target declaration type T
  2. If successful, checks if the declaration matches the given name and scope
  3. If a match is found and isDefining is true, returns the defining declaration
  4. If a match is found and isDefining is false, returns the declaration itself
  5. If no match at the current node, recursively searches all child nodes
Parameters
rootPointer to the root SgNode from which to begin the search. If NULL, the function returns NULL immediately.
nameThe name of the declaration to search for. This is matched against the symbol name obtained from the declaration's symbol table.
scopePointer to the scope statement to constrain the search. If NULL, the search will match declarations regardless of their scope.
isDefiningIf true, returns the defining declaration of the matched declaration. If false, returns the matched declaration directly.
Returns
Pointer to the found declaration of type T, or NULL if no matching declaration is found. When isDefining is true, returns the defining declaration; otherwise returns the first matching declaration.
Warning
If isDefining is true and a matching declaration is found but has no defining declaration, an assertion failure will occur.
For function members with defining declarations defined outside of their class, the declaration may not be found in the child traversal list.
Precondition
The template type T must be a declaration type that supports search_for_symbol_from_symbol_table(), get_scope(), get_definingDeclaration(), and get_firstNondefiningDeclaration() methods.
Postcondition
If a non-NULL value is returned, it points to a valid declaration of type T whose symbol name matches the specified name parameter.
Note
This is a template function that can be instantiated for various ROSE declaration types such as SgFunctionDeclaration, SgVariableDeclaration, etc.
A NULL scope parameter is explicitly allowed and will cause the search to ignore scope constraints when matching declarations.

◆ findEnclosingLoop()

SgScopeStatement * SageInterface::findEnclosingLoop ( SgStatement * s,
const std::string & label,
bool stopOnSwitches )

Finds the enclosing loop statement for a given statement, optionally matching a specific label.

This function traverses up the AST from the given statement to find the nearest enclosing loop construct. It supports various loop types including C/C++ loops (for, while, do-while), Fortran loops (SgFortranDo, SgFortranNonblockedDo), and Java constructs (foreach, labeled statements). The search can be constrained by a label name, which is useful for handling labeled break and continue statements in Fortran and Java. The function iterates through parent statements until it finds a matching loop or reaches the top of the AST.

The algorithm handles the following loop types:

  • SgDoWhileStmt: C/C++ do-while loop, matches only when label is empty
  • SgForStatement: C/C++ for loop, matches only when label is empty
  • SgFortranDo and SgFortranNonblockedDo: Fortran DO loops, matches when label is empty or matches the loop label
  • SgWhileStmt: C/C++ while loop, matches when label is empty or matches the loop label
  • SgSwitchStatement: Optionally stops at switch statements based on stopOnSwitches parameter
  • SgJavaForEachStatement: Java enhanced for loop, matches only when label is empty
  • SgJavaLabelStatement: Java labeled statement, matches when label is empty or matches the statement label
Parameters
sThe starting statement from which to search upward for an enclosing loop. The search begins at this statement and traverses through its parent chain.
labelThe label to match against loop labels. If empty, the function returns the innermost enclosing loop. If non-empty, the function searches for a loop with a matching Fortran label or Java label.
stopOnSwitchesIf true, the search will stop and return when a switch statement is encountered. If false, switch statements are ignored and the search continues upward.
Returns
A pointer to the enclosing SgScopeStatement representing the found loop, or NULL if no matching enclosing loop is found.
Precondition
The parameter s should be a valid pointer to an SgStatement within a properly constructed AST, or NULL.
Postcondition
The returned scope statement, if non-NULL, is guaranteed to be an ancestor of the input statement s in the AST hierarchy.
Note
When the label parameter is empty, the function returns the innermost enclosing loop. This is particularly important for Java where labeled statements require detecting the innermost labeled statement while skipping intermediate constructs.
For Fortran, the label corresponds to the numeric label associated with DO loops. For Java, the label corresponds to the identifier used in labeled statements.
Warning
If the input statement s is NULL, the function will immediately return NULL without performing any search.

◆ findEnclosingOmpClauseBodyStatement()

SgOmpClauseBodyStatement * SageInterface::findEnclosingOmpClauseBodyStatement ( SgStatement * s)

Finds the enclosing OpenMP clause body statement from a given statement.

This function traverses up the AST hierarchy starting from the given statement to find an enclosing SgOmpClauseBodyStatement node. If the input statement is already an SgOmpClauseBodyStatement, it is returned directly without further traversal. The function walks up the parent chain by repeatedly checking if the current node is an SgOmpClauseBodyStatement, and if not, moving to its parent statement.

Parameters
sThe starting statement from which to search for an enclosing OpenMP clause body statement. This parameter may be NULL, in which case the function returns NULL.
Returns
A pointer to the enclosing SgOmpClauseBodyStatement if found, or the input statement itself if it is already an SgOmpClauseBodyStatement. Returns NULL if no enclosing SgOmpClauseBodyStatement is found or if the input statement is NULL.
Note
The function allows the input parameter to be NULL and will gracefully return NULL in such cases rather than asserting.
This function only traverses upward through statement nodes. If a non-statement parent is encountered, the traversal will terminate.
Precondition
None. The function handles NULL input gracefully.
Postcondition
The returned pointer, if non-NULL, points to a valid SgOmpClauseBodyStatement that is either the input statement itself or an ancestor of the input statement in the AST.

◆ findEnclosingSwitch()

SgSwitchStatement * SageInterface::findEnclosingSwitch ( SgStatement * s)

Finds the nearest enclosing switch statement for a given statement.

This function traverses the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) upward from the given statement node to locate the nearest enclosing SgSwitchStatement. The search proceeds by iteratively examining parent nodes until either a switch statement is found or the traversal can no longer continue. The algorithm uses a simple parent-pointer traversal pattern common in AST navigation within the ROSE compiler infrastructure.

Parameters
sThe starting statement node from which to begin the upward search for an enclosing switch statement. This parameter should be a valid pointer to a statement that is expected to be nested within a switch statement.
Returns
A pointer to the nearest enclosing SgSwitchStatement if found.
Warning
This function will trigger a ROSE_ASSERT failure if no enclosing switch statement is found. The caller must ensure that the input statement is actually contained within a switch statement.
Precondition
The parameter s must be a non-null pointer to a valid SgStatement node that is part of a properly constructed AST.
The statement s must be nested within a switch statement somewhere in its ancestor chain.
Postcondition
The returned pointer is guaranteed to be a valid SgSwitchStatement pointer (non-null) due to the assertion check.
Note
This function is part of the SageInterface namespace which provides utility functions for working with the SAGE III intermediate representation in the ROSE compiler framework.
The function assumes proper AST structure where parent pointers are correctly set for all statement nodes.

◆ findFirstDefiningFunctionDecl()

SgFunctionDeclaration * SageInterface::findFirstDefiningFunctionDecl ( SgScopeStatement * scope)

Finds the first defining function declaration within a given scope.

This function searches through the declarations or statements within the specified scope to locate the first function declaration that is also its own defining declaration. The search considers only declarations that either belong to the same file as the scope or are transformations marked for output in code generation.

The algorithm handles two cases based on the scope's content:

  1. If the scope contains only declarations, it iterates through the declaration list.
  2. Otherwise, it iterates through the statement list.

For each item in the appropriate list, the function checks if the file information matches the scope's file or if the item is a transformation intended for code generation output. If the item is a function declaration and is its own defining declaration, it is returned as the result.

Parameters
scopeA pointer to the SgScopeStatement within which to search for the first defining function declaration. Must not be NULL.
Returns
A pointer to the first SgFunctionDeclaration that is a defining declaration found within the scope. Returns NULL if no such declaration is found.
Precondition
The scope parameter must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgScopeStatement.
Postcondition
The returned pointer, if non-NULL, points to a function declaration where get_definingDeclaration() returns the declaration itself.
Note
This function only considers declarations or statements that are either in the same file as the scope or are transformations marked for output during code generation. Declarations from included files that do not meet these criteria are skipped.
The function stops searching after finding the first matching defining function declaration and returns immediately.

◆ findFirstSgCastExpMarkedAsTransformation()

bool SageInterface::findFirstSgCastExpMarkedAsTransformation ( SgNode * n,
const std::string & s )

Searches for the first SgCastExp node marked as a transformation in an AST subtree.

This function traverses an AST subtree rooted at the given node to find SgCastExp (cast expression) nodes that have been marked as transformations. The search uses a preorder traversal via the AstSimpleProcessing framework. When examining each SgCastExp node, the function filters out cast expressions whose parent is an SgInitializer, as these are considered less interesting for transformation detection purposes. For qualifying cast expressions, the function checks if the associated file information indicates the node was created as part of a transformation.

The string parameter is used for diagnostic output purposes to help identify the context of the search during debugging.

Parameters
nPointer to the root SgNode of the AST subtree to be traversed. This node and all its descendants will be examined for SgCastExp nodes marked as transformations.
sA string identifier used for diagnostic output to provide context about the search operation being performed.
Returns
True if at least one SgCastExp node marked as a transformation is found in the subtree (excluding those with SgInitializer parents), false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter n must be a valid pointer to an SgNode within a properly constructed AST.
Each SgCastExp node in the subtree must have valid file information accessible via get_file_info().
Postcondition
The AST structure remains unchanged after the traversal.
Note
This function prints diagnostic messages to stdout indicating the search context and results, which may be useful for debugging transformation detection issues.
SgCastExp nodes whose parent is an SgInitializer are explicitly excluded from consideration as transformation candidates.
The function uses internal traversal class that inherits from AstSimpleProcessing to perform the AST walk.

SgFunctionDeclaration * SageInterface::findFunctionDeclaration ( SgNode * root,

Finds a function declaration within a given AST subtree by name and optional scope.

This function searches for a function declaration (SgFunctionDeclaration) within the abstract syntax tree (AST) rooted at the specified node. It is a convenience wrapper around the generic findDeclarationStatement template function, specialized for function declarations. The search can be constrained to a specific scope and can optionally require that the found declaration be a defining declaration (i.e., one that includes the function body).

Parameters
rootThe root node of the AST subtree to search within. This serves as the starting point for the traversal when looking for the function declaration.
nameThe name of the function to search for. This should be the unqualified function name as a string.

isDefiningIf true, the search will only match defining declarations (those with function bodies). If false, any declaration matching the name and scope criteria may be returned.
Returns
A pointer to the SgFunctionDeclaration if a matching function declaration is found, or nullptr if no matching declaration exists within the specified search criteria.

The root parameter should point to a valid AST node, or be nullptr.
The name parameter should be a non-empty string representing a valid function name.

The returned pointer, if non-null, points to a valid SgFunctionDeclaration node within the AST.

This function delegates to the template function findDeclarationStatement specialized for SgFunctionDeclaration types.

◆ findFunctionType()

SgFunctionType * SageInterface::findFunctionType ( SgType * return_type,
SgFunctionParameterTypeList * typeList )

Finds the function type matching a given return type and parameter type list.

This function searches the global function type table to find an existing SgFunctionType that matches the specified return type and parameter type list. It utilizes the mangled name generation mechanism of SgFunctionType to create a unique identifier for the function signature, which is then used to look up the corresponding function type in the global function type table.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Retrieves the global function type table from SgNode.
  2. Generates a mangled name using SgFunctionType::get_mangled() based on the return type and parameter type list.
  3. Looks up the function type in the table using the mangled name.
  4. Returns the found function type or NULL if no match exists.
Parameters
return_typePointer to the SgType representing the return type of the function. Must not be NULL.
typeListPointer to the SgFunctionParameterTypeList containing the parameter types of the function signature. Must not be NULL.
Returns
Pointer to the SgFunctionType that matches the given signature if found in the global function type table, or NULL if no matching function type exists.
Warning
This function uses a static member function (SgFunctionType::get_mangled) that cannot be used for SgMemberFunctionType without additional modifications.
Precondition
return_type must not be NULL.
typeList must not be NULL.
The global function type table must be properly initialized and accessible.
Postcondition
The global function type table remains unchanged.
Note
This function only searches for existing function types in the table and does not create new function types if a match is not found.

◆ findGotoStmts()

std::vector< SgGotoStatement * > SageInterface::findGotoStmts ( SgStatement * scope,

Finds all goto statements within a scope that target a specific label.

This function searches through a given scope in the abstract syntax tree (AST) to locate all SgGotoStatement nodes that reference a particular label statement. It uses the NodeQuery::querySubTree function to traverse the subtree rooted at the specified scope and collects all goto statements. Then it filters the results to include only those goto statements whose target label matches the provided label statement.

The implementation performs a two-step process:

  1. Query the AST subtree for all SgGotoStatement nodes
  2. Filter the results to retain only those targeting the specified label
Parameters
scopeThe statement node representing the scope within which to search for goto statements. This serves as the root of the subtree to query.
lThe label statement to match against. Only goto statements that target this specific label will be included in the result.
Returns
A vector containing pointers to all SgGotoStatement nodes found within the specified scope that target the given label. Returns an empty vector if no matching goto statements are found.
Precondition
scope must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgStatement node.
l must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgLabelStatement node.
Postcondition
The returned vector contains only goto statements where get_label() equals l.
The original AST remains unmodified.
Note
This function was updated to use std::vector instead of std::list for uniformity across ROSE (as of 9/25/2007).
The function performs a copy of results since the return type is IR node specific (SgGotoStatement*) while the query returns generic SgNode pointers.

◆ findHeader()

PreprocessingInfo * SageInterface::findHeader ( SgSourceFile * source_file,
const std::string & header_file_name,
bool isSystemHeader )

Finds the preprocessingInfo node representing a specific include directive within a source file.

This function searches for a PreprocessingInfo node that corresponds to either include <header.h> (system header) or include "header.h" (user header) within the given source file. The search is performed by examining the global scope and all declarations within it, checking their attached preprocessing information for matching include directives.

The function maintains a cache (fileHeaderDict) to store previously found headers, allowing for efficient repeated lookups. If the header has been found before, it returns the cached result. Otherwise, it performs a fresh search through the source file's global scope and its declarations.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Constructs the header key based on whether it is a system or user header
  2. Checks the cache for a previously found result
  3. If not cached, collects candidate nodes (global scope and its declarations)
  4. Iterates through each candidate's attached preprocessing info
  5. Searches for CpreprocessorIncludeDeclaration directives matching the header key
  6. Caches and returns the result if found
Parameters
source_filePointer to the SgSourceFile in which to search for the header. Must be a valid, non-null pointer to a source file node.
header_file_nameThe name of the header file to search for, without angle brackets or quotation marks (e.g., "vector" or "myheader.h").
isSystemHeaderBoolean flag indicating whether to search for a system header (enclosed in angle brackets) or a user header (enclosed in quotation marks). True for system headers, false for user headers.
Returns
Pointer to the PreprocessingInfo node representing the found include directive, or NULL if the specified header is not found in the source file.
Precondition
source_file must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgSourceFile node.
header_file_name should be a non-empty string containing the header file name.
Postcondition
If the header is found, it is cached in fileHeaderDict for future lookups.
The source file's AST structure is not modified by this function.
Note
This function only searches the global scope and its immediate declarations, as headers are typically inserted into the global scope.
The search uses string matching to find the header key within the preprocessing info content, which means partial matches may occur if header names are substrings of other header names.
Results are cached in the static fileHeaderDict map for performance optimization in repeated queries.

◆ findLastDeclarationStatement()

SgStatement * SageInterface::findLastDeclarationStatement ( SgScopeStatement * scope,
bool includePragma = false )

Finds the last declaration statement within a given scope.

This function iterates through all statements in the provided scope and identifies the last declaration statement. The function is useful for determining the appropriate insertion point when a new declaration statement needs to be prepended to a scope. By default, pragma declarations are excluded from consideration, but this behavior can be modified via the includePragma parameter.

The algorithm performs a linear scan through the statement list of the scope, tracking the most recent declaration statement encountered. For each statement, it checks whether the statement is a declaration statement and handles pragma declarations specially based on the includePragma flag.

Parameters
scopePointer to the scope statement to search within. This parameter must not be NULL.
includePragmaBoolean flag indicating whether pragma declarations should be considered as valid declaration statements. When set to false (default), pragma declarations are skipped. When set to true, pragma declarations are included in the search.
Returns
Pointer to the last declaration statement found in the scope. Returns NULL if no declaration statements are found, indicating that a declaration statement can be prepended to the scope.
Precondition
The scope parameter must not be NULL.
Postcondition
The returned statement, if non-NULL, is a declaration statement that exists within the provided scope.
Note
When the function returns NULL, it indicates that the scope contains no declaration statements (or no non-pragma declarations if includePragma is false), and therefore a new declaration statement can safely be inserted at the beginning of the scope.
Pragma declarations are typically excluded because inserting statements after pragmas may interfere with the intended behavior of those pragmas.

◆ findMain()

SgFunctionDeclaration * SageInterface::findMain ( SgNode * n)

Searches for the main function declaration within an AST subtree.

This function performs a recursive depth-first traversal of the abstract syntax tree starting from the given node to locate the defining declaration of the main function. The search algorithm iterates through all traversal successors of each node, checking if any node represents the main function. When a main function declaration is found, the function verifies that it is the defining declaration (not just a forward declaration) before returning it. This ensures that only the actual definition of main is returned, not prototype declarations.

The function uses the isMain helper function to determine if a node represents a main function, and checks the scope to ensure the main function is at global scope.

Parameters
nThe root node of the AST subtree to search. This can be any SgNode in the ROSE AST hierarchy, typically the SgProject or SgSourceFile node for a complete search. May be NULL, in which case the function returns NULL.
Returns
A pointer to the defining SgFunctionDeclaration for the main function if found, or NULL if no defining main function declaration exists in the subtree rooted at the given node.
Precondition
The input node, if non-NULL, must be a valid node within a properly constructed ROSE AST.
Postcondition
The returned pointer, if non-NULL, points to a defining declaration of the main function (i.e., get_definingDeclaration returns itself).
Note
This function only returns the defining declaration of main, skipping any non-defining (forward) declarations. This behavior was added to handle cases where main may have both a prototype and a definition.
The function performs a recursive traversal which may have performance implications on very large ASTs.

◆ findSurroundingStatementFromSameFile()

SgStatement * SageInterface::findSurroundingStatementFromSameFile ( SgStatement * targetStmt,
bool & surroundingStatementPreceedsTargetStatement )

Finds a surrounding statement from the same source file as the target statement.

This function locates a statement in the same source file as the given target statement, which can be used for relocating comments and preprocessor directives when removing or manipulating statements in the AST. The algorithm first searches backward (toward the beginning of the file) for a statement with the same file ID. If no suitable statement is found in that direction, it restarts from the target and searches forward (toward the end of the file).

The function maintains visited statement sets to detect and prevent infinite loops that could occur when iterating over cyclic statement structures. When searching backward, the function does not climb out of the current scope to avoid incorrectly moving preprocessing information from a child statement to its parent statement.

If the target statement is not associated with the original source code (indicated by a negative file ID), the function returns NULL as comment relocation is not supported for such statements. If the only statement in a file is being removed, the function returns the global scope (SgGlobal) as the surrounding statement.

Parameters
targetStmtPointer to the statement for which a surrounding statement from the same file is to be found. Must not be NULL.
surroundingStatementPreceedsTargetStatementOutput parameter that indicates whether the returned surrounding statement precedes the target statement in the source file. Set to true if the surrounding statement comes before the target, false if it comes after. This value is meaningless if the return value is SgGlobal (global scope).
Returns
Pointer to a statement from the same file as the target statement. Returns the global scope (SgGlobal) if no other suitable statement is found within the file. Returns NULL if the target statement is not associated with original source code (has a negative file ID) or if an infinite loop is detected during traversal.
Warning
If the target statement has a negative file ID (not associated with original source code), the function prints a warning message and returns NULL.
If an infinite loop is detected during statement traversal, an error message is printed and NULL is returned.
Precondition
targetStmt must not be NULL.
Postcondition
If a non-NULL value is returned and the target statement has a valid file ID, the returned statement will be from the same source file as the target statement.
Note
When the return value is SgGlobal (global scope), the surroundingStatementPreceedsTargetStatement parameter is set to false but this value is meaningless in that context.
This function is typically used during statement removal operations to determine where to relocate associated comments and preprocessor directives.
Debug output can be enabled by defining REMOVE_STATEMENT_DEBUG.

◆ findUnusedLabels()

std::set< SgLabelStatement * > SageInterface::findUnusedLabels ( SgNode * top)

Finds all unused label statements within a given AST subtree.

This function traverses the abstract syntax tree (AST) rooted at the specified node and identifies label statements that are not referenced by any goto statement. The implementation uses a visitor pattern through AstSimpleProcessing to collect two sets during a single preorder traversal: one containing all label statements found in the subtree, and another containing labels that are actually used as targets of goto statements. The function then computes the difference between these sets to determine which labels are unused.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Traverse the AST in preorder, collecting all SgLabelStatement nodes into an "all labels" set and all labels referenced by SgGotoStatement nodes into a "used labels" set.
  2. Remove each used label from the all labels set.
  3. Return the remaining labels as the set of unused labels.
Parameters
topThe root node of the AST subtree to analyze. This node and all its descendants will be examined for label statements and goto statements.
Returns
A set of pointers to SgLabelStatement nodes that are defined within the subtree but are not referenced by any goto statement.
Precondition
The parameter top must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgNode.
The AST rooted at top must be well-formed with properly linked parent and child relationships.
Postcondition
The returned set contains only label statements that exist within the subtree rooted at top and have no corresponding goto statements targeting them.
Note
This function is only available when USE_ROSE is not defined, as indicated by the ifndef USE_ROSE preprocessor guard.
The function uses an assertion to verify that every used label exists in the set of all labels found, which helps detect inconsistencies in the AST structure.
Labels that are targets of computed gotos or other indirect jump mechanisms may not be properly detected as used by this function.
Warning
The function assumes that all goto statements within the subtree reference labels that are also within the same subtree. If a goto references a label outside the analyzed subtree, the assertion may fail.

It serves as a wrapper that delegates the actual fixing logic to fixStructDeclaration, since class declarations in C++ share the same underlying representation and fixing requirements as struct declarations. Note
This function internally calls fixStructDeclaration since class and struct declarations share the same fixing mechanism in the SAGE III infrastructure.
