The parameter n should be a valid pointer to a node within a properly constructed AST.
Postcondition
The returned pointer, if non-null, points to a valid SgFunctionDefinition node that is an ancestor of (or equal to, if includingSelf is true) the input node.
Note
This function is equivalent to calling getEnclosingFunctionDefinition() directly. It exists to provide terminology consistency for users who prefer the term "procedure" over "function definition".
See also

◆ getEnclosingScope()

SgScopeStatement * SageInterface::getEnclosingScope ( SgNode * n,
const bool includingSelf = false )

Retrieves the enclosing scope statement for a given AST node.

This function determines the enclosing scope of a specified node in the abstract syntax tree (AST). It first obtains the scope associated with the node using getScope(). If the node itself is a scope statement and the caller does not want to include the node itself as the result, the function traverses up to the parent node to find the enclosing scope.

This is useful for AST traversal and transformation operations where understanding the lexical scope context of a node is necessary, such as when inserting new declarations or statements that need to be placed in an appropriate scope.

Parameters
nThe AST node for which to find the enclosing scope. This parameter should be a valid pointer to an SgNode in the AST.
includingSelfA boolean flag indicating whether the node itself should be considered as a valid result if it is a scope statement. When set to false (the default), if the node is itself a scope, the function returns the parent scope instead. When set to true, the node itself may be returned if it is a scope statement.
Returns
A pointer to the SgScopeStatement representing the enclosing scope of the given node. Returns the node itself if it is a scope and includingSelf is true. Returns NULL if no enclosing scope can be found.
Precondition
The parameter n should be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgNode that is part of a properly constructed AST.
Postcondition
The returned scope statement, if non-null, is an ancestor of the input node n in the AST hierarchy (or n itself if includingSelf is true and n is a scope statement).
Note
This function relies on the getScope() helper function to determine the scope associated with a node and uses the parent pointer of nodes to traverse upward in the AST when necessary.

SgSourceFile * SageInterface::getEnclosingSourceFile ( SgNode * n,

Retrieves the enclosing source file node for a given AST node.

This function traverses the AST hierarchy upward from the specified node to find the enclosing SgSourceFile node. It is a convenience wrapper around the templated getEnclosingNode function, specialized for SgSourceFile type. The SgSourceFile represents the root of a source file's AST representation in the ROSE compiler infrastructure.

Parameters
nThe AST node from which to begin the search for the enclosing source file. This pointer may be NULL, in which case the function will return NULL.
includingSelfA boolean flag indicating whether the search should consider the input node itself as a potential match. If true and n is already an SgSourceFile, n will be returned. If false, the search begins from the parent of n.
Returns
A pointer to the enclosing SgSourceFile node if found, or NULL if no enclosing source file exists in the ancestor chain or if the input node is NULL.
Precondition
The input node n, if not NULL, should be a valid node within a properly constructed AST with parent pointers correctly set.

The returned pointer, if not NULL, points to a valid SgSourceFile node that is an ancestor of n (or n itself if includingSelf is true).

This function relies on the parent pointers being correctly established in the AST. If parent pointers are not set, the function may fail to find the enclosing source file even if one exists.

◆ getEnclosingStatement()

SgStatement * SageInterface::getEnclosingStatement ( SgNode * n)

Finds the nearest enclosing statement node for a given AST node.

This function traverses up the abstract syntax tree (AST) starting from the given node, searching for the nearest ancestor that is a statement node (SgStatement). The traversal follows parent pointers until either a statement node is found or the root of the tree is reached. This is useful for determining the statement context in which a particular expression or sub-expression resides within the ROSE compiler infrastructure.

The algorithm uses a simple iterative approach, checking each ancestor node using the isSgStatement dynamic cast function until a statement is found or the parent chain is exhausted.

Parameters
nThe starting AST node from which to begin the upward traversal. May be NULL, in which case the function returns NULL.
Returns
A pointer to the nearest enclosing SgStatement node if one exists, or NULL if no enclosing statement is found or if the input is NULL.
Precondition
The node n, if non-NULL, should be part of a properly constructed AST with valid parent pointers set.
Postcondition
The returned statement, if non-NULL, is guaranteed to be an ancestor of the input node n in the AST hierarchy.
Note
If the input node n is itself a statement, the function will return n directly without traversing to its parent.
This function does not modify the AST or any of its nodes.

◆ getFirstStatement()

SgStatement * SageInterface::getFirstStatement ( SgScopeStatement * scope,
bool includingCompilerGenerated = false )

Retrieves the first statement within a given scope.

This function returns the first statement contained within the specified scope statement. The behavior differs based on whether the scope contains only declarations or a mix of statements. The function can optionally include or exclude compiler-generated statements based on the includingCompilerGenerated parameter.

When includingCompilerGenerated is false, the function filters out statements that are not from the same file as the scope or are not transformation-generated statements marked for output in code generation. This filtering is necessary because some content from included headers may not be properly marked as compiler-generated.

The implementation has been optimized for performance by using references instead of copies for statement lists and by using the empty() member function for O(1) complexity checks instead of size() which has O(n) complexity.

scopePointer to the SgScopeStatement from which to retrieve the first statement. Must not be NULL.
includingCompilerGeneratedBoolean flag indicating whether to include compiler-generated statements in the search. Defaults to false, meaning compiler-generated statements are skipped by default.

Precondition
The scope parameter must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgScopeStatement.
Postcondition
The returned statement, if non-NULL, belongs to the provided scope and satisfies the filtering criteria based on the includingCompilerGenerated flag.
Note
The function distinguishes between scopes that contain only declarations and those that contain general statements, using different internal lists accordingly.
When filtering statements, the function checks if the statement originates from the same file as the scope or if it is a transformation-generated statement that is marked for output in code generation.
Performance optimizations were applied to avoid unnecessary list copies and to use constant-time emptiness checks.
Warning
The functions isCompilerGenerated() and isOutputInCodeGeneration() alone are not sufficient for determining if a statement should be included, as some content from included headers may not be marked as compiler-generated.

◆ getForLoopInformations()

bool SageInterface::getForLoopInformations ( SgForStatement * for_loop,
SgVariableSymbol *& iterator,
SgExpression *& lower_bound,
SgExpression *& upper_bound,
SgExpression *& stride )

Extracts loop control information from a canonical for-loop statement.

This function analyzes a given SgForStatement and extracts its key components: the loop iterator variable, lower bound, upper bound, and stride expression. The function expects the for-loop to be in a canonical form where:

  • The initialization statement is a simple assignment to the iterator variable
  • The test condition uses a relational operator comparing the iterator to a bound
  • The increment expression modifies the iterator using standard increment patterns

The function handles various comparison operators in the test condition including less-than, less-than-or-equal, greater-than, and greater-than-or-equal. It also supports multiple increment patterns such as prefix increment/decrement operators, compound assignment operators (+=, -=), and explicit assignment with arithmetic expressions (i = i + step).

When the loop condition is non-inclusive (using strict inequality), the upper bound is automatically adjusted by adding or subtracting 1 to provide a normalized inclusive bound representation.

Parameters
for_loopPointer to the SgForStatement node representing the for-loop to analyze.
iteratorReference to a pointer that will be set to the loop iterator variable symbol.
lower_boundReference to a pointer that will be set to the expression representing the initial value of the iterator.
upper_boundReference to a pointer that will be set to the expression representing the upper bound of the loop iteration range. This value is adjusted to be inclusive if the original condition was strict.
strideReference to a pointer that will be set to the expression representing the step size of each iteration.
Returns
True if the loop information was successfully extracted, false otherwise. Currently always returns true if no assertion fails.
Warning
This function uses assertions that will abort the program if the for-loop does not conform to the expected canonical form. Future versions should replace assertions with error messages and return false.
The function does not handle variable declarations in the initialization statement (e.g., for(int i = 0; ...)).
Equality (==) and inequality (!=) operators in the test condition will cause the program to abort.
Precondition
The for_loop parameter must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgForStatement.
The for-loop must have exactly one initialization statement.
The initialization must be an assignment expression.
The test condition must be a binary relational expression.
The iterator must appear on exactly one side of the test condition.
Postcondition
If successful, iterator points to a valid SgVariableSymbol.
If successful, lower_bound points to the initial value expression.
If successful, upper_bound points to the (possibly adjusted) bound expression.
If successful, stride points to the step expression.
Note
The function strips cast expressions when analyzing the test condition operands.
For non-inclusive bounds, new AST nodes are created using SageBuilder to represent the adjusted upper bound.
The output parameters are initialized to NULL at the start of the function.

◆ getFrontendSpecificNodes()

std::set< SgNode * > SageInterface::getFrontendSpecificNodes ( )

Retrieves all AST nodes that are exclusively marked as frontend-specific.

This function traverses the entire ROSE AST memory pool to identify and collect nodes that are marked as frontend-specific. Frontend-specific nodes are those generated by the ROSE frontend during parsing and are not part of the original source code representation.

The algorithm works by performing a complete memory pool traversal using a custom visitor pattern. For each node encountered, it checks the associated file information to determine if the node is frontend-specific. The function recursively collects all data member pointers from each node to ensure complete coverage of the AST structure.

Two sets are maintained during traversal: one for frontend-specific nodes and one for non-specific nodes. The final result is computed using set difference to return only those nodes that appear exclusively in the frontend-specific set and not in the non-specific set. This ensures that nodes which appear in both contexts are excluded from the result.

The recursive collection mechanism prevents infinite loops by checking if a node has already been inserted into the collection before processing its children.

Returns
A set containing pointers to all SgNode objects that are exclusively marked as frontend-specific. The returned set may be empty if no such nodes exist in the current AST.
Note
This function traverses the entire memory pool, which may be computationally expensive for large ASTs. The traversal visits every allocated SgNode in memory.
Nodes that have file information indicating both frontend-specific and non-specific contexts will be excluded from the result due to the set difference operation.
If a node does not have associated file information but is itself an Sg_File_Info node, it will be classified based on its own isFrontendSpecific status without recursive collection of its data members.
Precondition
The ROSE AST memory pool must be properly initialized and contain valid nodes.
Postcondition
The returned set contains only nodes that are exclusively frontend-specific. The original AST remains unmodified.

◆ getFunctionDeclaration()

SgFunctionDeclaration * SageInterface::getFunctionDeclaration ( SgFunctionCallExp * functionCallExp)

Retrieves the function declaration associated with a function call expression.

This function extracts the SgFunctionDeclaration node associated with a given SgFunctionCallExp node. It handles multiple forms of function call expressions including direct function calls, member function calls through dot notation, and member function calls through arrow notation.

The implementation examines the function expression within the call and determines its type:

  • For SgDotExp (e.g., obj.method()), it extracts the right-hand side operand and retrieves the associated member function declaration.
  • For SgFunctionRefExp (e.g., func()), it directly retrieves the associated function declaration.
  • For SgArrowExp (e.g., ptr->method()), it extracts the right-hand side operand and retrieves the associated member function declaration.

This function provides a more general interface compared to calling the lower-level functions directly on SgFunctionRefExp or SgMemberFunctionRefExp, as those are more robust when not called directly on SgFunctionCallExp.

Parameters
functionCallExpPointer to the SgFunctionCallExp node from which to extract the function declaration. Must not be NULL.
Returns
Pointer to the SgFunctionDeclaration associated with the function call. Returns NULL if the function declaration cannot be determined or if the expression type is not one of the handled cases (SgDotExp, SgFunctionRefExp, or SgArrowExp with a valid member function reference).
Precondition
functionCallExp must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgFunctionCallExp node.
The function expression within functionCallExp must be non-NULL.
Postcondition
The returned declaration, if non-NULL, represents the function being called.
Note
This function was added to provide a more general mechanism for extracting function declarations from call expressions.
Not all function call expression types may be handled. If the expression type is not recognized, NULL is returned.
For member function calls, the function relies on SgMemberFunctionRefExp being present in the right-hand side of dot or arrow expressions.

Extracts the integer constant value from a ROSE SgValueExp node.

This function retrieves the underlying integer constant value from various types of ROSE AST value expression nodes. ◆ getLiveVariables()

void SageInterface::getLiveVariables ( LivenessAnalysis * liv,
SgForStatement * loop,
std::set< SgInitializedName * > & liveIns,
std::set< SgInitializedName * > & liveOuts )

Retrieves the live-in and live-out variables for a given for loop.

This function computes the set of variables that are live at the entry point (live-in) and exit point (live-out) of a specified for loop statement. It utilizes the provided liveness analysis results and the control flow graph (CFG) representation of the for loop to determine these variable sets.

The implementation works by examining the CFG node corresponding to the for statement after the test expression (CFG index 2). For SgForStatement, there are 5 CFG nodes with indices 0 through 4, where index 0 and 4 represent the beginning and end CFG nodes respectively, index 1 is after the init statement, index 2 is after the test expression, and index 3 is before the increment. The function uses index 2 because this node has two outgoing edges representing the true (entering loop body) and false (exiting loop) conditions.

The live-in variables for the loop are determined by examining the live-in set of the first statement inside the loop body (reached via the true edge). The live-out variables are determined by examining the live-in set of the first statement after the loop (reached via the false edge).

Parameters
livPointer to the LivenessAnalysis object containing precomputed liveness information for the program. Must not be NULL.
loopPointer to the SgForStatement representing the for loop to analyze. Must not be NULL.
liveInsReference to a set that will be populated with the SgInitializedName pointers representing variables that are live at the entry of the loop.
liveOutsReference to a set that will be populated with the SgInitializedName pointers representing variables that are live at the exit of the loop.
Precondition
The liv parameter must point to a valid LivenessAnalysis object with completed liveness analysis.
The loop parameter must point to a valid SgForStatement node within the analyzed program.

Retrieves the body statement of a loop construct.

This function extracts and returns the body of a given loop statement. It supports three types of loop constructs in the ROSE AST: while loops, for loops, and do-while loops. The function handles the following loop types:

  • SgForStatement: Returns the body via get_loop_body()

This function will trigger a ROSE_ASSERT failure if the provided statement is not a recognized loop type (while, for, or do-while). This will cause program termination in debug builds.

loopStmt must be one of the following types: SgWhileStmt, SgForStatement, or SgDoWhileStmt.

The returned pointer points to the body statement of the loop, which may be a single statement or a block statement (SgBasicBlock).

◆ getLoopIndexVariable()

SgInitializedName * SageInterface::getLoopIndexVariable ( SgNode * loop)

Returns the loop index variable for a C/C++ for loop or Fortran Do loop.

This function extracts and returns the loop index variable (induction variable) from a given loop construct. It supports both Fortran Do loops and C/C++ for loops with various initialization styles.

For Fortran Do loops, the function extracts the variable from the assignment operation in the loop initialization.

For C/C++ for loops, the function handles several initialization patterns:

  • C99-style declarations: for (int i = 0; ...)
  • Traditional assignment: for (i = 0; ...)
  • Comma expressions with multiple initializations: for (i = 1, len1 = 0, len2 = 0; ...) In this case, the leftmost variable in the comma expression is returned.

Other loop types such as while loops and do-while loops are not supported and will return NULL.

Parameters
loopA pointer to an SgNode representing the loop construct. This should be either an SgFortranDo node or an SgForStatement node.
Returns
A pointer to the SgInitializedName representing the loop index variable, or NULL if the loop type is not supported, the initialization statement format is unrecognized, or if there are zero or multiple initialization statements in a C/C++ for loop.
Warning
This function only supports single initialization statements in C/C++ for loops. Loops with no initialization or more than one initialization statement will cause the function to return NULL and print a warning message.
For comma expressions in the initialization, only the leftmost assignment is considered as the loop index variable, which may not always be the intended induction variable.
Precondition
The loop parameter must not be NULL.
Postcondition
If a valid loop index variable is found, the returned pointer references the declaration of that variable. The original AST is not modified.
Note
While loops, do-while loops, and other non-for/non-Do loop constructs are explicitly not supported and will return NULL without error.
The function uses ROSE assertion macros to validate internal assumptions about the AST structure.

◆ getScope()

Retrieves the enclosing scope statement for a given AST node.

This function determines the scope statement that contains or is associated with the provided AST node. The function employs multiple strategies to locate the scope:

First, it checks if the node is of a type that directly provides scope information through a get_scope() method, including SgSymbol, SgInitializedName, SgTemplateArgument, and SgQualifiedName nodes.

If the node does not have a direct scope accessor, the function traverses up the parent chain until it finds an SgScopeStatement. Special handling is provided for function parameter lists and constructor initializer lists, which are siblings of SgFunctionDefinition rather than children. In these cases, the function returns the function definition scope rather than continuing to the global scope.

The search is inclusive, meaning if the input node itself is a scope statement, that same node will be returned.

astNodePointer to the AST node for which the enclosing scope is to be found. Must not be NULL for meaningful results.
Returns
Pointer to the SgScopeStatement that encloses or is associated with the given AST node. Returns NULL if the node traces back to an SgType or SgSymbol without an associated statement. The function aborts if it cannot trace back to a valid scope statement and the parent is not an SgType or SgSymbol.
Warning
The function will call ROSE_ABORT() if it cannot trace back to an SgScopeStatement and the terminating parent node is not an SgType or SgSymbol. This indicates an unexpected AST structure.
The function prints an error message and returns NULL when the parent chain terminates at an SgType or SgSymbol node, indicating that no associated SgStatement could be located.
Precondition
The astNode parameter should point to a valid node within a properly constructed ROSE AST.
Postcondition
The returned scope statement, if non-NULL, is a valid SgScopeStatement that contains or is associated with the input node.
Note
This function is primarily used for name qualification support of template arguments.
The function returns a non-const pointer by using const_cast on the internally computed const scope statement.
For function parameter lists and constructor initializer lists, the function attempts to return the function definition scope. If no defining declaration exists, it continues traversing up the parent chain.

This function parses an abstract handle string representation and resolves it to the corresponding SgNode in the ROSE AST. The function first builds an abstract handle for the current project, then trims the input string to remove any leading project handle prefix (looking for the "SourceFile<" marker), and finally constructs a new abstract handle from the trimmed string to locate the target node.

The abstract handle mechanism provides a portable way to reference specific nodes in the AST using string-based identifiers. This is useful for tools that need to communicate node references across different ROSE sessions or between different components.

On MSVC compilers, covariant return types are not supported for the get_node() method, which will cause the function to abort.

◆ getSgNodeListFromMemoryPool()

static

Retrieves all nodes of a specific type from the ROSE memory pool.

This function traverses the ROSE compiler infrastructure memory pool to collect all nodes of the specified template type NodeType. It utilizes a custom traversal class derived from ROSE_VisitTraversal to visit each node in the memory pool associated with the given NodeType. During traversal, each visited node is dynamically cast to the target type, and if successful, the node pointer is added to the result list.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. A local traversal class MyTraversal is defined that inherits from ROSE_VisitTraversal.
  2. The visit method performs a dynamic_cast to convert each SgNode pointer to NodeType.
  3. The traverseMemoryPoolNodes static method of NodeType is invoked to iterate through all nodes of that type stored in the memory pool.

NodeTypeThe ROSE AST node type to search for in the memory pool. Must be a class derived from SgNode that provides a static traverseMemoryPoolNodes method.

The ROSE memory pool must be properly initialized before calling this function.
NodeType must be a valid ROSE AST node type derived from SgNode.
NodeType must provide a static traverseMemoryPoolNodes method that accepts a ROSE_VisitTraversal reference.
Postcondition
The returned vector contains valid pointers to all nodes of type NodeType currently in the memory pool.
The memory pool remains unchanged after the traversal.
Note
This function performs a dynamic_cast for type safety, with an assertion to verify the cast succeeds. In the context of traverseMemoryPoolNodes, all visited nodes should be of the correct type.
The returned pointers are owned by the ROSE memory pool and should not be deleted by the caller.

Retrieves the block size for a UPC shared modifier type.

This function extracts the block size (layout) information from a UPC shared modifier type node in the ROSE abstract syntax tree. UPC (Unified Parallel C) uses shared arrays with a block size that determines how array elements are distributed across threads. The function accesses the UPC modifier within the type modifier chain to obtain the layout value. If the block size is unspecified (indicated by a value of -1), the function treats it as having a default block size of 1, which corresponds to cyclic distribution in UPC semantics.

The parameter mod_type must not be null.
The parameter mod_type must be a valid UPC shared modifier type, as determined by isUpcSharedModifierType(mod_type) returning true.
Postcondition
The returned value is always a positive size_t value (at least 1).
Note
An unspecified block size in UPC (represented internally as -1) is normalized to 1, which represents cyclic distribution where each successive element is placed on the next thread.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if called with a modifier type that is not a UPC shared modifier type.

The input for-loop statement remains unmodified.

◆ HasNoThrowAssign()

bool SageInterface::HasNoThrowAssign ( const SgType *const inputType)

Determines whether a type has a non-throwing assignment operator.

This function analyzes a given type to determine if assignment operations on that type are guaranteed not to throw exceptions. The function first strips typedef and array qualifiers from the input type, then performs several checks to determine the no-throw property.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Strips typedef and array type qualifiers from the input type
  2. Returns false immediately for const types (cannot be assigned)
  3. Returns false immediately for reference types
  4. Returns true if the type has a trivial assignment operator
  5. For class types, examines all member functions in the class hierarchy to find assignment operators (operator=) and verifies they have the GNU nothrow attribute

The function currently checks for the GNU nothrow attribute on assignment operators. Support for C++11 noexcept expressions is noted as a future enhancement.

inputTypePointer to the SgType object representing the type to be analyzed. Must not be null. The pointer itself is const, and the pointed-to type is also const.

inputType must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
The input type remains unchanged.
Note
For non-class types that are not const, not references, and have trivial assignment, the function returns true.
The function uses the ENSURE_CLASS_TYPE macro which may cause early return with false if the type is not a class type.
Debug output can be enabled via the DEBUG_QUADRATIC_BEHAVIOR preprocessor definition to track the number of member functions being examined.
C++11 noexcept specifier support is not yet implemented and is marked as a TODO item.
Warning
This function does not currently support the C++11 noexcept expression, which may lead to incorrect results for modern C++ code that uses noexcept instead of the GNU nothrow attribute.

For class types, the function examines all member functions in the class hierarchy to find default constructors (constructors with zero arguments) and verifies that they have the GNU no-throw attribute.

The algorithm iterates through all member functions in the class hierarchy, identifies default constructors, and returns false if any default constructor lacks the no-throw attribute. If all default constructors have the no-throw attribute, or if the type has a trivial constructor, the function returns true.

If the type has a trivial copy constructor, the function immediately returns true since trivial copy constructors cannot throw.

For class types, the function examines all member functions in the class hierarchy to locate copy constructors. A copy constructor is identified as a constructor that accepts exactly one argument matching the class type (ignoring const, reference, and typedef qualifiers). ◆ hasSameGlobalScope()

bool SageInterface::hasSameGlobalScope ( SgStatement * statement_1,

Determines whether two statements share the same global scope.

This function checks if two given SgStatement nodes belong to the same global scope within the ROSE AST (Abstract Syntax Tree). It retrieves the enclosing SgGlobal node for each statement and compares them for equality. This functionality is particularly useful for recognizing functions in header files that may originate from two different ASTs, allowing for proper identification of shared declarations across translation units.

The function uses the getEnclosingNode template function to traverse up the AST hierarchy from each statement to find their respective global scope nodes. The comparison is done by pointer equality, meaning both statements must reside in exactly the same SgGlobal instance to be considered as having the same global scope.

Debug output can be enabled by setting the DEBUG_HAS_SAME_SCOPE macro to a non-zero value, which will print detailed information about the statements, their global scopes, and associated source files.

Parameters
statement_1Pointer to the first SgStatement node to be compared. Must not be null.
statement_2Pointer to the second SgStatement node to be compared. Must not be null.
Returns
True if both statements share the same global scope (i.e., their enclosing SgGlobal nodes are identical), false otherwise.
Precondition
statement_1 must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgStatement node.
statement_2 must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgStatement node.
Both statements must be part of a properly constructed AST with valid enclosing scopes.
Postcondition
The AST structure remains unchanged.
Note
This function includes the statement itself in the search for the enclosing global scope (includingSelf is set to true), so if either statement is itself an SgGlobal, it will be returned as its own enclosing global scope.
The DEBUG_HAS_SAME_SCOPE preprocessor macro controls debug output. When enabled, it prints information about the statements, their global scopes, and parent source files.

◆ hasSimpleChildrenList()

bool SageInterface::hasSimpleChildrenList ( SgScopeStatement * scope)

Determines whether a scope statement has a simple children list.

This function checks if the given scope statement type has a simple, flat list of children statements. Some scope statements, such as SgBasicBlock, maintain a straightforward list of statements as their children, while others like SgIfStmt have more complex structures with multiple branches or conditional components that do not form a simple linear list.

The function uses a switch statement on the variant type of the scope to categorize it. Scope types like SgBasicBlock, SgClassDefinition, SgFunctionDefinition, SgGlobal, and SgNamespaceDefinitionStatement are considered to have simple children lists. Control flow statements such as SgIfStmt, SgForStatement, SgWhileStmt, SgDoWhileStmt, SgSwitchStatement, and similar constructs are considered to have complex children structures.

Parameters
scopePointer to the SgScopeStatement to be analyzed. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the scope statement has a simple children list, false otherwise. Returns false for unrecognized or unhandled scope types.
Precondition
The scope parameter must not be NULL.
Postcondition
The scope statement remains unchanged.
Warning
Unrecognized or unhandled scope types will trigger a console warning message and return false by default.
Note
This function is useful for determining how to iterate over or manipulate the children of a scope statement. Simple children lists can typically be processed with straightforward iteration, while complex structures may require specialized handling for each component.

◆ hasTemplateSyntax()

bool SageInterface::hasTemplateSyntax ( const SgName & name)

Determines whether a given name contains C++ template instantiation syntax.

This function examines a name string to detect the presence of template syntax, which is characterized by the presence of both angle brackets (less-than and greater-than symbols). The function is used to identify template instantiations in names associated with classes, member functions, and functions within the ROSE compiler infrastructure.

The algorithm performs a simple string search for both the opening angle bracket and closing angle bracket characters. A name is considered to have template syntax only if both characters are present. However, a special case exists for the name "<unnamed>" which is explicitly excluded from being identified as template syntax, as this is a placeholder name used in certain compiler contexts (notably observed with the Intel v16 compiler and its mutex header file in C++11 code).

Parameters
nameThe SgName object containing the name string to be examined for template syntax. This may represent a class name, function name, or member function name.
Returns
True if the name contains both opening and closing angle brackets and is not the special case "<unnamed>"; false otherwise.
Note
This function specifically avoids false positives from operator overloads such as "operator<()" by requiring both angle bracket characters to be present.
The special handling of "<unnamed>" was added to address compatibility issues with C++11 code compiled using the Intel v16 compiler, particularly in relation to mutex header files.
Precondition
The name parameter should contain a valid string representation accessible via the getString() method.
Postcondition
The function does not modify the input parameter or any global state.

◆ hasTrivialDestructor()

bool SageInterface::hasTrivialDestructor ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given ROSE type has a trivial (built-in) destructor.

This function analyzes a ROSE compiler infrastructure type node to determine if the type has a trivial destructor. A trivial destructor is one that is implicitly defined by the compiler and performs no actions, which is the case for built-in types, pointers, references, enumerations, and function types.

The algorithm uses a switch statement on the type variant to handle different type categories:

  • Built-in primitive types (int, char, float, double, etc.) return true immediately
  • Pointer and reference types return true as they have trivial destructors
  • Array types, modifier types, and typedef types recursively check their base type
  • Class types require inspection of the class definition to check for an explicitly declared destructor. If a destructor is found, the function returns false; otherwise, it returns true
  • Function declarations and enum declarations associated with types return true

The function supports various ROSE-specific type variants including C99 complex and imaginary types, C99/C++11 char16_t and char32_t types, and 128-bit signed integers used in automated builtin function generation.

Parameters
tPointer to the SgType node representing the type to be analyzed. Must be a valid, non-null pointer to a ROSE type node.
Returns
True if the type has a trivial destructor, false otherwise. Returns false for class types with explicitly declared destructors or for unrecognized type variants.
Precondition
The parameter t must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType node within a properly constructed ROSE abstract syntax tree.
Postcondition
The input type node t remains unchanged.
Note
For class types, this function only checks for the presence of an explicitly declared destructor. It does not perform deep analysis of whether the destructor body is trivial.
The function returns false for class types whose definition is not available (forward declarations only).
Warning
This function may not correctly handle all edge cases for complex template instantiations or types with inherited destructors.

◆ hasUpcSharedType()

bool SageInterface::hasUpcSharedType ( SgType * sg_type,
SgModifierType ** mod_type_out )

Determines whether a given SAGE type contains a UPC shared type modifier.

This function recursively traverses a SAGE type hierarchy to detect the presence of a UPC (Unified Parallel C) shared type modifier. UPC shared types are used in parallel programming to indicate data that is distributed across multiple threads. The function handles various type wrappers including modifier types, pointer types, reference types, array types, and typedef types by recursively examining their base types until a UPC shared modifier is found or the type hierarchy is exhausted.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. If the type is a modifier type, check if it is a UPC shared modifier type. If so, return true and optionally output the modifier type. Otherwise, recursively check the base type.
  2. For pointer, reference, array, and typedef types, recursively check their base types.
  3. If no UPC shared type is found after traversal, return false.
Parameters
sg_typePointer to the SAGE type node to be examined. Must not be NULL.
mod_type_outOptional output parameter. If not NULL and a UPC shared modifier type is found, this will be set to point to that modifier type. If no UPC shared type is found, this will be set to NULL.
Returns
True if the type contains a UPC shared type modifier, false otherwise.
Precondition
sg_type must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
If the function returns true and mod_type_out is not NULL, mod_type_out will point to the SgModifierType containing the UPC shared modifier.
If the function returns false and mod_type_out is not NULL, mod_type_out will be set to NULL.
Note
This function uses ROSE_ASSERT to verify that sg_type is not NULL. Passing a NULL pointer will trigger an assertion failure.
The function only examines the type chain through specific type wrappers. Other composite types may not be fully traversed.
Warning
This function performs recursive calls which could lead to stack overflow for extremely deep type hierarchies, though such cases are rare in practice.

The function first strips typedef and array type qualifiers from the input type to obtain the underlying type. It then retrieves all member functions from the entire class hierarchy and searches for a function that is both marked as virtual and is a destructor.

The algorithm iterates through all member functions in the class hierarchy, checking each function's modifiers to determine if it qualifies as a virtual destructor. The search terminates early upon finding the first virtual destructor.

◆ insertAfterUsingCommaOp()

SgCommaOpExp * SageInterface::insertAfterUsingCommaOp ( SgExpression * new_exp,

Inserts a new expression after an anchor expression while preserving side effects using comma operators.

This function inserts a new expression (new_exp) after another expression (anchor_exp) that may have side effects, with minimal changes to the original program semantics. The transformation is achieved by using two comma operators to create the following pattern:

Given: type T1; ... anchor_exp ... Result: type T1; ... ((T1 = anchor_exp, new_exp), T1) ...

Where T1 is a temporary variable that saves the value produced by anchor_exp, ensuring that any side effects of anchor_exp are preserved and its value is correctly propagated. The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Determines the type of anchor_exp
  2. Creates a temporary variable declaration of that type before the enclosing statement
  3. Builds a nested comma expression that assigns anchor_exp to the temp, executes new_exp, then returns the temp value
  4. Replaces the original anchor_exp with the constructed comma expression
Parameters
new_expPointer to the new expression to be inserted after the anchor expression. Must not be NULL and must be different from anchor_exp.
anchor_expPointer to the anchor expression after which new_exp will be inserted. Must not be NULL. This expression may have side effects that need to be preserved.
temp_declOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, will be set to point to the generated temporary variable declaration statement.
temp_refOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, will be set to point to the first variable reference to the temporary variable (the one in the assignment T1 = anchor_exp).
Returns
Pointer to the top-level SgCommaOpExp that replaces the original anchor_exp. This represents the expression ((T1 = anchor_exp, new_exp), T1).
Precondition
new_exp must not be NULL.
anchor_exp must not be NULL.
new_exp and anchor_exp must be different expression nodes.
anchor_exp must have a valid parent node.
anchor_exp must be enclosed within a statement.
anchor_exp must have a valid type.
Postcondition
A new temporary variable declaration is inserted before the enclosing statement of anchor_exp.
The original anchor_exp is replaced by a comma operator expression in the AST.
The global gensym_counter is incremented.
If temp_decl is non-NULL, it points to the new variable declaration.
If temp_ref is non-NULL, it points to the variable reference in the assignment expression.
Note
The temporary variable name is generated using the pattern "_t_N" where N is a unique counter value.
A deep copy of anchor_exp is made for the assignment, so the original anchor_exp node is replaced rather than moved in the AST.
This transformation is useful for instrumentation or code transformation scenarios where additional code needs to be executed at a specific point without altering the evaluation order or losing side effects of the original expression.
Warning
The caller is responsible for ensuring that the transformation is semantically valid in the context where it is applied.
The type of anchor_exp must be assignable to a variable for this transformation to produce valid code.

◆ insertBeforeUsingCommaOp()

SgCommaOpExp * SageInterface::insertBeforeUsingCommaOp ( SgExpression * new_exp,

Inserts an expression before another expression using the comma operator.

This function inserts a new expression before an anchor expression that may have possible side effects, while minimizing changes to the original semantics. The insertion is achieved by constructing a comma operator expression of the form (new_exp, anchor_exp). In C/C++, the comma operator evaluates its left operand first, discards the result, then evaluates and returns the right operand. This ensures that new_exp is executed before anchor_exp while preserving the overall expression value.

The implementation creates a new SgCommaOpExp node, replaces the anchor expression in the AST with this comma operator expression, and then sets the anchor expression as the right-hand side operand of the comma operator. The new expression becomes the left-hand side operand.

new_expPointer to the new expression to be inserted before the anchor. Must not be NULL and must be different from anchor_exp.

anchor_exp has a valid parent node in the AST.

anchor_exp becomes the right-hand side operand of the returned comma expression.
new_exp becomes the left-hand side operand of the returned comma expression.

PreprocessingInfo * SageInterface::insertHeader ( const string & filename,

Inserts a header file include directive into the AST.

This function inserts a C preprocessor include directive for the specified header file into the ROSE AST. The function creates a PreprocessingInfo object representing the include directive and attaches it to an appropriate declaration statement in the global scope.

The function supports both system headers (using angle brackets) and user headers (using double quotes). It also handles token-based unparsing by marking the surrounding whitespace of affected statements as containing transformations, which ensures the added header is properly output during unparsing.

When unparsing header files is enabled and the target scope is within a header file, the function adjusts the source scope accordingly to ensure the include directive is inserted into the correct file. Header file suffixes recognized include: h, hpp, hh, H, hxx, h++, and tcc.

The algorithm iterates through declarations in the global scope to find an appropriate location for attaching the include directive. The directive is attached to the first declaration that either belongs to the same file as the source scope or is marked as a transformation.

Parameters
filenameThe name of the header file to include, without the surrounding angle brackets or quotes.
positionThe relative position where the include directive should be placed. Defaults to PreprocessingInfo::after.
isSystemHeaderIf true, the header is treated as a system header and will be enclosed in angle brackets. If false, double quotes are used. Defaults to false.
scopeThe scope statement indicating where to insert the header. If NULL, the top of the scope stack is used. Defaults to NULL.
Returns
A pointer to the newly created PreprocessingInfo object representing the include directive, or NULL if the insertion failed.
Precondition
The scope parameter, if provided, must be a valid SgScopeStatement pointer.
If scope is NULL, the scope stack must not be empty.
The source file must contain at least one declaration statement for the header to be attached to.
Postcondition
If successful, a new PreprocessingInfo object is created and attached to a declaration in the global scope.
The returned PreprocessingInfo object is marked as a transformation.
When token-based unparsing is enabled, the affected statement is marked with containsTransformationToSurroundingWhitespace set to true.
Warning
This function will trigger an assertion failure if the source file is empty, as preprocessing information must be attached to a located node such as a statement.
When using token-based unparsing, additional handling is required to ensure the header appears in the output, which this function attempts to address.
Note
The caller is responsible for handling cases where insertion fails, such as when translating an empty file for OpenMP where no headers need to be inserted.
For inserting headers into header files, the unparseHeaderFiles option must be enabled in the source file settings.

Inserts a include directive header into a source file.

This function inserts a C preprocessor include directive into the specified source file. It constructs the appropriate include statement based on whether the header is a system header (using angle brackets) or a user header (using double quotes). The function searches through the global scope declarations to find the first eligible located statement to which the include directive can be attached as preprocessing information.

The algorithm iterates through all declarations in the global scope and attaches the include directive to the first statement that either belongs to the same file as the global scope or is marked as a transformation-generated statement. The resulting PreprocessingInfo object is marked as a transformation to ensure proper output handling, particularly for shared IR nodes when multiple files are processed.

This is the recommended version of the insertHeader function that provides control over header placement and header type specification.

source_filePointer to the SgSourceFile where the header should be inserted. Must not be NULL.
filenameThe name of the header file to include, without the surrounding brackets or quotes.

A pointer to the newly created PreprocessingInfo object representing the include directive, or NULL if the insertion failed.
Warning
Empty source files are not supported. If the source file contains no declarations, the function will output an error message and abort. A statement must be inserted first before a header can be added.
The caller is responsible for handling cases where the return value is NULL, which indicates that the insertion failed.

source_file must not be NULL.
source_file must have a valid global scope.

If successful, a new PreprocessingInfo object is created and attached to the first eligible statement in the global scope.
The returned PreprocessingInfo object (if non-NULL) is marked as a transformation.

The function allows failed insertions in certain scenarios, such as when translating an empty file for OpenMP where no headers need to be inserted. The caller should decide how to handle insertion failures.

Inserts a header file inclusion directive into a source file.

This function adds a include preprocessor directive for a specified header file into the given source file. The function supports both system headers (using angle brackets) and user headers (using double quotes). The implementation handles two different unparsing modes: standard unparsing and token-based unparsing.

For standard unparsing, the include directive is attached directly to the global scope as preprocessing information. For token-based unparsing, an empty declaration statement is created and prepended to the global scope, with the include directive attached to that statement. This approach is necessary because in token-based unparsing, the global scope may not be marked as a transformation.

When header unparsing is also enabled, the function ensures that the physical file ID of the empty declaration matches the target file to be unparsed.

Parameters
source_filePointer to the source file where the header inclusion will be added. Must not be NULL.
header_file_nameThe name of the header file to include. This should be the filename without the angle brackets or quotes.
isSystemHeaderIf true, the header is treated as a system header and will be included using angle brackets. If false, double quotes are used.
positionSpecifies whether the include directive should be placed before or after the attachment point. Must be either PreprocessingInfo::before or PreprocessingInfo::after.
Returns
A pointer to the newly created PreprocessingInfo object representing the include directive. The returned object is marked as a transformation.
Precondition
source_file must not be NULL.
position must be either PreprocessingInfo::before or PreprocessingInfo::after.
Postcondition
A new include directive is added to the source file, either attached to the global scope or to a newly created empty declaration statement.
The returned PreprocessingInfo object has its file info marked as a transformation.
Note
When token-based unparsing is enabled, an SgEmptyDeclaration is created and prepended to the global scope to serve as an attachment point for the directive.
The preprocessing information is marked as a transformation to ensure proper output handling, particularly for shared IR nodes when multiple files are processed on the command line.

void SageInterface::insertHeader ( SgStatement * stmt,
PreprocessingInfo * newheader,
bool asLastHeader )

Inserts a new header preprocessing directive before a statement at a specified position.

This function inserts a new header (represented as a PreprocessingInfo object) into the preprocessing information attached to a given statement. The insertion position is determined relative to any existing header directives already attached to the statement.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. If the statement has no attached preprocessing information, the new header is simply attached with the appropriate relative position (before or after based on asLastHeader).
  2. If preprocessing information exists, the function scans through all attached directives to find the first and last existing include directives, as well as endif directives.
  3. When inserting as the last header, the new header is placed after the last existing include or endif directive to handle cases where includes are enclosed in ifdef/endif blocks.
  4. When inserting as the first header, the new header is placed before the first existing include directive.

The implementation specifically handles the case where the final include directive is enclosed within an ifdef/endif block, ensuring the inserted header remains visible in the generated output file.

Parameters
stmtPointer to the statement before which the header should be inserted. Must not be NULL.
newheaderPointer to the PreprocessingInfo object representing the new header directive to be inserted. Must not be NULL.
asLastHeaderBoolean flag indicating the insertion position. If true, the new header is inserted as the last header among existing headers. If false, it is inserted as the first header.
Precondition
stmt must be a valid non-NULL pointer to an SgStatement.
newheader must be a valid non-NULL pointer to a PreprocessingInfo object.
Postcondition
The newheader is attached to the preprocessing information of stmt at the appropriate position based on the asLastHeader flag.
Note
This function was updated to handle cases where include directives are enclosed within ifdef/endif preprocessor blocks, as encountered in applications like wget.
When no existing headers are found, the new header is simply appended after the statement regardless of the asLastHeader setting.
Warning
The function assumes that the PreprocessingInfo object passed as newheader is properly initialized and represents a valid header directive.

◆ insertStatement()

void SageInterface::insertStatement ( SgStatement * targetStmt,
SgStatement * newStmt,
bool insertBefore,
bool autoMovePreprocessingInfo )

Inserts a new statement before or after a target statement in the AST.

This function inserts a new statement relative to an existing target statement in the ROSE Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). The insertion can occur either before or after the target statement based on the insertBefore parameter. The function handles various complex scenarios including:

  • Label statements as parents: When the target statement's parent is a SgLabelStatement, the function traverses up to find the appropriate parent for insertion.
  • Control flow statements: Special handling is provided for if statements, while loops, do-while loops, for loops, UPC forall statements, and OpenMP body statements. When inserting relative to the body of these constructs, a padding SgBasicBlock is created to properly contain both the original and new statements.
  • Preprocessing information: By default, comments and CPP directives attached to the target statement are automatically relocated to the new statement when appropriate. This behavior can be disabled via the autoMovePreprocessingInfo parameter.
  • Function declaration linking: After insertion, if the new statement is a function declaration, the defining and non-defining declaration links are updated within the scope.
Parameters
targetStmtPointer to the existing statement relative to which the new statement will be inserted. Must not be NULL and must have a valid parent.
newStmtPointer to the new statement to be inserted. Must not be NULL and must be different from targetStmt. Should not have attached preprocessing information if autoMovePreprocessingInfo is true.
insertBeforeIf true, the new statement is inserted before the target statement. If false, the new statement is inserted after the target statement.
autoMovePreprocessingInfoIf true (default), preprocessing information such as comments and CPP directives attached to the target statement will be automatically moved to the new statement when appropriate. If false, preprocessing information is left unchanged.
Warning
If the new statement being inserted already has attached comments or CPP directives and autoMovePreprocessingInfo is true, a warning is issued as this case is not fully supported.
Special rules apply when inserting a SgBasicBlock that has attached comments or CPP directives; comment relocation is disabled in this case.
Precondition
targetStmt must not be NULL.
newStmt must not be NULL.
targetStmt and newStmt must be different statement nodes.
targetStmt must have a valid non-NULL parent pointer.
Postcondition
The new statement is inserted into the AST at the specified position relative to the target statement.
The parent pointer of newStmt is set to the appropriate scope.
If autoMovePreprocessingInfo is true, relevant preprocessing information is transferred from targetStmt to newStmt.
If newStmt is a function declaration and not in frontend construction mode, defining and non-defining links are updated.
Note
The function may recursively call itself when handling special parent types such as control flow statements.
When the target statement is a conditional or test expression of a control flow statement, the insertion is performed relative to the entire control flow statement instead.
The function uses fixStatement internally to handle symbol table updates for the new statement.

Inserts a statement after the last declaration within a given scope.

This function locates the last declaration statement within the specified scope and inserts the provided statement immediately after it. If no declaration statement exists within the scope, the statement is prepended to the beginning of the scope instead. This is useful for ensuring that new statements are placed in a logical position relative to existing declarations, maintaining proper code structure where declarations typically appear before executable statements.

The function uses findLastDeclarationStatement to search for the last declaration in the scope. If found, insertStatementAfter is called to place the new statement after it. Otherwise, prependStatement is used to add the statement at the beginning of the scope.

scope must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgScopeStatement.
The statement should not already be attached to another location in the AST.
Postcondition
The statement is inserted into the scope either after the last declaration statement or at the beginning of the scope if no declarations exist.
The AST is updated to reflect the new statement placement.
Note
If the scope contains no declaration statements, the behavior is to prepend the statement to the scope, making it the first statement in that scope.
This function does not verify whether the statement type is appropriate for the given scope context.

Inserts a list of statements after the last declaration within a scope.

The statements are inserted in order, with the first statement placed after the last declaration, and subsequent statements inserted sequentially after each preceding statement from the list.

The algorithm works as follows:

All statements from stmt_list are inserted into scope after the last declaration statement, or at the beginning if no declarations exist.
The statements maintain their relative order from the input list.
Note
If stmt_list is empty, the function performs no operations.
This function relies on insertStatementAfterLastDeclaration for single statements and insertStatementAfter for chaining subsequent statements.
Warning
The scope parameter must not be NULL; a NULL value will trigger an assertion failure.

void SageInterface::insertStatementList ( SgStatement * targetStmt,

Inserts a list of statements before or after a target statement.

This function inserts multiple statements from a vector into the AST relative to a specified target statement. The insertion can be performed either before or after the target statement based on the insertBefore flag.

When inserting before the target statement, the statements are inserted in their original order from the vector (index 0 first). When inserting after the target statement, the statements are inserted in reverse order so that the final ordering in the AST matches the original order in the input vector. This reverse iteration ensures that after all insertions, the statements appear in the same sequence as they were provided in the newStmts vector.

The function delegates the actual insertion work to insertStatementBefore and insertStatementAfter helper functions for each individual statement.

Parameters
targetStmtPointer to the target statement relative to which the new statements will be inserted. Must be a valid, non-null statement that exists within an AST.
newStmtsA vector of pointers to statements that will be inserted. Each statement in the vector should be a valid SgStatement pointer. The statements will maintain their relative order after insertion.
insertBeforeBoolean flag indicating the insertion position. If true, statements are inserted before the target statement. If false, statements are inserted after the target statement.
Precondition
targetStmt must be a valid non-null pointer to an existing statement in the AST.
All statement pointers in newStmts must be valid and not already attached to another location in the AST.
Postcondition
All statements from newStmts are inserted into the AST in their original vector order, either immediately before or after targetStmt.
The parent and scope information for each inserted statement is properly updated.
Note
When inserting after, the reverse iteration ensures correct final ordering since each subsequent insertion places the statement immediately after the target, pushing previously inserted statements further down.
Warning
If targetStmt is null or invalid, the behavior is undefined.
If any statement in newStmts is null, the behavior depends on the underlying insertStatementBefore and insertStatementAfter implementations.

bool SageInterface::insideSystemHeader ( SgLocatedNode * node)

Determines whether a given AST node is located within a system header file.

This function checks if the specified located node originates from a system header file by examining its file information. The function identifies system headers by searching for specific path patterns that correspond to ROSE compiler infrastructure staging directories, installation directories, and standard system include paths. The function checks against multiple known system header locations including GCC and G++ header staging directories in both build and install trees, as well as the standard /usr/include system header path.

Parameters
nodePointer to an SgLocatedNode representing an AST node with associated source location information. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the node is located within a recognized system header file path, false otherwise. Returns false if the node has no associated file information.
Precondition
The node parameter must not be NULL.
Postcondition
The state of the input node remains unchanged.
Note
The function recognizes the following system header path patterns:
  • include-staging/gcc_HEADERS (build tree GCC headers)
  • include-staging/g++_HEADERS (build tree G++ headers)
  • include/edg/gcc_HEADERS (install tree GCC headers)
  • include/edg/g++_HEADERS (install tree G++ headers)
  • /usr/include (standard system headers)
This function only checks for substring matches in the filename path, so it may produce false positives if user code paths contain these substrings.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if the node parameter is NULL.

int SageInterface::instrumentEndOfFunction ( SgFunctionDeclaration * func,
SgStatement * s )

Inserts a statement right before each return statement in a function.

This function instruments the end of a given function by inserting a specified statement immediately before every return statement found within the function body. The function uses a subtree query to locate all SgReturnStmt nodes within the function declaration. For return statements that contain non-trivial expressions (i.e., expressions that are not simple value expressions), the return expression is first split to ensure proper instrumentation order. If the function contains no return statements, the statement is appended to the end of the function body. When multiple return statements exist, the input statement is copied for each insertion after the first to avoid reusing the same statement object.

Parameters
funcPointer to the function declaration to be instrumented. Must not be NULL. The function must have a valid definition with a non-empty body if no return statements are present.
sPointer to the statement to be inserted before each return statement. Must not be NULL. This statement will be copied if multiple insertions are required.
Returns
The number of instrumentation points where the statement was inserted. Returns at least 1 if the function has a valid body, representing either the number of return statements instrumented or 1 if the statement was appended to a function with no return statements.
Precondition
func must not be NULL and must point to a valid SgFunctionDeclaration.
s must not be NULL and must point to a valid SgStatement.
If the function has no return statements, it must have a valid definition with a non-NULL body.
Postcondition
The statement s (or copies of it) has been inserted before each return statement in the function, or appended to the function body if no return statements exist.
Return expressions containing non-trivial expressions have been split to ensure correct execution order.
Warning
The function will call ROSE_ABORT() if a function without return statements has an empty (NULL) body, terminating program execution.
For return statements with complex expressions, the splitExpression function is called which may modify the AST structure around the return statement.
Note
The original statement s is used for the first insertion, while copies are created for subsequent insertions to avoid AST corruption from reusing the same statement node.
Value expressions in return statements (e.g., return 0) are not split as they do not require reordering for correct instrumentation.
