◆ IsAbstract()

bool SageInterface::IsAbstract ( const SgType *const inputType)

Determines whether a given type represents an abstract class.

This function checks if the provided type corresponds to an abstract class in the C++ sense. An abstract class is one that contains at least one pure virtual function and cannot be instantiated directly. The function first strips any typedef and array type qualifiers from the input type to obtain the underlying type. It then verifies that the type is a class type before checking for abstract class properties using the ROSE compiler infrastructure SageInterface utilities along with a class hierarchy wrapper.

The function relies on the ENSURE_CLASS_TYPE macro for type validation and uses SageInterface::isPureVirtualClass to perform the actual abstract class detection by analyzing the class hierarchy.

Parameters
inputTypeA pointer to the SgType object representing the type to be analyzed. This parameter should not be null and must point to a valid SgType instance.
Returns
True if the input type represents an abstract class (i.e., a class containing at least one pure virtual function). Returns false if the type is not a class type or if the class is not abstract.
Precondition
inputType must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgType object.
The project context must be properly initialized and accessible via getProject() for class hierarchy analysis.
Postcondition
The input type object remains unchanged.
Note
This function strips typedef and array type qualifiers before analysis, so typedef aliases to abstract classes will correctly return true.
The function constructs a ClassHierarchyWrapper internally for each call, which may have performance implications if called repeatedly.
Warning
If inputType is null or invalid, behavior depends on the ENSURE_CLASS_TYPE macro implementation and may result in undefined behavior or early return with false.

◆ isAddressTaken()

bool SageInterface::isAddressTaken ( SgExpression * refExp)

Determines whether the address-of operator is applied to a given expression.

This function checks if a given expression (either a variable reference or a member function reference) has its address taken via the unary address-of operator (&). The function examines the parent node of the input expression to determine if it is an SgAddressOfOp node, which indicates that the address-of operator is being applied to the expression.

This functionality is useful for detecting when name qualification may be required for pointer-to-member expressions, as well as for general analysis of address-taking operations in the AST.

Parameters
refExpPointer to an SgExpression that must be either an SgVarRefExp (variable reference expression) or an SgMemberFunctionRefExp (member function reference expression). This parameter must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the address-of operator is applied to the given expression, false otherwise.
Precondition
refExp must not be NULL.
refExp must be either an SgVarRefExp or an SgMemberFunctionRefExp.
Postcondition
The input expression and its parent nodes remain unchanged.
Note
This function was generalized to support member function references in addition to variable references to handle name qualification requirements for pointer-to-member expressions.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if refExp is NULL or if refExp is neither an SgVarRefExp nor an SgMemberFunctionRefExp.

◆ isAncestor()

bool SageInterface::isAncestor ( SgNode * node1,
SgNode * node2 )

Determines whether one AST node is an ancestor of another.

This function checks if node1 is an ancestor of node2 in the ROSE abstract syntax tree (AST) hierarchy. It traverses upward from node2 through the parent chain until either node1 is found (indicating node1 is an ancestor) or the root of the tree is reached (indicating node1 is not an ancestor). The function uses an iterative approach, following parent pointers from node2 until the search terminates.

Note that a node is not considered an ancestor of itself. If node1 and node2 are the same node, the function returns false.

Parameters
node1The potential ancestor node to check. Must not be null.
node2The node from which to search upward through the parent chain. Must not be null.
Returns
True if node1 is a proper ancestor of node2 (i.e., node1 appears somewhere in the parent chain of node2). False if node1 is not an ancestor of node2, or if node1 and node2 are the same node.
Precondition
node1 must not be null.
node2 must not be null.
The AST must have properly initialized parent pointers for accurate traversal.
Postcondition
The AST structure remains unchanged.
Note
This function only checks the direct parent chain. It does not consider other relationships such as siblings or descendants.
The function performs a linear traversal up the tree, so its time complexity is O(h) where h is the height of node2 in the AST.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if either node1 or node2 is null.

◆ isAssignable()

bool SageInterface::isAssignable ( SgType * type)

Determines whether a given C++ type supports assignment operations.

This function analyzes a ROSE AST type node to determine if values of that type can be assigned using the assignment operator (=). The function handles various type categories including primitive types, class types, modifier types, typedef types, and special types.

For class types, the function performs a detailed analysis by:

  1. Checking for user-defined public assignment operators (operator=)
  2. If a non-public assignment operator exists, the type is not assignable
  3. If no user-defined assignment operator exists, recursively checking that all non-static data members are assignable

The function recognizes that certain types are inherently non-assignable in C++:

  • Array types (cannot be directly assigned)
  • Function types and member function types
  • Reference types (cannot be reseated after initialization)
  • Ellipsis types
  • Decltype expressions

Most primitive types (int, char, float, double, pointers, enums, etc.) are considered assignable.

Parameters
typePointer to an SgType node representing the type to be analyzed. Must not be NULL. For class types, the type must have a valid defining declaration with a complete class definition.
Returns
True if values of the given type can be assigned, false otherwise.
Precondition
The type parameter must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType node.
For class types, the class must have a defining declaration with a complete definition available in the AST.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unchanged.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if an unknown or unsupported type variant is encountered.
For class types, the function creates a temporary SgReferenceType object when checking assignment operator signatures, which may have memory management implications.
The logic for detecting assignment operators checks for the constructor modifier combined with the name "operator=", which may not correctly identify all assignment operator declarations.
Note
The function handles modifier types and typedef types by recursively analyzing their base types.
C99 complex and imaginary types are considered assignable.
Support for 128-bit signed integers and C++11 char16_t and char32_t types is included.

◆ isAssignmentStatement()

bool SageInterface::isAssignmentStatement ( SgNode * s,
SgExpression ** lhs,
SgExpression ** rhs,
bool * readlhs )

Determines whether a given AST node represents an assignment statement.

This function analyzes a SAGE III AST node to determine if it represents an assignment statement. It handles both expression statements containing assignments and direct assignment expressions. The function recognizes various forms of assignment operators including simple assignment (=) and compound assignment operators (+=, -=, &=, |=, *=, /=, %=, ^=).

The implementation first attempts to extract an expression from the node, either by casting to SgExprStatement and retrieving its expression, or by directly casting to SgExpression. It then checks the variant type of the expression against known assignment operator types. For compound assignments, the left-hand side variable is also being read (e.g., in x += 1, x is both read and written).

This code is derived from AstInterface::IsAssignment().

Parameters
sThe AST node to analyze. Can be either an SgExprStatement or an SgExpression node. May be NULL, in which case the function returns false.
lhsOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, will be set to point to the left-hand side expression of the assignment if one is found.
rhsOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, will be set to point to the right-hand side expression of the assignment if one is found. If the right-hand side is an SgAssignInitializer, the operand is extracted.
readlhsOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, will be set to true if the assignment is a compound assignment (where the left-hand side is also read), or false for simple assignment.
Returns
True if the node represents an assignment statement, false otherwise.
Note
The output parameters lhs, rhs, and readlhs are only modified when the function returns true and the corresponding pointer is non-NULL.
For compound assignment operators (+=, -=, etc.), readlhs is set to true because the left-hand side value must be read before the operation. For simple assignment (=), readlhs is set to false.
Precondition
The input node s, if non-NULL, should be a valid SAGE III AST node.
Postcondition
If the function returns true and output parameters are provided, they will contain valid pointers to the corresponding AST components.

◆ IsBaseOf()

bool SageInterface::IsBaseOf ( const SgType *const inputBaseType,
const SgType *const inputDerivedType )

Determines whether one class type is a base class of another class type.

This function checks if the first type parameter represents a base class of the second type parameter in a class inheritance hierarchy. The function first strips typedef and modifier qualifiers from both input types to obtain the underlying class types. It then verifies that both types are class types and that the derived type is a complete type with a defining declaration.

The algorithm uses the ClassHierarchyWrapper to retrieve all ancestor classes of the derived type, including the derived type itself. It then iterates through this set of ancestors to find a match with the base type. Type comparison is performed after stripping typedef, array, and modifier qualifiers from each ancestor's type.

Parameters
inputBaseTypePointer to the SgType representing the potential base class type. Must not be null. The type will be stripped of typedef and modifier qualifiers before comparison.
inputDerivedTypePointer to the SgType representing the potential derived class type. Must not be null and must represent a complete class type with a defining declaration available.
Returns
True if inputBaseType is a base class of inputDerivedType or if they represent the same class type. Returns false if either type is not a class type or if no inheritance relationship exists between them.
Precondition
inputBaseType must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgType.
inputDerivedType must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgType.
inputDerivedType must represent a complete class type with a defining declaration.
A valid project must be accessible via getProject() for class hierarchy analysis.
Postcondition
The function does not modify either input type.
Warning
The function requires inputDerivedType to be a complete type. If the derived type does not have a defining declaration, an assertion failure will occur.
This function constructs a ClassHierarchyWrapper for each call, which may have performance implications if called frequently.
Note
The function considers a class to be a base of itself, as the derived class definition is included in the set of ancestors being checked.
Debug output for quadratic behavior analysis can be enabled via the DEBUG_QUADRATIC_BEHAVIOR preprocessor macro.

◆ isBodyStatement()

bool SageInterface::isBodyStatement ( SgStatement * s)

Determines whether a statement is the body of a control structure.

This function checks if the given statement serves as the body of various control flow constructs in the ROSE AST. It examines the parent node of the statement and determines if the statement is used as the loop body, conditional body, or other body component of control structures such as for loops, while loops, do-while loops, switch statements, if statements, case options, catch blocks, and OpenMP body statements.

The function uses a switch statement on the parent node's variant type to identify the specific control structure and then compares the statement against the appropriate body accessor method for that structure.

Supported parent control structures include:

  • SgForStatement (loop body)
  • SgUpcForAllStatement (UPC parallel for-all loop body)
  • SgWhileStmt (while loop body)
  • SgDoWhileStmt (do-while loop body)
  • SgSwitchStatement (switch body)
  • SgCaseOptionStmt (case body)
  • SgDefaultOptionStmt (default case body)
  • SgCatchOptionStmt (catch block body)
  • SgIfStmt (true body or false body)
  • SgOmpBodyStatement (OpenMP body statements)
Parameters
sPointer to the SgStatement to be checked. Must not be null and must have a valid parent node that is a SgLocatedNode.
Returns
True if the statement is the body of a recognized control structure, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter s must not be null.
The parent of s must be a valid SgLocatedNode.
Postcondition
The input statement and its parent remain unchanged.
Note
This function only checks immediate parent relationships. It does not recursively check ancestor nodes.
For SgIfStmt, the function returns true if the statement is either the true body or the false body of the if statement.
The default case handles OpenMP body statements through the isSgOmpBodyStatement dynamic cast check.

◆ isCallToParticularFunction() [1/2]

bool SageInterface::isCallToParticularFunction ( const std::string & qualifiedName,
size_t arity,
SgExpression * e )

Determines whether an expression is a function call to a specific function with a given arity.

This function checks if the provided expression represents a function call to a function with the specified fully qualified name and the expected number of arguments. The function performs a series of checks to validate that the expression is indeed a function call expression, that it contains a function reference expression, and that both the qualified name and argument count match the expected values.

The implementation first attempts to cast the expression to an SgFunctionCallExp. If successful, it then extracts the function reference expression from the call. The qualified name is obtained from the function symbol's declaration and compared against the provided qualified name. The arity is verified by comparing the size of the argument expression list with the expected count.

Parameters
qualifiedNameThe fully qualified name of the function to match against. This should include any namespace or class scope prefixes as they appear in the ROSE AST representation.
arityThe expected number of arguments that the function call should have.
eA pointer to the SgExpression to be examined. This expression is tested to determine if it represents a call to the specified function.
Returns
True if the expression is a function call to the specified function with the exact number of arguments matching arity. False otherwise, including cases where the expression is not a function call, does not contain a direct function reference, the qualified name does not match, or the argument count differs.
Precondition
The parameter e may be NULL, in which case the function will return false.
If e is non-NULL, it should point to a valid SgExpression node in the AST.
Postcondition
The AST remains unmodified by this function.
Note
This function only matches direct function calls through SgFunctionRefExp. It will not match calls made through function pointers, member function calls, or other indirect calling mechanisms.
The qualified name comparison is exact and case-sensitive.

◆ isCallToParticularFunction() [2/2]

bool SageInterface::isCallToParticularFunction ( SgFunctionDeclaration * decl,
SgExpression * e )

Determines whether an expression is a function call to a specific function declaration.

This function checks if a given expression represents a function call expression that invokes a particular function identified by the provided function declaration. The function performs a series of checks to verify that the expression is indeed a function call expression, that it contains a function reference expression, and that the referenced function's declaration matches the specified declaration.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Attempts to cast the expression to an SgFunctionCallExp
  2. If successful, extracts the function reference expression from the call
  3. Compares the declaration associated with the function reference's symbol against the provided declaration
Parameters
declPointer to the SgFunctionDeclaration representing the target function to check against. This is the function declaration that the caller wants to determine if the expression is calling.
ePointer to the SgExpression to be examined. This expression is tested to determine if it represents a call to the function specified by decl.
Returns
True if the expression e is a function call expression that calls the function specified by decl. Returns false if e is not a function call expression, if the function call does not use a direct function reference, or if the called function's declaration does not match decl.
Precondition
The decl parameter should point to a valid SgFunctionDeclaration object.
The expression e should be a valid SgExpression pointer, or NULL.
Postcondition
The function does not modify any input parameters or global state.
Note
This function only handles direct function calls through function reference expressions. It will return false for indirect calls such as calls through function pointers or member function calls.
The comparison is performed using pointer equality on the declaration obtained from the function symbol, which means it checks for the exact same declaration object rather than semantically equivalent declarations.

◆ isCanonicalDoLoop()

bool SageInterface::isCanonicalDoLoop ( SgFortranDo * loop,
SgInitializedName ** ivar,
SgExpression ** lb,
SgExpression ** ub,
SgExpression ** step,
SgStatement ** body,
bool * hasIncrementalIterationSpace,
bool * isInclusiveUpperBound )

Determines whether a Fortran DO loop is in canonical form and extracts its key features.

This function analyzes a Fortran DO loop to determine if it conforms to a canonical loop structure. A canonical Fortran DO loop must have an initialization expression of the form i=expr where i is an integer loop index variable. The function validates that the loop index has a strict integer type and that the increment expression is properly defined (not null). If the loop is canonical, the function can optionally return various loop components including the induction variable, lower bound, upper bound, step expression, and loop body.

Fortran DO loops are treated as always having an inclusive upper bound. The function attempts to determine whether the iteration space is incremental by examining the step value when it is a constant integer.

Parameters
loopPointer to the SgFortranDo node representing the Fortran DO loop to analyze.
ivarOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, receives a pointer to the SgInitializedName representing the loop induction variable.
lbOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, receives a pointer to the SgExpression representing the lower bound of the loop.
ubOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, receives a pointer to the SgExpression representing the upper bound of the loop.
stepOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, receives a pointer to the SgExpression representing the loop increment/step expression.
bodyOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, receives a pointer to the SgStatement representing the loop body.
hasIncrementalIterationSpaceOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, receives true if the loop iterates in an increasing direction, false otherwise. This is determined by examining the step value if it is a constant integer.
isInclusiveUpperBoundOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, always receives true since Fortran DO loops have inclusive upper bounds by definition.
Returns
True if the loop is in canonical form, false otherwise.
Precondition
The loop parameter must not be NULL.
The loop must have been normalized using doLoopNormalization() so that the increment expression is not a null expression.
Postcondition
If the function returns true and output parameters are provided, they will contain valid pointers to the corresponding loop components.
If the function returns false, the values of output parameters are undefined.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if the increment expression is a SgNullExpression, indicating that doLoopNormalization() should be called first.
Note
The loop index variable must have a strict integer type for the loop to be considered canonical.
Unlike C/C++ for loops, Fortran DO loops always have inclusive upper bounds.
The determination of incremental iteration space is only accurate when the step is a constant integer value. For non-constant steps, hasIncrementalIterationSpace defaults to true.

◆ isCanonicalForLoop()

bool SageInterface::isCanonicalForLoop ( SgNode * loop,
SgInitializedName ** ivar,
SgExpression ** lb,
SgExpression ** ub,
SgExpression ** step,
SgStatement ** body,
bool * hasIncrementalIterationSpace,
bool * isInclusiveUpperBound )

Determines whether a given loop node represents a canonical for loop.

This function analyzes an SgNode representing a loop to determine if it conforms to the canonical for loop pattern commonly required for parallelization and optimization transformations. A canonical for loop has a specific structure with a well-defined initialization, test condition, and increment expression that allows for static analysis of the iteration space.

The function checks the following criteria for a canonical for loop:

  1. Initialization statement must be either a variable declaration with assignment initializer (C99 style: for(int i=0;...)) or a simple assignment statement (for(i=0;...)).
  2. The loop index variable must have a strict integer type.
  3. The test expression must use one of the comparison operators: <=, <, >=, or >. The left operand must be the loop index variable.
  4. The increment expression must follow one of the allowed forms:
    • ++var or var++
    • –var or var–
    • var += incr or var -= incr
    • var = var + incr, var = incr + var, or var = var - incr
  5. The loop body must be a structured block (single entry, single exit).
Parameters
loopPointer to the SgNode representing the loop to be analyzed. Must not be NULL.
ivarOptional output parameter. If not NULL, receives a pointer to the SgInitializedName of the loop index variable.
lbOptional output parameter. If not NULL, receives a pointer to the SgExpression representing the lower bound of the loop.
ubOptional output parameter. If not NULL, receives a pointer to the SgExpression representing the upper bound of the loop.
stepOptional output parameter. If not NULL, receives a pointer to the SgExpression representing the step or increment value of the loop.
bodyOptional output parameter. If not NULL, receives a pointer to the SgStatement representing the loop body.
hasIncrementalIterationSpaceOptional output parameter. If not NULL, set to true if the loop iterates in increasing order (uses < or <=), false if decreasing (uses > or >=).
isInclusiveUpperBoundOptional output parameter. If not NULL, set to true if the upper bound is inclusive (<= or >=), false otherwise.
Returns
True if the loop is a canonical for loop meeting all criteria, false otherwise.
Precondition
The loop parameter must not be NULL.
If loop is not an SgForStatement, the function returns false immediately.
Postcondition
If the function returns true, all non-NULL output parameters are populated with valid pointers to the corresponding loop components.
If the function returns false, the values of output parameters are undefined.
Warning
The step expression returned when the increment is ++ or – is a newly created SgIntVal node with value 1, which may cause memory management concerns as it is not attached to the AST.
This function currently only supports C for loops. Fortran DO loops are not supported in this implementation.
Note
The function does not verify that the loop index variable is not modified within the loop body. A TODO comment in the source indicates this check should be added.
The != operator in the test expression is not currently allowed, though there is commented-out code suggesting it was considered.

◆ isConstantFalse()

bool SageInterface::isConstantFalse ( SgExpression * e)

Determines whether an expression is a compile-time constant that evaluates to false.

This function analyzes a SAGE III expression node to determine if it represents a constant false value at compile time. The function handles several expression types including boolean literals, integer literals, cast expressions, and logical NOT operations. For boolean values, it checks if the value is explicitly false. For integer values, it checks if the value is zero (which is equivalent to false in C/C++). Cast expressions are handled recursively by examining the operand. Logical NOT expressions are evaluated by checking if the operand is a constant true value (since NOT of true equals false).

Parameters
ePointer to the SgExpression node to be evaluated. This expression is analyzed to determine if it represents a constant false value. Must not be null.
Returns
True if the expression is determined to be a compile-time constant that evaluates to false, false otherwise. Returns false for expression types that are not explicitly handled or cannot be determined to be constant false at compile time.
Precondition
The parameter e must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgExpression node.
Postcondition
The input expression e is not modified.
Note
This function only handles a limited set of expression types. Complex expressions involving arithmetic operations, function calls, or other constructs will return false even if they might evaluate to false at runtime.
This function works in conjunction with isConstantTrue to handle logical NOT expressions.
Warning
Passing a null pointer will result in undefined behavior.

◆ isConstantTrue()

bool SageInterface::isConstantTrue ( SgExpression * e)

Determines whether a given expression evaluates to a constant true value.

This function analyzes a ROSE AST expression node to determine if it represents a compile-time constant that evaluates to true. The function handles several expression types including boolean literals, integer literals, cast expressions, logical not operations, and address-of operations. For cast expressions and logical not operations, the function recursively evaluates the operand. The implementation includes platform-specific handling for MSVC compilers due to differences in how boolean values are represented internally.

The algorithm uses a switch statement on the expression variant type to dispatch to the appropriate evaluation logic for each supported expression kind. For boolean values, it checks if the value is true (or non-zero on MSVC). For integer values, any non-zero value is considered true. Address-of operations always return true since the address of any valid object is non-null. For logical not operations, the function delegates to isConstantFalse on the operand.

Parameters
ePointer to the SgExpression node to be evaluated. This expression is analyzed to determine if it represents a constant true value.
Returns
True if the expression is determined to be a constant true value, false otherwise. Returns false for expression types that are not explicitly handled or cannot be determined to be constant true.
Precondition
The parameter e must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgExpression node.
Postcondition
The input expression e remains unmodified.
Note
For V_SgBoolValExp, the comparison differs between MSVC and other compilers due to internal representation differences of the p_value member.
This function only handles a limited set of expression types. Complex expressions or those not explicitly listed in the switch statement will return false even if they might evaluate to true at runtime.
Warning
The function assumes the input pointer is valid. Passing a null pointer will result in undefined behavior.
See also
isConstantFalse

◆ isConstType()

bool SageInterface::isConstType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given SAGE III type is const-qualified.

This function recursively analyzes a SAGE III type node to determine if it represents a const-qualified type. The function handles type indirection through typedef types and modifier types, unwrapping these layers to find the underlying const qualification.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. If the type is a typedef type, it recursively checks the base type of the typedef.
  2. If the type is a modifier type, it examines the const-volatile modifier. If the const modifier is set, the function returns true. Otherwise, it recursively checks the base type of the modifier.
  3. If the type is neither a typedef nor a modifier type, the function returns false.

Note that reference types are not specially handled in this implementation, as indicated by the commented-out code. Reference types typically cannot be cv-qualified directly in C++.

Parameters
tPointer to the SgType node to be analyzed for const qualification. This should be a valid SAGE III type node from the abstract syntax tree. May be nullptr, in which case the behavior depends on the SAGE III type-checking macros.
Returns
True if the type is const-qualified, either directly or through typedef or modifier type indirection. Returns false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType node within a properly constructed SAGE III abstract syntax tree.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unmodified.
Note
This function uses SAGE III dynamic type checking functions (isSgTypedefType, isSgModifierType) to determine the specific type category.
The function does not handle all possible type wrappers. Types that are not typedef types or modifier types will return false even if they contain const-qualified components (e.g., pointer to const).

◆ isCopyConstructible()

bool SageInterface::isCopyConstructible ( SgType * type)

Determines whether a given ROSE SgType is copy constructible.

This function analyzes a ROSE compiler infrastructure SgType node to determine if values of that type can be copy constructed according to C++ semantics. The function handles various type categories through a switch statement on the type's variant tag.

For array types, function types, member function types, ellipsis types, and decltype types, the function returns false as these are not copy constructible.

For class types, the function performs a detailed analysis including:

  • Checking for user-defined copy constructors and their accessibility (public vs non-public)
  • Detecting pure virtual functions which prevent copy construction
  • Recursively verifying that all non-static data members are copy constructible
  • Recursively verifying that all base classes are copy constructible

For modifier types and typedef types, the function recursively checks the underlying base type.

Primitive types, pointer types, reference types, enum types, and other built-in types are considered copy constructible and return true.

Parameters
typePointer to the SgType node to be analyzed for copy constructibility. Must not be null. The type can be any valid ROSE type representation.
Returns
True if the type is copy constructible, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter type must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType node.
For class types, the class must have a defining declaration available.
Postcondition
The function does not modify the input type or any associated AST nodes.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if an unknown or unhandled type variant is encountered.
For class types, the function assumes that the defining declaration and class definition are accessible; assertion failures will occur if these are null.
Note
Array types are explicitly marked as not copy constructible as of 3/3/2009.
The function uses recursive calls to handle nested types, modifier types, typedef types, class member types, and base class types.
Support for V_SgTypeSigned128bitInteger was added on 9/7/2016 for automated generation of builtin functions.
Support for V_SgTypeChar16 and V_SgTypeChar32 was added on 2/16/2018 for C99 and C++11 specific types.
The naming of SgTypeComplex was changed on 8/27/2006 for consistency, and SgTypeImaginary was added for C99 complex support.

◆ isDataMemberReference()

bool SageInterface::isDataMemberReference ( SgVarRefExp * varRefExp)

Determines whether a variable reference expression refers to a non-static data member access.

This function analyzes a variable reference expression to determine if it represents a data member access through an object (e.g., "x.member" or "ptr->member") rather than a simple qualified reference to a data member (e.g., "X::member"). The distinction is important for name qualification purposes in code generation and transformation.

The function checks the following conditions to identify a data member reference:

  1. The parent of the variable reference must be an arrow expression (->), dot expression (.), or address-of operator (&).
  2. For arrow expressions, it excludes cases where the expression is used within a sizeof operator with objectless nonstatic data member reference semantics.
  3. The referenced variable must not be declared as static.
  4. The variable must be declared within a class definition scope.

This function specifically targets non-static data members, as static data members require different name qualification handling.

Parameters
varRefExpPointer to the variable reference expression to analyze. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the variable reference represents a non-static data member access through an object instance, false otherwise.
Precondition
varRefExp must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgVarRefExp node.
The parent node of varRefExp must be properly set in the AST.
Postcondition
The AST remains unmodified.
Note
This function is used to support name qualification of data member references separately from name qualification of variables that might be members.
Static data members are excluded from this check as they are qualified differently and do not use member data name qualification.
Debug output can be enabled by setting DEBUG_IS_DATA_MEMBER_REFERENCE to a non-zero value.
Warning
If the variable reference is not associated with a variable declaration, the function cannot determine if it is a static data member and will return false.

◆ isDefaultConstructible()

bool SageInterface::isDefaultConstructible ( SgType * type)

Determines whether a given ROSE AST type is default constructible.

This function analyzes a ROSE compiler infrastructure SgType node to determine if the represented C++ type can be default constructed. The implementation recursively examines the type structure and handles various type categories including arrays, modifier types, class types, typedef types, and primitive types.

For class types, the function performs a detailed analysis by examining the class definition to find constructors. It checks for the presence of a public default constructor (a constructor that can be called with no arguments, either because it has no parameters or all parameters have default values). If no user-defined constructors exist, it verifies that all non-static data members are themselves default constructible.

The algorithm handles the following cases:

  • Array types: Recursively checks the base element type
  • Modifier types: Recursively checks the underlying base type
  • Class types: Searches for public default constructors or implicitly generated ones
  • Typedef types: Recursively checks the aliased type
  • Reference types: Always returns false (references must be initialized)
  • Primitive types (int, char, float, etc.): Always returns true
  • Pointer types: Always returns true
  • Enum types: Always returns true

typePointer to the SgType node representing the type to be analyzed. Must not be null.
Returns

Warning
The implementation comment notes that this function may not work properly in all cases. Use with caution for complex type scenarios.
For class types, the logic for checking non-static data members appears to return true if any member is default constructible rather than checking if all members are default constructible, which may be a bug in the implementation.
Precondition
The type parameter must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType node.
Postcondition
The function does not modify the input type or any related AST nodes.
Note
This function uses ROSE compiler infrastructure types and functions such as isSgArrayType, isSgClassType, isSgClassDeclaration, etc.
The function will trigger an assertion failure if an unknown type variant is encountered.
Support for C99 and C++11 specific types including char16_t, char32_t, complex types, and 128-bit signed integers is included.

The stripType method is called with flags to remove both typedef aliases and type modifiers (such as const, volatile) before checking if the type is an enum.

◆ isEqualToIntConst()

bool SageInterface::isEqualToIntConst ( SgExpression * e,
int value )

Checks whether an expression is an integer constant equal to a specified value.

This function determines if a given SAGE III expression node represents an integer constant (SgIntVal) and whether that constant is equal to the provided integer value. The function performs a two-step check: first verifying that the expression is of type SgIntVal using the isSgIntVal dynamic cast function, and then comparing the stored integer value against the specified target value.

This utility is commonly used in AST analysis and transformation passes where specific constant values need to be identified, such as checking for sentinel values, loop bounds, or special constants like 0 or 1.

Parameters
ePointer to the SgExpression node to be examined. May be NULL or point to any type of expression node in the SAGE III AST.
valueThe integer value to compare against if the expression is an integer constant.
Returns
True if the expression is a non-NULL SgIntVal node whose stored value equals the specified value parameter. Returns false if the expression is NULL, is not an SgIntVal, or has a different integer value.
Precondition
The expression pointer e should be a valid pointer to an SgExpression node or NULL.
Postcondition
The AST is not modified by this function.
Note
This function only checks for SgIntVal nodes and does not handle other integer literal types such as SgLongIntVal, SgShortVal, or SgUnsignedIntVal. For comprehensive integer constant checking, consider using additional type checks or a more general utility function.
The function safely handles NULL input by relying on the behavior of isSgIntVal, which returns NULL for NULL input.

◆ isEquivalentFunctionType()

bool SageInterface::isEquivalentFunctionType ( const SgFunctionType * lhs,
const SgFunctionType * rhs )

Determines whether two function types are semantically equivalent.

This function compares two SgFunctionType objects to determine if they represent equivalent function types. The equivalence check is performed by comparing the return types and all argument types of both function types. Two function types are considered equivalent if and only if their return types are equivalent and they have the same number of arguments with each corresponding argument type being equivalent.

The algorithm proceeds as follows:

  1. First checks if both pointers refer to the same object (identity check)
  2. Compares the return types using isEquivalentType
  3. If return types match, verifies both functions have the same number of arguments
  4. Iterates through all argument types, comparing each pair using isEquivalentType
  5. Returns true only if all comparisons succeed
Parameters
lhsPointer to the first SgFunctionType to compare. Must not be NULL.
rhsPointer to the second SgFunctionType to compare. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the two function types are equivalent (same return type and all argument types match), false otherwise.
Precondition
lhs must not be NULL.
rhs must not be NULL.
Postcondition
The input function type objects remain unchanged.
Note
This function relies on isEquivalentType for comparing individual types, so the definition of type equivalence depends on that function's behavior.
If both pointers point to the same SgFunctionType object, the function returns true immediately without performing detailed comparisons.
The comparison short-circuits on the first non-matching argument type for efficiency.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if either lhs or rhs is NULL.

◆ isEquivalentType()

bool SageInterface::isEquivalentType ( const SgType * lhs,
const SgType * rhs )

Determines whether two SgType pointers represent equivalent types.

This function performs a comprehensive comparison of two ROSE AST type nodes to determine if they are semantically equivalent. The comparison is performed recursively, unwrapping and comparing various type layers including typedefs, references, pointers, arrays, modifier types, function types, member function types, and template types (SgNonrealType).

The algorithm works by first stripping typedef layers from both types, then recursively comparing the underlying type structures. For compound types such as references, pointers, and arrays, the function extracts and compares their base types. For modifier types, it checks whether the modifiers are equivalent and recursively compares base types. Identity modifiers (modifiers with default settings) are skipped during comparison.

The function includes protection against infinite recursion through a static counter that limits the recursion depth to 350 levels. This is necessary because complex template instantiations in STL and Boost libraries can create deeply nested type chains.

Special handling is provided for:

  • SgTypedefType: Stripped automatically at the beginning of each recursive call
  • SgReferenceType: Base types compared when both sides are references
  • SgPointerType: Base types compared when both sides are pointers
  • SgArrayType: Base types and index expressions compared when both sides are arrays
  • SgModifierType: Modifiers compared, with identity modifiers being skipped
  • SgNonrealType: Template parameter positions and parent declarations compared
  • SgFunctionType and SgMemberFunctionType: Direct pointer comparison
Parameters
lhsPointer to the first SgType to compare. Must not be NULL.
rhsPointer to the second SgType to compare. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the two types are semantically equivalent, false otherwise.
Precondition
lhs is not NULL
rhs is not NULL
Postcondition
The function returns without modifying either input type
The internal recursion counter is restored to its original value
Warning
This function uses a static counter to prevent infinite recursion. The recursion limit is set to 350 levels. If this limit is exceeded, the function will call ROSE_ABORT() and terminate the program.
The function may not correctly handle all edge cases involving complex template types or deeply nested type structures.
Note
This function is called internally by SgType::isEquivalentType().
For array types, the current implementation may not fully verify expression equivalence for array index expressions when they differ by pointer identity.
The DEBUG_TYPE_EQUIVALENCE macro can be enabled to produce detailed debugging output showing the type comparison process.
For function types, the comparison currently uses direct pointer equality rather than structural comparison of return types and parameter lists.

Determines whether a declaration statement has extern storage class.

This function checks if the given declaration statement has the extern storage modifier applied to it. It accesses the declaration modifier of the statement, then retrieves the storage modifier, and finally queries whether the extern specifier is set. The extern storage class indicates that the declared entity has external linkage and its definition may exist in another translation unit.

Parameters
stmtPointer to the SgDeclarationStatement node to be examined. This parameter must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the declaration statement has the extern storage modifier, false otherwise.
Precondition
stmt must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgDeclarationStatement object.
Postcondition

Note

Warning
Passing a null pointer will trigger an assertion failure.

◆ isIndexOperator()

bool SageInterface::isIndexOperator ( SgExpression * exp)

Determines whether an expression represents an index operator (operator[] or operator()).

This function checks if the given expression is a member function reference expression that corresponds to an index operator. It specifically looks for overloaded operator[] (subscript operator) or operator() (function call operator) member functions. These operators are commonly used for array-like or functor-like access patterns in C++ classes such as std::vector, std::map, or custom container types.

The function first verifies that the expression is a member function reference expression, then retrieves the associated member function declaration to check if its name matches either "operator[]" or "operator()" and that it has a valid type.

Parameters
expPointer to an SgExpression node to be analyzed. This expression is checked to determine if it represents a call to an index operator. May be NULL.
Returns
True if the expression represents a member function reference to operator[] or operator() with a valid type, false otherwise. Returns false if exp is NULL or not a member function reference expression.
Precondition
The input expression, if not NULL, should be part of a valid SAGE III AST.
Postcondition
The AST remains unmodified; this is a query-only function.
Note
This function only detects member function versions of these operators, not non-member overloads or built-in array subscript operations.
Both operator[] and operator() are considered index operators for the purposes of this function, as both can be used for element access in container-like classes.

◆ isInSubTree()

bool SageInterface::isInSubTree ( SgExpression * subtree,
SgExpression * exp )

Determines whether a given expression node exists within a specified subtree.

This function checks if a target expression node is contained within an AST subtree rooted at the specified subtree node. It performs a preorder traversal of the subtree using the ROSE compiler infrastructure's AstSimpleProcessing visitor pattern. During traversal, each visited node is compared against the target expression to determine membership in the subtree.

The implementation defines an internal Visitor class that inherits from AstSimpleProcessing. This visitor maintains a pointer to the target expression and a boolean flag that is set to true when the target is found during traversal. The traversal visits all nodes in preorder (parent before children) until the entire subtree has been processed.

Parameters
subtreePointer to the root of the expression subtree to search within. This defines the scope of the search operation.
expPointer to the target expression node to search for within the subtree. This is the node whose presence in the subtree is being tested.
Returns
True if the expression exp is found within the subtree rooted at subtree, false otherwise.
Precondition
subtree must be a valid pointer to an SgExpression node representing the root of the subtree to search.
exp must be a valid pointer to an SgExpression node to search for.
Postcondition
The AST structure remains unchanged after the search operation.
Note
This function performs a complete traversal of the subtree even after finding the target expression. For large subtrees where early termination is desired, a different traversal approach may be more efficient.
The comparison is based on pointer equality, not structural or semantic equality of the expressions.

◆ isJovialOutParam()

bool SageInterface::isJovialOutParam ( SgInitializedName * name)

Determines whether a parameter name is a Jovial output parameter.

This function checks if the given initialized name represents an output parameter in the Jovial programming language. In Jovial, output parameters are parameters that can be modified by the called procedure and have their modified values returned to the caller. The determination is made by checking if the parameter is mutable, as Jovial output parameters are characterized by their mutability.

The implementation delegates to the isMutable function, which performs the actual check for mutability of the parameter.

Parameters
namePointer to an SgInitializedName node representing the parameter to be checked. This should be a valid pointer to a parameter declaration in the AST.
Returns
True if the parameter is a Jovial output parameter (i.e., mutable), false otherwise.
Precondition
The name parameter should be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgInitializedName node representing a function parameter.
Postcondition
The state of the name parameter and the AST remains unchanged.
Note
This function is specific to Jovial language support in ROSE and relies on the mutability property to identify output parameters.
Jovial is a legacy programming language primarily used in military and aerospace applications.

◆ isLambdaCapturedVariable()

bool SageInterface::isLambdaCapturedVariable ( SgVarRefExp * varRef)

Determines whether a variable reference is a lambda captured variable.

This function checks if a given variable reference expression represents a variable that has been captured by a lambda expression. The detection is performed by analyzing the AST structure surrounding the variable reference. Specifically, the function looks for a pattern where the variable reference is accessed through an arrow expression with a this pointer on the left-hand side, and that this pointer belongs to a lambda closure class.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Check if the parent of the variable reference is an arrow expression (SgArrowExp)
  2. Verify that the left operand of the arrow expression is a this expression (SgThisExp)
  3. Retrieve the class symbol from the this expression and its associated class declaration
  4. Check if the class declaration's parent is a lambda expression (SgLambdaExp)
  5. Confirm that the class declaration is indeed the lambda closure class by comparing it with the lambda expression's lambda_closure_class pointer
Parameters
varRefPointer to the variable reference expression to be examined. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the variable reference represents a lambda captured variable, false otherwise.
Warning
This function does not work properly when compiled with MSVC. When built with the Microsoft Visual C++ compiler, the function always returns false due to compiler-specific limitations.
Precondition
varRef must be a valid non-NULL pointer to an SgVarRefExp node.
The AST must be properly constructed with valid parent pointers.
Postcondition
The input AST remains unchanged.
Note
The lambda closure class is a compiler-generated class that holds captured variables. Its parent in the AST is the SgLambdaExp node, and the lambda_closure_class member of SgLambdaExp points back to this class declaration.
On non-MSVC compilers, the function performs full analysis. On MSVC, a pragma message warning is emitted at compile time indicating the limitation.

◆ isLambdaFunction()

bool SageInterface::isLambdaFunction ( SgFunctionDeclaration * func)

Determines whether a function declaration represents a lambda function.

This function checks if the given function declaration is the internal function associated with a lambda expression in the ROSE abstract syntax tree (AST). It does this by examining the parent node of the function declaration and verifying whether it is an SgLambdaExp node whose lambda function matches the provided function declaration.

The implementation traverses up one level in the AST hierarchy to find the parent node, then attempts to cast it to an SgLambdaExp. If the cast succeeds and the lambda expression's associated function matches the input function, the function is identified as a lambda function.

Parameters
funcPointer to the SgFunctionDeclaration node to be checked. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the function declaration represents a lambda function, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter func must not be NULL.
The function declaration must have a valid parent node in the AST.
Postcondition
The AST remains unchanged; this is a read-only query operation.
Warning
This function will trigger an assertion failure if func is NULL or if the parent node of func is NULL.
Note
This function is marked with a TODO comment indicating it should be exposed to the SageInterface namespace.
The function relies on ROSE's internal AST structure where lambda functions are represented as children of SgLambdaExp nodes.

◆ isLastStatement()

bool SageInterface::isLastStatement ( SgStatement * stmt)

Checks if a statement is the last statement within its enclosing scope.

This function determines whether the given statement is positioned as the last statement within its immediately enclosing scope. It retrieves the parent scope of the statement, generates a list of all statements contained within that scope, and compares the last element of the list with the provided statement to determine if they are the same.

The function uses generateStatementList() to obtain a comprehensive list of statements in the scope, which handles both declaration-only scopes and mixed statement scopes uniformly.

Parameters
stmtPointer to the SgStatement node to be checked. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the statement is the last statement in its enclosing scope, false otherwise.
Precondition
The stmt parameter must not be NULL.
The statement must have a valid parent scope (get_scope() must return a non-NULL value).
The scope must contain at least one statement.
Postcondition
The input statement and its scope remain unchanged.
Warning
This function will trigger an assertion failure if stmt is NULL.
This function will trigger an assertion failure if the statement has no valid scope.
If the scope's statement list is empty, accessing the last element may result in undefined behavior.
Note
The function uses generateStatementList() rather than getStatementList() or getDeclarationList() to handle all scope types uniformly.

◆ IsLiteralType()

bool SageInterface::IsLiteralType ( const SgType *const inputType)

Determines whether a given type is a literal type according to C++ standards.

This function checks if the provided type qualifies as a literal type. A literal type is a type that can be used in constant expressions. The function first strips away typedef aliases, array qualifiers, and type modifiers to examine the underlying type. It then checks if the resulting type is a scalar type, reference type, or pointer type, all of which are considered literal types.

The current implementation only handles scalar types, reference types, and pointer types. For other types such as class types with constexpr constructors, the function is not yet implemented and will trigger an assertion failure.

Parameters
inputTypeA pointer to the SgType object representing the type to be checked. Must not be null.
Returns
True if the input type is a literal type (scalar, reference, or pointer type). The function does not return false under normal circumstances as unhandled types cause an assertion failure.
Warning
This function is incomplete. It will abort execution with an assertion failure if the type is not a scalar, reference, or pointer type. Class types and other complex literal types are not yet implemented.
Precondition
inputType must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
The function either returns true or aborts execution due to an unhandled type.
Note
The function uses ROSE compiler infrastructure types and utilities including SgType::stripType for removing type qualifiers and the isScalarType, isReferenceType, and isPointerType helper functions.
The ENSURE_CLASS_TYPE macro is present but unreachable due to the preceding abort call.

◆ isLoopIndexVariable()

bool SageInterface::isLoopIndexVariable ( SgInitializedName * ivar,
SgNode * subtree_root )

Determines whether a given variable is used as a loop index in any enclosing loop.

This function performs a bottom-up traversal starting from the specified subtree root to find all enclosing loops. For each enclosing loop encountered, it checks whether the provided initialized name (ivar) is used as the loop index variable. The traversal continues outward through nested loop structures until either a match is found or there are no more enclosing loops to examine.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. Find the innermost enclosing loop from the subtree root
  2. Extract the loop index variable from the current loop
  3. Compare the extracted index variable with the target variable (ivar)
  4. If they match, return true; otherwise, move to the next outer enclosing loop
  5. Repeat until no more enclosing loops exist
Parameters
ivarPointer to the SgInitializedName representing the variable to check. This is the variable being tested to determine if it serves as a loop index in any enclosing loop scope. Must not be NULL.
subtree_rootPointer to the SgNode representing the starting point for the bottom-up traversal. The search for enclosing loops begins from the statement enclosing this node. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the variable ivar is used as a loop index variable in any of the enclosing loops; false otherwise.
Precondition
ivar must be a valid non-NULL pointer to an SgInitializedName node.
subtree_root must be a valid non-NULL pointer to an SgNode within the AST.
Postcondition
The AST remains unmodified; this is a read-only query operation.
Note
The function uses findEnclosingLoop which is inclusive, meaning it may return the current node if it is itself a loop. This is handled by getting the parent of the current loop when moving to the next outer enclosing loop.
This function only checks for direct equality between the loop index variable and ivar using pointer comparison.

◆ isMain()

bool SageInterface::isMain ( const SgNode * n)

Determines whether a given AST node represents a main program entry point.

This function checks if the provided AST node corresponds to the main entry point of a program. The detection logic varies depending on the source language being analyzed:

For Fortran programs, the function checks if the node is an SgProgramHeaderStatement, which represents the Fortran main program entry point.

For Java programs, the function checks if the node is a function declaration with the name "main". Java does not require the main method to be at global scope since it is always a class member.

For C and C++ programs, the function verifies that the node is a function declaration named "main" and that it exists at global scope. This ensures that nested functions or methods named "main" are not incorrectly identified as the program entry point.

Parameters
nPointer to the AST node to be examined. May be nullptr, in which case the function returns false.
Returns
True if the node represents the main program entry point for the current source language, false otherwise.
Precondition
The source language context should be properly set before calling this function, as the detection logic depends on whether the source is Fortran, Java, or C/C++.
Postcondition
The input node remains unchanged.
Note
This function uses SageInterface language query functions (is_Fortran_language, is_Java_language) to determine the appropriate detection strategy.
For C/C++ programs, only functions declared at global scope are considered as potential main entry points. Functions named "main" within classes or nested scopes will return false.

◆ isMemberFunctionMemberReference()

bool SageInterface::isMemberFunctionMemberReference ( SgMemberFunctionRefExp * memberFunctionRefExp)

Determines whether a member function reference expression represents an instance member function access.

This function analyzes a given SgMemberFunctionRefExp node to determine if it represents an access to a non-static member function through an object instance, as opposed to a qualified reference to a static member function or a direct class-qualified reference.

The function checks whether the member function reference is used in the context of a member access expression (via arrow operator, dot operator, or address-of operator). If so, it further verifies that the referenced function is not declared as static and that it belongs to a class definition. This distinguishes between instance member function accesses like "x.memberFunc()" or "ptr->memberFunc()" versus static or class-qualified references like "X::staticFunc()".

The implementation shares a similar design pattern with isDataMemberReference() for handling data members.

Parameters
memberFunctionRefExpPointer to the SgMemberFunctionRefExp node to be analyzed. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the member function reference represents an instance member function access through an object (via dot, arrow, or address-of operator) and the function is non-static and defined within a class. False otherwise.
Precondition
memberFunctionRefExp must not be NULL.
memberFunctionRefExp must have a valid parent node in the AST.
The symbol associated with memberFunctionRefExp must be valid and have an associated function declaration.
Postcondition
The AST remains unchanged; this function performs read-only analysis.
Note
This function uses conditional compilation with DEBUG_IS_MEMBER_FUNCTION_MEMBER_REFERENCE macro to enable debug output when needed.
The function considers SgAddressOfOp as a valid parent context to support member pointers to functions, similar to how member pointers to data are handled.
The function uses SgFunctionSymbol instead of SgMemberFunctionSymbol for generality in symbol handling.

◆ isNonconstReference()

bool SageInterface::isNonconstReference ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given type is a non-constant reference type.

This function analyzes a ROSE compiler infrastructure SgType node to determine if it represents a non-constant (mutable) reference type. The function handles several type representations including direct reference types, typedef types, and modifier types. It recursively traverses through type layers such as typedefs and modifiers to reach the underlying reference type and check if the referenced base type is non-const.

The algorithm works as follows:

  • If the type is a direct reference type (SgReferenceType), it checks whether the base type of the reference is not const.
  • If the type is a typedef (SgTypedefType), it recursively examines the underlying base type.
  • If the type is a modifier type (SgModifierType), it first checks if the modifier itself adds const qualification. If so, it returns false. Otherwise, it recursively examines the base type.
  • For all other type kinds, the function returns false.
Parameters
tPointer to an SgType node representing the type to be analyzed. May be nullptr, in which case the function returns false.
Returns
True if the type represents a non-constant reference type, false otherwise. Returns false if the type is not a reference type, if the reference is to a const-qualified type, or if any enclosing modifier adds const qualification.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType node within a properly constructed ROSE AST, or be nullptr.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unmodified.
Note
This function is part of the ROSE compiler infrastructure type analysis utilities. It relies on ROSE-specific type casting functions such as isSgReferenceType, isSgTypedefType, and isSgModifierType.
The function also depends on an external helper function isConstType to determine if a base type is const-qualified.

The function uses ROSE's dynamic type checking functions (isSgOmp*) to determine the node type.

Note that there is a TODO indicating that all Omp*statement types should eventually be moved under a common parent SgOmpStatement class, which would simplify this type checking logic.

Parameters

Returns
True if the node is an OpenMP statement of one of the recognized types, false otherwise.

The recognized types are: SgOmpBarrierStatement, SgOmpBodyStatement, SgOmpDeclareSimdStatement, SgOmpFlushStatement, SgOmpThreadprivateStatement, and SgOmpTaskwaitStatement.

◆ isOverloaded()

bool SageInterface::isOverloaded ( SgFunctionDeclaration * functionDeclaration)

Determines whether a given function declaration is overloaded.

This function examines whether the input function declaration has any other function declarations with the same name that would constitute function overloading. For member functions, the search is limited to the scope where the member function is defined, specifically within the class definition. For non-member functions, the implementation is not yet complete and will abort.

The algorithm iterates through all member declarations in the containing class definition and counts how many member functions or template declarations share the same name as the input function. If more than one declaration with the same name is found, the function is considered overloaded.

Note that this approach has known limitations:

  • For member functions, overloaded functions declared in base classes are not detected.
  • For non-member functions, friend function declarations in classes are not considered.
  • Functions declared in different namespace definitions (since namespaces are re-entrant) may not be properly detected.
Parameters
functionDeclarationPointer to the SgFunctionDeclaration to check for overloading. Must not be NULL. Can be either a member function declaration or a non-member function declaration (though non-member case is not yet implemented).
Returns
True if the function is overloaded (more than one function with the same name exists in the relevant scope), false otherwise.
Warning
The non-member function case is not implemented and will cause the program to abort with ROSE_ABORT() if encountered.
When the scope is an SgDeclarationScope, the function returns false without proper analysis. This is a known limitation tracked in ROSE-1378.
This function may not detect all overloaded functions, particularly those declared in base classes or in different namespace definitions.
Precondition
functionDeclaration must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgFunctionDeclaration.
Postcondition
The input functionDeclaration and the AST remain unchanged.
Note
For member functions, the function checks both SgMemberFunctionDeclaration and SgTemplateDeclaration nodes within the class definition to detect overloading.
Friend functions defined within a class may potentially be overloaded, but this case is not fully handled and a diagnostic message is printed when encountered.

◆ IsPod()

bool SageInterface::IsPod ( const SgType *const inputType)

Determines whether a given type is a Plain Old Data (POD) type.

This function checks if the provided type qualifies as a POD type according to C++ standards. A POD type is one that is both trivial and has standard layout. The function first strips any typedef and array type qualifiers from the input type before performing the checks. This ensures that the underlying base type is evaluated rather than any type aliases or array wrappers.

The determination is made by verifying two conditions:

  1. The type must be trivial (checked via IsTrivial with POD checking disabled)
  2. The type must have standard layout (checked via IsStandardLayout)

POD types are significant in C++ as they guarantee compatibility with C-style memory operations such as memcpy and memset, and can be safely used in low-level data manipulation scenarios.

Parameters
inputTypePointer to the SgType object representing the type to be analyzed. This parameter must not be null.
Returns
True if the type is a POD type (both trivial and standard layout), false otherwise.
Precondition
inputType must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
The input type object remains unchanged.
Note
The function uses SgType::STRIP_TYPEDEF_TYPE and SgType::STRIP_ARRAY_TYPE flags to obtain the underlying type before evaluation.
The IsTrivial function is called with the checkPod parameter set to false to avoid recursive POD checking.
Warning
Passing a null pointer for inputType will result in undefined behavior.

◆ isPointerToNonConstType()

bool SageInterface::isPointerToNonConstType ( SgType * type)

Determines whether a given type is a pointer to a non-const type.

This function recursively analyzes a ROSE compiler infrastructure SgType node to determine if it represents a pointer to a non-const type. The function handles type indirection through typedef declarations and modifier types by recursively unwrapping these layers to reach the underlying pointer type. Once a pointer type is found, it checks whether the pointed-to type is non-const using the SageInterface utility function.

The algorithm follows this logic:

  • If the type is a typedef, recursively check its base type
  • If the type is a pointer type, return true if the base type is not const
  • If the type is a modifier type, recursively check its base type
  • Otherwise, return false (the type is not a pointer to non-const)
