typeA pointer to an SgType node representing the type to be analyzed. May be a typedef, pointer type, modifier type, or any other SgType. Can be nullptr, in which case the behavior depends on the underlying ROSE type checking functions.
Returns
True if the type represents a pointer to a non-const type, false otherwise. Returns false if the type is not a pointer type after unwrapping typedefs and modifiers.
Precondition
The type parameter should be a valid SgType pointer from the ROSE AST, or nullptr.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unchanged.
Note
This function relies on ROSE compiler infrastructure functions including isSgTypedefType, isSgPointerType, isSgModifierType, and SageInterface::isConstType.
The function uses recursion to handle nested typedefs and modifier types, so deeply nested type definitions may result in deep recursion.

◆ isPointerType()

bool SageInterface::isPointerType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given SAGE type represents a pointer type.

This function checks if the provided SgType is a pointer type by examining the type and recursively unwrapping typedef and modifier layers. The function handles three cases: direct pointer types (SgPointerType), typedef types that may alias pointer types (SgTypedefType), and modifier types that wrap pointer types (SgModifierType). For typedef and modifier types, the function recursively examines the underlying base type to determine if the ultimate type is a pointer.

This recursive approach ensures that pointer types hidden behind multiple layers of typedefs or type modifiers (such as const or volatile qualifiers) are correctly identified as pointer types.

Parameters
tPointer to an SgType object representing the type to be examined. May be a direct pointer type, a typedef type, a modifier type, or any other SAGE type representation.
Returns
True if the type represents a pointer type (either directly or through typedef or modifier indirection), false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType object. Behavior is undefined if t is a null pointer or points to an invalid memory location.
Postcondition
The input type object remains unchanged after the function call.
Note
This function is part of the ROSE compiler infrastructure and operates on SAGE III intermediate representation types.
The function does not handle reference types or array types that decay to pointers; it only identifies explicit pointer types.
Warning
Deep nesting of typedefs and modifiers may lead to deep recursion, though this is unlikely in practice with well-formed type hierarchies.

◆ IsPolymorphic()

bool SageInterface::IsPolymorphic ( const SgType *const inputType)

Determines whether a given type is polymorphic.

This function checks if the specified type is polymorphic by examining whether the type or any of its base classes contains at least one virtual member function. A polymorphic type in C++ is one that declares or inherits at least one virtual function, enabling runtime polymorphism through virtual dispatch.

The algorithm first strips type modifiers, typedefs, and array types from the input to obtain the underlying type. It then verifies that the resulting type is a class type. If so, it retrieves all member functions from the entire class hierarchy (including inherited members) and iterates through them to check if any function has the virtual modifier set.

Parameters
inputTypePointer to the SgType object representing the type to be checked for polymorphism. Must not be null.
Returns
True if the type is polymorphic (contains at least one virtual member function in its class hierarchy), false otherwise. Also returns false if the input type is not a class type.
Precondition
inputType must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
The input type and its associated class hierarchy remain unchanged.
Note
This function uses the ENSURE_CLASS_TYPE macro to validate that the stripped type is indeed a class type before proceeding with the analysis.
Template types at the point of analysis may not be fully handled, as indicated by a comment in the implementation.
Debug output showing the number of member functions found can be enabled by defining DEBUG_QUADRATIC_BEHAVIOR.
Warning
The function traverses the entire class hierarchy to collect member functions, which may have performance implications for deep or complex inheritance hierarchies.

◆ isPostfixOperator()

bool SageInterface::isPostfixOperator ( SgExpression * exp)

Determines whether an expression represents a postfix operator.

This function checks if the given expression is a postfix operator by verifying that it is neither a prefix operator nor an index operator. A postfix operator is identified through a process of elimination: if the expression does not qualify as a prefix operator and does not qualify as an index operator, then it is considered a postfix operator. This approach relies on the helper functions isPrefixOperator() and isIndexOperator() to perform the classification.

Parameters
expPointer to the SgExpression node to be examined. This represents an expression in the SAGE III abstract syntax tree that may be an operator expression.
Returns
True if the expression is a postfix operator (i.e., it is neither a prefix operator nor an index operator), false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter exp should point to a valid SgExpression node or be NULL.
Postcondition
The input expression remains unmodified.
Note
This function uses a negative definition approach, classifying an operator as postfix if it fails to match other operator categories. This means the accuracy of this function depends on the correctness of isPrefixOperator() and isIndexOperator().
If exp is NULL or not an operator expression, the behavior depends on the implementation of isPrefixOperator() and isIndexOperator().
See also
SageInterface::isPrefixOperator
SageInterface::isIndexOperator

◆ isPrefixOperator()

bool SageInterface::isPrefixOperator ( SgExpression * exp)

Empty function or ill-formed function detected.

Determines whether a given expression represents a prefix operator.

This function analyzes an expression node to determine if it represents a prefix operator (such as prefix increment ++x, prefix decrement –x, unary plus +x, unary minus -x, logical not !x, bitwise not ~x, dereference *x, or address-of &x). The function supports both member function and non-member function implementations of overloaded operators.

The algorithm works by first extracting the function name and number of operands from either a SgMemberFunctionRefExp or SgFunctionRefExp. It then checks if the function name corresponds to a prefix operator using isPrefixOperatorName(). For operators that can be both prefix and postfix (such as ++ and –), the distinction is made based on the number of operands:

  • For member functions: prefix operators have 0 parameters, postfix have 1 (dummy int)
  • For non-member functions: prefix operators have 1 parameter, postfix have 2
Parameters
expPointer to the SgExpression node to be analyzed. This should be either a SgFunctionRefExp or SgMemberFunctionRefExp representing an operator call. If the expression is neither of these types, the function will print a diagnostic message and return false.
Returns
True if the expression represents a prefix operator, false otherwise. Returns false if the expression type is not recognized or if the operator signature matches a postfix operator.
Warning
If the expression is neither a SgFunctionRefExp nor a SgMemberFunctionRefExp, a diagnostic message is printed to stdout indicating an unknown case.
Precondition
The parameter exp must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgExpression.
Postcondition
The input expression is not modified by this function.
Note
This function was reimplemented to support more prefix operators and to handle both member function and non-member function definitions of operators.
The function relies on isPrefixOperatorName() to determine if a given function name corresponds to a prefix operator.
For the dereference operator (*) and multiply operator (*), additional context such as return type may be needed to distinguish between them, as noted in the implementation comments.

◆ isPrefixOperatorName()

bool SageInterface::isPrefixOperatorName ( const SgName & functionName)

Determines whether a given function name represents a C++ prefix operator.

This function checks if the provided function name corresponds to one of the recognized C++ prefix unary operators. Prefix operators are those that appear before their operand, such as increment (++x), decrement (–x), address-of (&x), logical not (!x), dereference (*x), unary plus (+x), unary minus (-x), and bitwise complement (~x).

The function performs a string comparison against a predefined list of prefix operator names. Note that some operators like operator* and operator& can be either prefix unary operators or binary operators depending on context. This function only checks the name and does not distinguish based on the number of parameters or return type.

Parameters
functionNameThe SgName object containing the function name to be checked. This should be in the standard C++ operator notation format (e.g., "operator++", "operator&", "operator~").
Returns
True if the function name matches one of the recognized prefix operator names, false otherwise. Also returns false if the function name is null.
Warning
This function cannot distinguish between prefix and postfix versions of operator++ and operator-- based solely on the name. Additional context such as parameter count would be needed for complete disambiguation.
The dereference operator (operator*) and address-of operator (operator&) share names with the binary multiplication and bitwise AND operators respectively. The return type or parameter count may need to be examined to distinguish between these cases.
Precondition
The functionName parameter should be a valid SgName object.
Postcondition
The function does not modify any state; the return value reflects whether the name matches a known prefix operator.
Note
The list of recognized prefix operators includes: operator++, operator--, operator&, operator!, operator*, operator+, operator-, and operator~.

◆ isPrototypeInScope()

bool SageInterface::isPrototypeInScope ( SgScopeStatement * scope,
SgFunctionDeclaration * functionDeclaration,
SgDeclarationStatement * startingAtDeclaration )

Checks whether a function prototype already exists within a given scope.

This function searches for an existing function prototype (forward declaration) within the specified scope that matches the given function declaration. The search begins at a specified starting declaration and proceeds linearly through the declaration list until the end is reached or a matching prototype is found.

The function specifically looks for template instantiation member function declarations (SgTemplateInstantiationMemberFunctionDecl) that match both the target scope and name of the provided function declaration. Only forward declarations are considered as valid prototypes; defining declarations are excluded from the match.

This is useful for avoiding duplicate prototype insertions when transforming or generating code, particularly for template member functions.

Parameters
scopeThe scope statement in which to search for the prototype. Must not be NULL and must be a scope that contains only declarations (i.e., containsOnlyDeclarations() returns true). SgDeclarationScope is currently not fully supported.
functionDeclarationThe function declaration whose prototype is being searched for. Must not be NULL. The function's scope and name are used for matching.
startingAtDeclarationThe declaration statement from which to begin the search. Must not be NULL and should exist within the scope's declaration list. The search starts at this position and continues to the end of the list.
Returns
True if a matching forward declaration (prototype) is found in the scope starting from the specified declaration; false otherwise. Also returns false if the scope is an SgDeclarationScope or if the starting declaration is not found in the scope.
Warning
SgDeclarationScope handling is not fully implemented. If the scope is an SgDeclarationScope, the function prints a TODO message and returns false.
Precondition
scope is not NULL.
functionDeclaration is not NULL.
startingAtDeclaration is not NULL.
scope->containsOnlyDeclarations() returns true.
startingAtDeclaration exists within the scope's declaration list for meaningful results.
Postcondition
The scope and its declaration list remain unchanged.
Note
This function performs a linear search through the declaration list starting from the specified position, which may have performance implications for large scopes.
Only SgTemplateInstantiationMemberFunctionDecl declarations are considered for matching. Other types of function declarations are ignored during the search.
See ROSE-1378 for information about SgDeclarationScope handling limitations.

◆ isPureVirtualClass()

bool SageInterface::isPureVirtualClass ( SgType * type,
const ClassHierarchyWrapper & classHierarchy )

Determines whether a given type represents a pure virtual (abstract) class.

This function analyzes a class type to determine if it is a pure virtual class, meaning it has at least one pure virtual member function that is not implemented by any concrete function in the class or its ancestor classes. The algorithm works by first collecting all ancestor classes from the class hierarchy, then gathering all pure virtual functions and concrete functions from the class and its ancestors. Finally, it checks whether each pure virtual function has a corresponding concrete implementation by matching function names, argument counts, and argument types.

The function handles cases where the defining declaration is not available by conservatively returning false, as the analysis cannot be performed without the class definition.

This function is conditionally compiled and is only available when ROSE_USE_INTERNAL_FRONTEND_DEVELOPMENT is not defined.

Parameters
typePointer to the SgType to be analyzed. This should be a class type for meaningful analysis. If NULL or not a class type, the function returns false.
classHierarchyA reference to a ClassHierarchyWrapper object that provides information about the class inheritance hierarchy, used to retrieve ancestor classes.
Returns
True if the type represents a pure virtual class (i.e., has at least one unimplemented pure virtual function), false otherwise. Also returns false if the type is not a class type or if the defining declaration cannot be found.
Precondition
The classHierarchy parameter must be properly initialized with the relevant class hierarchy information for accurate ancestor class retrieval.
The type parameter, if representing a class, should have its declaration and definition available in the AST for complete analysis.
Postcondition
The function does not modify any input parameters or global state.
Note
The function performs a simple signature matching for determining if a concrete function implements a pure virtual function, comparing only function names, argument counts, and argument types. It does not account for covariant return types or other advanced matching rules.
If the defining declaration of the class cannot be found, the function conservatively returns false rather than true.
Warning
This function relies on pointer equality for type comparison of function arguments, which may not correctly handle all type equivalence scenarios such as typedefs or template instantiations.

◆ isReferenceType()

bool SageInterface::isReferenceType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given type is a reference type.

This function checks if the provided SAGE III type node represents a constant or non-constant reference type. The function recursively traverses through typedef and modifier type layers to determine if the underlying base type is a reference type. This is useful for type analysis in source-to-source transformation tools built on the ROSE compiler infrastructure.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. If the type is directly an SgReferenceType, return true.
  2. If the type is a typedef, recursively check the base type of the typedef.
  3. If the type is a modifier type (e.g., const, volatile), recursively check the base type of the modifier.
  4. Otherwise, return false indicating the type is not a reference type.
Parameters
tPointer to an SgType node representing the type to be checked. May be NULL, in which case the function returns false.
Returns
True if the type is a reference type (either directly or through typedef or modifier indirection), false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType node within a properly constructed SAGE III AST, or be NULL.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unmodified.
Note
This function handles both lvalue references. It recursively unwraps typedef and modifier types to find the underlying reference type.
The function uses ROSE compiler infrastructure type checking functions such as isSgReferenceType, isSgTypedefType, and isSgModifierType.

◆ isRestrictType()

bool SageInterface::isRestrictType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given type has the restrict qualifier.

This function recursively examines a ROSE AST type node to determine if it represents a restrict-qualified type. The restrict qualifier is a C99 feature that indicates a pointer is the only reference to the underlying object, allowing for certain compiler optimizations.

The function handles type indirection by recursively unwrapping typedef types and modifier types. For typedef types, it examines the underlying base type. For modifier types, it checks if the restrict modifier is set; if not, it continues to examine the base type of the modifier. This recursive approach ensures that restrict qualifiers are detected regardless of how deeply they are nested within typedef or modifier type wrappers.

Parameters
tPointer to an SgType node representing the type to be examined. May be NULL, in which case the function returns false.
Returns
True if the type has the restrict qualifier applied at any level of its type hierarchy, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType node within a properly constructed ROSE AST, or be NULL.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unmodified.
Note
This function is specific to the ROSE compiler infrastructure and relies on ROSE's type system classes such as SgTypedefType, SgModifierType, and SgTypeModifier.
The restrict qualifier is primarily used in C99 and later standards. In C++, restrict is not a standard keyword, though some compilers support it as an extension.

◆ isSameFunction()

bool SageInterface::isSameFunction ( SgFunctionDeclaration * func1,
SgFunctionDeclaration * func2 )

Determines whether two function declarations refer to the same function.

This function compares two SgFunctionDeclaration pointers to determine if they represent the same function. The comparison strategy varies depending on the source language being processed. For languages like C, C99, PHP, CUDA, OpenCL, Python, and Fortran, the comparison is based solely on the function name. For C++ and Java, the comparison uses both the qualified name and the mangled name to account for function overloading and namespaces. If the two pointers are identical (pointing to the same object), they are immediately considered to represent the same function.

Parameters
func1Pointer to the first SgFunctionDeclaration to compare. Must not be null.
func2Pointer to the second SgFunctionDeclaration to compare. Must not be null.
Returns
True if both function declarations refer to the same function according to the language-specific comparison rules, false otherwise.
Warning
This function will call ROSE_ABORT() if the current source language is not one of the supported languages (C, C99, PHP, CUDA, OpenCL, Python, C++, Java, or Fortran).
Precondition
func1 must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgFunctionDeclaration.
func2 must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgFunctionDeclaration.
The source language must be properly set before calling this function.
Postcondition
The function declarations remain unchanged.
Note
For C++ and Java, the function concatenates the qualified name and mangled name strings for comparison, which handles function overloading scenarios where functions may share the same qualified name but have different parameter signatures.
For simpler languages without function overloading (C, Fortran, etc.), only the function name is compared since overloading is not supported.

◆ isScalarType()

bool SageInterface::isScalarType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given ROSE type represents a scalar type.

This function checks if the provided SgType pointer represents a scalar type in the ROSE compiler infrastructure. Scalar types include all fundamental arithmetic types (integers, floating-point numbers), character types, boolean, string, void, and complex/imaginary types. The function first strips any typedef chains and type modifiers (such as const, volatile) from the input type before performing the classification. The classification is performed using a switch statement on the type's variant identifier.

The following type categories are considered scalar:

  • Character types: char, signed char, unsigned char, wchar_t, char16_t, char32_t
  • Integer types: short, int, long, long long (signed and unsigned variants)
  • Floating-point types: float, double, long double
  • Special types: void, bool, string
  • Complex types: complex, imaginary (C99 types)
Parameters
tPointer to an SgType object representing the type to be checked. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the type is a scalar type, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
The input type object remains unchanged.
Note
This function uses ROSE_ASSERT to verify that the input pointer is not NULL. If a NULL pointer is passed, the assertion will fail and the program will terminate in debug builds.
The function handles typedef chains by calling stripTypedefsAndModifiers() to obtain the underlying base type before classification.
Support for char16_t and char32_t types was added for C99 and C++11 compatibility.
Warning
Passing a NULL pointer will trigger an assertion failure.

◆ IsStandardLayout()

bool SageInterface::IsStandardLayout ( const SgType *const inputType)

Determines whether a given C++ type qualifies as a standard-layout type according to the C++ standard.

This function checks if the provided type meets all the criteria for being a standard-layout type as defined by the C++ standard. A standard-layout type is important for compatibility with C code and for certain low-level operations like memcpy.

The function performs the following checks:

  1. Scalar types and pointer types are considered standard-layout.
  2. For class types, the function verifies:
    • No virtual functions exist in the class.
    • No virtual base classes are present.
    • All non-static data members have the same access control (private, protected, or public).
    • If the most derived class has non-static data members, no base class can have non-static data members.
    • If the most derived class has no non-static data members, at most one base class can have non-static data members.
    • All base classes must themselves be standard-layout types (recursive check).
    • No base class can be of the same type as the first non-static data member (to avoid empty base optimization conflicts).

The function uses the ClassHierarchyWrapper to traverse the class inheritance hierarchy and GetAllVariableDeclarationsInAncestors to collect variable declarations from ancestor classes.

Parameters
inputTypeA pointer to the SgType representing the type to be checked. The pointer itself is const, and the SgType it points to is also treated as const.
Returns
True if the type is a standard-layout type according to the C++ standard rules, false otherwise.
Precondition
inputType must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
For class types, a defining declaration with a complete class definition must be available.
Postcondition
The input type and the AST remain unmodified.
Note
This function strips modifiers, typedefs, array types, and reference types from the input type before performing the standard-layout analysis.
The function uses the ENSURE_CLASS_TYPE macro which returns false if the type is not a class type after stripping scalar and pointer types.
Debug output can be enabled via the DEBUG_QUADRATIC_BEHAVIOR preprocessor macro to monitor the sizes of ancestor collections during analysis.
The function relies on getProject() to obtain the project context for building the class hierarchy.
Warning
The function assumes that the class type has a complete definition available. If only a forward declaration exists, the function will trigger an assertion failure.
This implementation may have quadratic time complexity when analyzing deep class hierarchies due to repeated traversal of ancestor classes.

◆ isStatic()

Determines whether a declaration statement has static storage class.

This function checks if the given declaration statement has the static storage modifier applied to it. It accesses the declaration modifier of the statement, then retrieves the storage modifier, and finally queries whether the static specifier is set. This is useful for analyzing variable and function declarations to determine their linkage and storage duration characteristics.

Parameters
stmtPointer to the SgDeclarationStatement node to be examined for static storage class specification.
Returns
True if the declaration statement has the static storage modifier, false otherwise.
Precondition
stmt must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgDeclarationStatement object.
Postcondition
The state of stmt remains unchanged after this call.
Note
This function uses ROSE_ASSERT to verify that the input pointer is not null. If a null pointer is passed, the program will abort in debug builds.
Warning
Passing a null pointer will trigger an assertion failure and terminate the program.

◆ isStrictIntegerType()

bool SageInterface::isStrictIntegerType ( SgType * t)

Determines if a given type is a strict integer type.

This function checks whether the provided SgType pointer represents a strict integer type. Unlike the similar function SgType::isIntegerType(), this function uses a more restrictive definition that excludes char, wchar, and bool types. The function first resolves any typedef layers to obtain the underlying base type, then checks if that base type matches one of the recognized strict integer types.

The strict integer types recognized by this function include:

  • short, signed short, unsigned short
  • int, signed int, unsigned int
  • long, signed long, unsigned long
  • long long, signed long long, unsigned long long
Parameters
tPointer to an SgType object representing the type to be checked. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the type is a strict integer type, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t must be a valid non-NULL pointer to an SgType object.

Postcondition
The input type object remains unchanged.
Note
This function recursively resolves typedef types to find the underlying base type before performing the integer type check.
This function is more restrictive than SgType::isIntegerType() as it does not consider char, wchar, or bool as integer types.

The function will trigger an assertion failure if t is NULL or if any typedef in the chain has a NULL base type.

Determines whether a given AST node represents a struct declaration.

This function checks if the provided AST node is a class declaration of type struct. It first attempts to cast the node to an SgClassDeclaration, and if successful, examines the class type to determine if it is specifically a struct declaration (as opposed to a class or union declaration). In C++, structs are represented internally as a special case of class declarations with a distinct class type enumeration value.

nodeA pointer to the SgNode to be examined. This node is checked to determine if it represents a struct declaration in the AST.

True if the node is a valid SgClassDeclaration with class type e_struct, false otherwise (including when the node is not a class declaration).

The node parameter must not be NULL. The function asserts this condition and will terminate if violated.
Postcondition
The AST remains unchanged. This is a query function with no side effects.
Note
This function distinguishes between struct declarations and other class-like declarations (class, union) by checking the class_type attribute of the SgClassDeclaration node.
Warning
Passing a NULL pointer will trigger an assertion failure and program termination via ROSE_ASSERT.

◆ isStructType()

bool SageInterface::isStructType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given type represents a struct type.

This function checks if the provided SgType pointer represents a struct type in the ROSE abstract syntax tree. It first attempts to cast the type to an SgClassType, and if successful, retrieves the associated declaration statement and delegates to isStructDeclaration to determine if the declaration is specifically a struct declaration rather than a class or union.

Parameters
tPointer to the SgType object to be examined. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the type represents a struct type, false otherwise. Returns false if the type is not an SgClassType or if the underlying declaration is not a struct declaration.
Precondition
The parameter t must not be NULL. The function will trigger an assertion failure if t is NULL.
Postcondition
The input type t remains unchanged.
Note
This function relies on the isStructDeclaration helper function to perform the final determination of whether the declaration is a struct.
In C++, structs and classes are both represented as SgClassType in ROSE, so additional checking via the declaration is necessary to distinguish between them.
Warning
An assertion failure will occur if a NULL pointer is passed as the parameter t.

◆ isStructurallyEquivalentAST()

bool SageInterface::isStructurallyEquivalentAST ( SgNode * tree1,
SgNode * tree2 )

Determines if two AST subtrees are structurally equivalent.

This function tests whether two AST subtrees rooted at the given nodes are structurally equivalent by comparing their node types in a synchronized traversal. The comparison is performed using RoseAst iterators that traverse both trees simultaneously, checking that each corresponding pair of nodes has the same variant type (node kind).

The algorithm iterates through both ASTs in parallel using RoseAst iterators. At each step, it compares the variant type of the current nodes from both trees. If any mismatch is found, the function returns false immediately. If the traversal completes successfully with all nodes matching, the function returns true.

Note that this function is conditionally compiled and only performs the actual comparison when CMake is not used (controlled by the USE_CMAKEx preprocessor macro). When CMake is used, the function simply returns true without performing any comparison, as the required libraries may not be configured.

Parameters
tree1Pointer to the root node of the first AST subtree to compare. This tree is referred to as the "copy" in the implementation.
tree2Pointer to the root node of the second AST subtree to compare. This tree is referred to as the "original" in the implementation.
Returns
True if both AST subtrees are structurally equivalent (all corresponding nodes have the same variant type), or if the comparison is skipped due to CMake configuration. Returns false if any structural mismatch is detected.
Warning
When compiled with CMake (USE_CMAKEx defined), this function always returns true without performing any actual comparison.
Precondition
Both tree1 and tree2 should point to valid SgNode objects.
Both trees should have the same structure and size for the function to return true.
Postcondition
The input AST trees remain unmodified.
Note
This function only compares the structural layout (node types) of the ASTs, not the actual content or attribute values within the nodes.
The function assumes that if the trees are structurally equivalent, they will have the same number of nodes, which is verified by assertions.

This function checks if the provided SAGE III AST node is any type of template instantiation node. It examines the node against several template instantiation IR node types including template instantiation declarations, definitions, function declarations, member function declarations, typedef declarations, and directive statements. The function focuses primarily on declaration-related template instantiation nodes.

The function performs type checking using SAGE III dynamic cast functions (isSgTemplateInstantiation*) to determine if the node matches any of the supported template instantiation types.

Parameters
nodePointer to the SgNode to be checked. May be NULL, in which case all type checks will return false and the function will return false.

True if the node is any of the following template instantiation types: SgTemplateInstantiationDecl, SgTemplateInstantiationDefn, SgTemplateInstantiationFunctionDecl, SgTemplateInstantiationMemberFunctionDecl, SgTemplateInstantiationTypedefDeclaration, or SgTemplateInstantiationDirectiveStatement. Returns false otherwise.
Note
The function includes SgTemplateInstantiationDefn in its checks, though this was a design decision made to allow these IR nodes as of January 2016.
This function is part of the SageInterface namespace which provides utility functions for working with the SAGE III intermediate representation.
Precondition
None. The function handles NULL input gracefully.
Postcondition
The input node is not modified.

◆ isUnionDeclaration()

bool SageInterface::isUnionDeclaration ( SgNode * node)

Determines whether a given AST node represents a union declaration.

This function checks if the provided ROSE AST node is a union declaration. It first attempts to cast the node to an SgClassDeclaration, and if successful, examines the class type to determine if it is specifically a union (as opposed to a class or struct). In ROSE, unions are represented as a special case of SgClassDeclaration with the class type set to e_union.

Parameters
nodeA pointer to the SgNode to be examined. This node is tested to determine if it represents a union declaration in the AST.
Returns
True if the node is an SgClassDeclaration with class type e_union, false otherwise (including when the node is not an SgClassDeclaration).
Precondition
The parameter node must not be NULL. The function will trigger an assertion failure if a NULL pointer is passed.
Postcondition
The input node remains unchanged. This function performs read-only inspection of the AST node.
Note
This function uses ROSE_ASSERT to validate that the input node is not NULL, which will terminate the program in debug builds if violated.
In ROSE, SgClassDeclaration is used to represent classes, structs, and unions. The distinction is made through the class_type attribute.

◆ isUpcArrayWithThreads()

bool SageInterface::isUpcArrayWithThreads ( SgArrayType * t)

Determines if a UPC array type has a thread-based dimension.

This function checks whether a given SgArrayType represents a UPC (Unified Parallel C) array that includes a thread-related dimension in its index expression. Specifically, it examines the array's index expression to determine if it is a multiplication operation where the right-hand operand is either an SgUpcThreads node (representing the THREADS keyword in UPC) or an SgIntVal node (representing a statically compiled thread count as an integer value).

The function supports both dynamic UPC thread specifications using the THREADS keyword and static compilation modes where the thread count is resolved to a constant integer at compile time.

Parameters
tPointer to an SgArrayType node representing the array type to be examined. Must not be NULL.
Returns
True if the array type has an index expression that is a multiplication operation with either THREADS or an integer value as the right operand, indicating a UPC array with thread-based dimensioning. Returns false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgArrayType object.
Postcondition
The input SgArrayType node remains unchanged.
Note
This function uses ROSE_ASSERT to verify that the input pointer is not NULL, which will terminate the program if the assertion fails in debug builds.
The static compilation case (SgIntVal check) was added to handle scenarios where UPC threads are compiled to integer values rather than using the dynamic THREADS keyword.

◆ isUpcPhaseLessSharedType()

bool SageInterface::isUpcPhaseLessSharedType ( SgType * t)

Determines if a UPC shared type is phase-less.

This function checks whether a given SAGE type represents a UPC (Unified Parallel C) phase-less shared type. In UPC, a shared type is considered phase-less when its block size is either 1, 0, or unspecified (-1). Phase-less shared types have simpler memory distribution semantics compared to blocked shared types with explicit block sizes greater than 1.

The function first verifies that the input type is a UPC shared type by calling hasUpcSharedType(). If confirmed, it extracts the block size from the type's UPC modifier and determines if the type qualifies as phase-less based on the block size value.

Parameters
tPointer to the SAGE type node to be examined. This should be a valid SgType pointer that may or may not represent a UPC shared type.
Returns
True if the type is a UPC shared type with a phase-less block size (block size equals 1, 0, or -1). Returns false if the type is not a UPC shared type or if it has an explicit block size greater than 1.
Precondition
The parameter t should be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
Postcondition
The input type t remains unchanged.
Note
Block size values have the following meanings in UPC:
  • Block size of 1: Default cyclic distribution (phase-less)
  • Block size of 0: Indefinite block size (phase-less)
  • Block size of -1: Unspecified block size (phase-less)
  • Block size greater than 1: Explicit blocked distribution (has phase)
Warning
The function uses ROSE_ASSERT to verify internal consistency. If hasUpcSharedType() returns true but fails to provide a valid modifier type, an assertion failure will occur.

◆ isUpcPrivateToSharedType()

bool SageInterface::isUpcPrivateToSharedType ( SgType * t)

Determines if a UPC type is a private-to-shared pointer type.

This function analyzes a UPC (Unified Parallel C) type to determine whether it represents a private-to-shared pointer type. In UPC, a private-to-shared pointer is a local pointer that points to shared memory. This is distinguished from a shared pointer by the order of type modifiers: if the pointer type appears before the UPC shared modifier in the type chain, it indicates a private-to-shared type.

The algorithm traverses the type hierarchy starting from the given type, unwrapping nested type constructs (modifiers, pointers, references, arrays, and typedefs) until it reaches the UPC shared modifier. During traversal, it tracks whether a pointer type is encountered before the shared modifier. If a pointer is found first, the type is classified as private-to-shared.

Parameters
tPointer to the SgType node representing the type to be analyzed. This should be a valid SAGE III type node from the AST.
Returns
True if the type is a UPC private-to-shared pointer type (i.e., the pointer modifier appears before the UPC shared modifier in the type chain). Returns false if the type does not contain a UPC shared modifier, or if the shared modifier appears before any pointer type.
Precondition
The parameter t must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgType object.
The type system must be properly initialized with UPC type support.
Postcondition
The input type t remains unchanged.
Note
This function relies on hasUpcSharedType() to first verify that the type contains a UPC shared modifier before performing the detailed analysis.
The function handles complex nested types including modifier types, pointer types, reference types, array types, and typedef types during traversal.
Warning
The function assumes that if hasUpcSharedType() returns true, a UPC shared modifier will eventually be found during type traversal. If this invariant is violated, the while loop may not terminate properly.

◆ isUpcSharedArrayType()

bool SageInterface::isUpcSharedArrayType ( SgArrayType * array_type)

Determines whether a given array type is a UPC shared array type.

This function checks if the provided SgArrayType represents a UPC (Unified Parallel C) shared array type. It does this by extracting the base element type of the array and then checking if that base type is a modifier type with UPC shared semantics. The function delegates to isUpcSharedModifierType to perform the actual shared modifier check when the base type is an SgModifierType.

Parameters
array_typePointer to the SgArrayType node to be examined. This parameter must not be null.
Returns
True if the array's element type is a UPC shared modifier type, false otherwise. Returns false if the base element type is not an SgModifierType.
Precondition
array_type must be a valid non-null pointer to an SgArrayType node.
Postcondition
The input array_type remains unchanged.
Note
This function only checks the immediate element type of the array. It relies on getArrayElementType to retrieve the base element type and isUpcSharedModifierType to determine if the modifier type has UPC shared semantics.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if array_type is null.

◆ isUpcSharedModifierType()

bool SageInterface::isUpcSharedModifierType ( SgModifierType * mod_type)

Determines whether a modifier type has the UPC shared qualifier.

This function checks if the given SgModifierType node represents a UPC (Unified Parallel C) shared type modifier. It accesses the type modifier's UPC modifier component and queries whether the shared attribute is set. UPC shared types are used in parallel programming to indicate data that is distributed across multiple threads in a partitioned global address space.

Parameters
mod_typePointer to an SgModifierType node to be examined. This parameter must not be null.
Returns
True if the modifier type has the UPC shared qualifier set, false otherwise.
Precondition
The mod_type parameter must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgModifierType object.
Postcondition
The state of the mod_type object remains unchanged.
Warning
This function will trigger an assertion failure if mod_type is null.
Note
This function is specific to UPC language extensions and is only meaningful when analyzing UPC source code. For non-UPC code, the shared modifier will typically not be set.

◆ isUpcSharedType()

bool SageInterface::isUpcSharedType ( SgType * t,
SgModifierType ** mod_type_out )

Check if a type is a UPC shared type, including shared array, shared pointers, etc.

This function determines whether a given SgType represents a UPC (Unified Parallel C) shared type. UPC shared types include shared arrays, shared pointers, and other shared-qualified types. The function performs this check by verifying that the type has a UPC shared qualifier and is not a private-to-shared type. A type is considered a UPC shared type if it passes the hasUpcSharedType check but fails the isUpcPrivateToSharedType check, effectively filtering out private-to-shared conversions.

Parameters
tPointer to the SgType node to be examined. This represents the type that will be checked for UPC shared qualification.
mod_type_outOptional output parameter. If non-NULL, this pointer will be set to point to the SgModifierType that contains the UPC shared modifier, if one is found. Can be NULL if the caller does not need this information.
Returns
True if the type is a UPC shared type (has UPC shared qualification and is not a private-to-shared type), false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType node.
Postcondition
The mod_type_out parameter, if non-NULL, may be modified to point to the relevant SgModifierType containing the shared modifier.
Note
This function distinguishes between true UPC shared types and private-to-shared pointer types, which are handled differently in UPC semantics.
The function relies on hasUpcSharedType and isUpcPrivateToSharedType helper functions to perform the actual type analysis.

◆ isUpcStrictSharedModifierType()

bool SageInterface::isUpcStrictSharedModifierType ( SgModifierType * mod_type)

Determines whether a UPC shared modifier type has the strict qualifier.

This function checks if a given SgModifierType node, which must already be a UPC shared modifier type, has the UPC strict qualifier applied. The strict qualifier in UPC (Unified Parallel C) enforces strict memory consistency semantics for shared data accesses, meaning all accesses to strict shared objects are sequentially consistent across all threads.

The function extracts the UPC modifier from the type modifier chain and queries whether the strict attribute is set.

Parameters
mod_typePointer to an SgModifierType node representing a UPC shared modifier type. This parameter must not be null and must represent a valid UPC shared modifier type.
Returns
True if the modifier type has the UPC strict qualifier, false otherwise.
Precondition
The mod_type parameter must be a valid UPC shared modifier type. This precondition is enforced via an assertion that calls isUpcSharedModifierType(mod_type).
Postcondition
The state of mod_type remains unchanged.
Warning
The function will trigger an assertion failure if mod_type is not a UPC shared modifier type. Callers should verify the type using isUpcSharedModifierType before calling this function.
Note
This function is specific to UPC language extensions in ROSE and is only meaningful when analyzing UPC source code.

◆ isUseByAddressVariableRef()

bool SageInterface::isUseByAddressVariableRef ( SgVarRefExp * ref)

Determines if a variable reference is used by its address.

This function checks whether a given variable reference expression is being used by its address. There are two main cases where this occurs:

Case 1: The variable reference is the operand of an address-of operator (SgAddressOfOp), such as in the expression "&a".

Case 2: In C++ code, the variable reference is passed as an argument to a function call where the corresponding parameter has a reference type. For example, when calling "foo(a)" where foo is declared as "type2 foo(Type& parameter)".

The algorithm works by examining the parent node of the variable reference to determine the context in which it is used. For function call arguments, it identifies the parameter index and then retrieves the corresponding parameter type from the function declaration to check if it is a reference type. The function handles both regular function calls and member function calls accessed through dot or arrow expressions.

Parameters
refPointer to the variable reference expression to be analyzed. Must not be NULL and must have a valid parent node in the AST.
Returns
True if the variable reference is used by address (either through the address-of operator or as an argument to a reference parameter), false otherwise.
Precondition
ref is not NULL.
ref has a valid parent node (ref->get_parent() is not NULL).
Postcondition
The AST is not modified by this function.
Note
This function only performs the C++ reference parameter check when the source language is C++ (determined by SageInterface::is_Cxx_language()).
For variadic functions (those using ellipsis parameters like printf), if the argument index exceeds the declared parameter list, the function checks if the reference itself has a reference type.
The function handles member function calls accessed via both dot expressions (object.method()) and arrow expressions (pointer->method()).
Warning
The function does not currently tolerate type casting operations between the variable reference and the address-of operator.
The function does not currently handle typedef chains when checking parameter types.

◆ isVolatileType()

bool SageInterface::isVolatileType ( SgType * t)

Determines whether a given SAGE III type has the volatile qualifier.

This function recursively examines a SAGE III type node to determine if it carries the volatile type qualifier. The function handles type indirection through typedef types and modifier types by recursively traversing to the underlying base types. For typedef types, it unwraps the typedef and checks the base type. For modifier types, it examines the const-volatile modifier to check for the volatile flag, and if not found, continues checking the base type. This recursive approach ensures that volatile qualifiers are detected regardless of how deeply they are nested within type wrappers.

Parameters
tPointer to the SgType node to be examined for volatile qualification. May be a direct type, a typedef type, or a modifier type. Can be nullptr, in which case the function returns false.
Returns
True if the type or any of its underlying base types has the volatile qualifier, false otherwise.
Precondition
The parameter t should point to a valid SgType node within the SAGE III abstract syntax tree, or be nullptr.
Postcondition
The input type node and the AST remain unmodified.
Note
This function only checks for volatile qualifiers and does not consider other type modifiers such as const or restrict.
The function uses SAGE III dynamic type checking functions (isSgTypedefType, isSgModifierType) to determine the actual type of the node.

◆ language_may_contain_nondeclarations_in_scope()

bool SageInterface::language_may_contain_nondeclarations_in_scope ( )

Determines whether the current source language may contain non-declaration statements within a scope.

This function checks if the current source language being processed is one that allows function definitions or other non-declaration statements to appear at locations other than the beginning of a scope. Specifically, in Fortran and Jovial, function definitions may be declared at the end of procedures. Python also permits non-declarations to appear freely within scopes. This information is useful for the ROSE compiler infrastructure when performing source-to-source transformations or analysis that depends on understanding the structural constraints of different programming languages.

The function performs a logical OR check across three language detection functions: is_Fortran_language(), is_Jovial_language(), and is_Python_language().

Returns
True if the current language is Fortran, Jovial, or Python, indicating that non-declaration statements may appear within scopes. Returns false otherwise.
Note
This function is part of the SageInterface namespace which provides utility functions for working with the SAGE III intermediate representation in ROSE.
The determination is based on the currently active source language context within the ROSE compiler framework.
Precondition
The ROSE compiler infrastructure must be properly initialized with a valid source language context established.
Postcondition
The function does not modify any state; it only queries the current language setting.

◆ lastFrontEndSpecificStatement()

SgStatement * SageInterface::lastFrontEndSpecificStatement ( SgGlobal * globalScope)

Finds the last front-end specific statement in the global scope.

This function iterates through the declaration statements in the provided global scope to locate the last statement that originates from the front-end specific preinclude file rose_edg_required_macros_and_functions.h. This is particularly useful when inserting new statements into global scope, as it is often desirable to insert them after all the compiler-generated front-end specific statements rather than at the very beginning of the scope.

The function traverses the declaration list sequentially, checking each statement's file information to determine if it is marked as front-end specific. The traversal stops when it encounters the first non-front-end-specific statement or reaches the end of the declaration list.

Parameters
globalScopePointer to the SgGlobal node representing the global scope whose declarations will be searched. Must not be NULL and should contain at least one front-end specific statement.
Returns
Pointer to the last SgStatement that is marked as front-end specific in the global scope's declaration list.
Precondition
globalScope must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to an SgGlobal node.
The global scope must contain at least one front-end specific statement from the rose_edg_required_macros_and_functions.h preinclude file.
Each declaration statement in the global scope should have valid file information (non-NULL get_file_info()).
Postcondition
The returned statement pointer is guaranteed to be non-NULL.
The returned statement is the last consecutive front-end specific statement starting from the beginning of the declaration list.
Warning
This function will trigger a ROSE_ASSERT failure if no front-end specific statement is found in the global scope.
Note
This function is typically used in conjunction with statement insertion operations to ensure that user code is placed after all automatically generated front-end declarations and definitions.
The function includes debug output that prints information about the last statement found.

◆ lastStatementOfScopeWithTokenInfo()

SgStatement * SageInterface::lastStatementOfScopeWithTokenInfo ( SgScopeStatement * scope,
std::map< SgNode *, TokenStreamSequenceToNodeMapping * > & tokenStreamSequenceMap )

Finds the last statement within a scope that has associated token stream information.

This function traverses a given scope statement to locate the last statement that has valid token stream mapping information. The function handles SgIfStmt scopes specially by checking the false body first, then the true body. For other scope types, it iterates through the statement list in reverse order to find the last statement with token information.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. For SgIfStmt scopes: Check the false body first for token info, then fall back to the true body if the false body has no token mapping.
  2. For other scopes: Generate a statement list and iterate from the end backwards, returning the first statement encountered that has a valid entry in the token stream sequence map.
Parameters
scopePointer to the scope statement to search within. This parameter must not be NULL.
tokenStreamSequenceMapA reference to a map associating SgNode pointers with their corresponding TokenStreamSequenceToNodeMapping objects. Used to determine which statements have token information.
Returns
Pointer to the last SgStatement in the scope that has token stream information, or NULL if no such statement exists or if the scope is empty.
Precondition
scope must not be NULL.
tokenStreamSequenceMap should be properly initialized with token mappings for statements that have token information.
Postcondition
The returned statement, if not NULL, will have a valid entry in the tokenStreamSequenceMap.
Note
This function prints diagnostic output to stdout when processing SgIfStmt scopes, which may be intended for debugging purposes.
For SgIfStmt scopes, the function prioritizes the false body over the true body when both have token information.
A statement is considered to have no token information if it is not found in the map or if its mapped value is NULL.

◆ listHeaderFiles()

void SageInterface::listHeaderFiles ( SgIncludeFile * includeFile)

Lists all header files included within a given include file hierarchy.

This function performs a preorder traversal of the include file tree starting from the specified SgIncludeFile node. It uses an internal traversal class derived from AstSimpleProcessing to visit each node in the tree and print information about any SgIncludeFile nodes encountered. The function outputs the filename of each include file found during the traversal to standard output.

The implementation defines a local PrefixTraversal class that overrides the visit method to check if each visited node is an SgIncludeFile. When an SgIncludeFile is found, its filename is printed. This provides a diagnostic view of the include file hierarchy rooted at the given include file.

Parameters
includeFilePointer to the SgIncludeFile node representing the root of the include file hierarchy to be traversed. This should be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgIncludeFile object.
Precondition
includeFile must be a valid, non-null pointer to an SgIncludeFile node.
Postcondition
All SgIncludeFile nodes reachable from the given includeFile through preorder traversal will have their filenames printed to standard output.
Note
This function is primarily intended for debugging and diagnostic purposes, as it outputs information directly to standard output using printf.
The traversal visits all nodes in the subtree, not just SgIncludeFile nodes, but only SgIncludeFile nodes produce output beyond the generic node information.
Warning
This function produces console output and should not be used in production code where such output is undesirable.

◆ lookupClassSymbolInParentScopes()

SgClassSymbol * SageInterface::lookupClassSymbolInParentScopes ( const SgName & name,
SgScopeStatement * cscope,
SgTemplateArgumentPtrList * templateArgumentList )

Searches for a class symbol by name through the current scope and all enclosing parent scopes.

This function performs an upward traversal through the scope hierarchy to locate a class symbol matching the specified name. Starting from the given scope (or the top of the scope stack if none is provided), it searches each scope level until either the symbol is found or the global scope is reached. The search terminates at the global scope level, as there are no parent scopes beyond it. This implementation properly handles SgAliasSymbols by resolving them to the underlying SgClassSymbol when the alias refers to a class symbol. Template arguments can be provided to match templated class symbols.

Parameters
nameThe name of the class symbol to search for. This is the identifier used to look up the class in each scope's symbol table.
cscopeThe starting scope from which to begin the search. If NULL is passed, the function will use the top of the SageBuilder scope stack as the starting point.
templateArgumentListA pointer to a list of template arguments used to match templated class symbols. Can be NULL if searching for non-templated classes or if template arguments are not needed for the lookup.
Returns
A pointer to the SgClassSymbol if found in the current scope or any enclosing parent scope. Returns NULL if no matching class symbol is found in any accessible scope.
Precondition
If cscope is provided (not NULL), it must be a valid SgScopeStatement with a properly initialized parent chain.
If cscope is NULL, the SageBuilder scope stack must not be empty.
Postcondition
The returned symbol, if not NULL, is a valid SgClassSymbol that exists in one of the scopes in the parent chain starting from the initial scope.
The original scope hierarchy remains unchanged.
Note
This function is considered a better implementation pattern compared to lookupVariableSymbolInParentScopes for scope-based symbol lookup.
The search stops at the global scope and does not continue beyond it, as global scope has no parent scope.
When the parent of a scope is not set, the traversal terminates to avoid undefined behavior.

◆ lookupEnumSymbolInParentScopes()

SgEnumSymbol * SageInterface::lookupEnumSymbolInParentScopes ( const SgName & name,
SgScopeStatement * cscope )

Searches for an enum symbol by name through the current scope and its parent scopes.

This function performs a hierarchical lookup for an enum symbol starting from the specified scope and traversing upward through parent scopes until the symbol is found or the global scope is reached. The search terminates when either the symbol is found or there are no more parent scopes to search. This implementation is similar to lookupClassSymbolInParentScopes and follows the same traversal pattern for scope hierarchy navigation.

The algorithm works as follows:

  1. If no scope is provided, the top of the scope stack from SageBuilder is used as the starting point.
  2. The function iteratively searches each scope level using the lookup_enum_symbol method.
  3. If the symbol is not found and the current scope is not the global scope, the search continues in the parent scope.
  4. The search stops when the symbol is found, the global scope is reached, or the parent pointer is NULL.
Parameters
nameThe name of the enum symbol to search for. This is passed as a constant reference to an SgName object.
cscopeThe starting scope from which to begin the search. If NULL is provided, the function will use the top of the SageBuilder scope stack as the starting scope.
Returns
A pointer to the SgEnumSymbol if found in the current scope or any of its parent scopes. Returns NULL if the symbol is not found in any accessible scope.
Precondition
If cscope is provided as non-NULL, it must be a valid SgScopeStatement pointer.
If cscope is NULL, the SageBuilder scope stack must not be empty.
Postcondition
The returned symbol, if non-NULL, corresponds to an enum declaration visible from the original search scope.
Note
This function may resolve SgAliasSymbols to their underlying SgEnumSymbol when the alias refers to an enum symbol.
A templated solution combining this with similar lookup functions like lookupClassSymbolInParentScopes could provide a more unified implementation.
The search does not continue beyond the global scope, as global scope has no parent.

Searches for a function symbol by name and type in the current scope and its enclosing parent scopes.

The search begins at the provided current scope and continues through each enclosing parent scope until either a matching function symbol is found or the global scope is reached. The algorithm terminates when a match is found, when the global scope has been searched, or when a scope with no parent is encountered.

If currentScope is provided (non-NULL), it must be a valid SgScopeStatement node within the AST.

◆ lookupFunctionSymbolInParentScopes() [2/2]

SgFunctionSymbol * SageInterface::lookupFunctionSymbolInParentScopes ( const SgName & functionName,

Searches for a function symbol by name through the parent scope hierarchy.

This function performs a hierarchical lookup for a function symbol starting from the specified scope and traversing upward through parent scopes until the symbol is found or the global scope is reached. The search algorithm iteratively checks each scope level by calling the lookup_function_symbol method on the current scope, then moves to the parent scope if the symbol is not found. The traversal stops when either the function symbol is located, the global scope is reached, or a scope with no parent is encountered.

If no current scope is provided (NULL), the function defaults to using the top of the scope stack maintained by SageBuilder. This function may return NULL when the function symbol is not found, which can occur when a function is referenced before it is defined, particularly in languages like Fortran where no prototype mechanism is required.

currentScopeThe starting scope from which to begin the upward search. If NULL, the search begins from the top of the SageBuilder scope stack.

Note
The search terminates at the global scope level and does not continue beyond it.
When the parent of a scope is not set (which may occur during the middle of translation), the search terminates to avoid errors from calling get_scope.
Precondition
If currentScope is not NULL, it must be a valid SgScopeStatement pointer.
The SageBuilder scope stack must be properly initialized if currentScope is NULL.
Postcondition
The returned pointer, if non-NULL, points to a valid SgFunctionSymbol that exists within the searched scope hierarchy.
Warning
This function may return NULL if the function symbol does not exist in any of the searched scopes. Callers should check the return value before use.

SgNamespaceSymbol * SageInterface::lookupNamespaceSymbolInParentScopes ( const SgName & name,

Searches for a namespace symbol by name in the current scope and its parent scopes.

A pointer to the SgNamespaceSymbol if found in the current scope or any of its parent scopes. Returns NULL if no matching namespace symbol is found in the entire scope hierarchy.
Precondition
If cscope is provided as non-NULL, it must be a valid SgScopeStatement pointer.
The SageBuilder scope stack must be properly initialized if cscope is NULL.
Postcondition
The returned symbol, if non-NULL, corresponds to a namespace with the given name that is visible from the original starting scope.
Note
The search stops at the global scope (SgGlobal) and does not attempt to traverse beyond it, as global scope has no parent scope in the ROSE AST hierarchy.
This function may resolve alias symbols to their underlying namespace symbols during the lookup process.
